If even one were left out, it would not be “all.” I have often been grateful that even the weak and troubled are specially included in Scripture. We are told not to criticise such people, but to comfort them. Those who need comfort most are the very ones God most desires to comfort—not the strong, but the weak. This is the glory of a religion of love. Christ was sent to comfort all who mourn. The God of all comfort sent His Son to bring comfort to a world full of sorrow. And throughout His life, Christ fulfilled this mission. When His disciples wanted Him to call down judgement on those who rejected Him, He rebuked them and said that He had not come to destroy lives but to save them. He welcomed sinners. He showed mercy where others showed condemnation. To the woman caught in sin, He said, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” (John 8:11) Everywhere, He stood on the side of those in need. That was His purpose—to save sinners. Two young girls were once talking about God, and one said, “I don’t think God loves me. I am too small and unimportant.” The other replied, “But that is exactly who God cares for—people like us who cannot manage on our own.” “Is that true?” said the first. “Then I do not need to worry anymore.” If anyone reading this feels afraid or troubled, let me say clearly: this is exactly what the Lord Jesus Christ is for—to care for and comfort all who mourn. All—every single one, including you. It would not be “all” if you were left out. Even if you feel completely cast down, He is described as the One “who comforts the downcast.” What a beautiful mission—to bring comfort into a world full of sorrow. And how I long for every troubled heart to experience this comfort from God. And our Comforter is not distant. He is near. He remains with us. When Christ was about to leave this world, He told His disciples He would not leave them alone, but would send “another Helper” to be with them forever. This Comforter would teach them and remind them of all truth. Then He added: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you… Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid.” (John 14:27) How can we remain fearful in the light of such words? “Comforter”—what a wonderful word, if only we truly understood it. Let us dwell on it until it becomes real to us. And not just a comforter who comes and goes, but one who remains—always present, always ready to bring joy in place of sorrow. An abiding Comforter—what an extraordinary truth. Even having a human friend stay with us in difficulty is a great help. But here is a divine Comforter who is always with us and whose ability to comfort never fails. There should never be a moment when we are without comfort. And yet many do not realise this. If they did, there would not be so many troubled Christians. You may ask whether this Comforter also corrects us, and whether that can truly be comforting. In fact, this is one of the ways He comforts us. What would we be like without someone to show us our faults and help us change? If I were walking with a fault in my appearance that I did not know about, it would be a kindness for a friend to point it out. In the same way, it is a comfort to know that the Spirit gently shows us our faults so that we are not left unaware of them. There is comfort even in correction, because it leads to healing. God “comforts all our waste places” by showing us what needs to be restored and then restoring it. You may feel unworthy of such comfort. That may be true—but that is exactly why you need it. Christ came to save sinners, not those who think themselves worthy. Your need is your qualification. The path to receiving God’s comfort often comes through recognising our need for it. This is why God sometimes allows sorrow. In difficult places, we are able to hear His voice more clearly. It is often in the wilderness that we hear His words of comfort. God knows that it is better for us to receive His comfort, even through trials, than never to experience it at all. What He gives is far greater than what we lose. Earthly things may pass, but what He gives is eternal. Like Paul, we can come to see that everything is loss compared to knowing Christ. And yet, strangely, when life is easy, we believe God is the God of all comfort—but when we truly need comfort, we struggle to believe it exists. It is as if we change the meaning of Scripture in our hearts. Instead of believing “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted,” we begin to think only the already happy will receive comfort. We may even twist words like “God who comforts the downcast” into something entirely different, as though He forgets or ignores those who are struggling. And in doing so, we lose the very comfort offered to us. But God says He will comfort us on every side. Nothing is left out. And yet, in times of trouble, we often believe there is no comfort exactly where we need it most. This is not because God has failed, but because we have doubted. It is like Israel of old. God declared His comfort, yet they said, “The Lord has forgotten me.” And His answer came full of tenderness: can a mother forget her child? Even if she could, God will not. We are always before Him. So be comforted. But you may still ask, how can you receive this comfort? The answer is simple: you must accept it. God is continually giving His comfort—but unless you receive it, you cannot experience it. Divine comfort does not come to us in a mysterious or arbitrary way. It comes through a clear and simple process. The indwelling Comforter brings to our remembrance comforting truths about our Lord, and if we believe them, we are comforted. A verse of Scripture may come to mind, or a line from a hymn, or a quiet reminder of Christ’s love and tender care. If we receive that in simple faith, comfort naturally follows. But if we refuse to listen to the voice of the Comforter and instead give attention to discouragement or despair, then no comfort can reach our souls. Even a mother can pour out all her love in vain on a child who refuses to be comforted. The child may sit stubborn and unmoved, rejecting every word. In the same way, comforting words can only comfort us if we believe them. God has spoken enough comforting words to soothe an entire world, yet many Christians remain anxious, burdened, and restless. Why? Because they do not allow those words to enter their hearts. Some even believe it is wrong to feel comfort—they feel too unworthy. And when comfort begins to rise within them, they push it away, refusing it, just as Scripture says, “they refused to be comforted.” (Jeremiah 31:15) We are told that everything written in Scripture is given so that, through endurance and the comfort it provides, we might have hope. But this comfort can only come through belief. Nothing God says can bring peace to a heart that doubts its truth. If a ship captain assures us the vessel is safe, we must believe him before we can relax. If a train conductor tells us we are on the right train, we must trust his word before we sit at ease. This is obvious in everyday life—yet in spiritual matters, we often ignore it. Some people even try to feel comfort before they believe God’s promises. But that reverses the order entirely. Just as a traveler cannot feel secure before trusting the guide, so we cannot feel comfort before believing God. God’s order is simple: believe first, then feel. We often reverse it: feel first, then believe. This reversal is the root of much of our struggle. Consider this: when we are overwhelmed with anxiety, God tells us not to be anxious, but to cast our cares upon Him because He cares for us. He points us to the birds of the air and the lilies of the field, assuring us that we are far more valuable than they. What greater comfort could there be than this—that the Creator of Heaven and earth takes responsibility for our care? And yet, many are not comforted. Why? Because they do not believe it. They admire the words, wish they were true, but hesitate to accept them personally. They wait for a feeling to confirm the truth, instead of trusting the truth itself. We say, “If only I could feel that it is true.” God says, “If only you would believe that it is true.” At the root of our lack of comfort is simply unbelief. The remedy is clear. If we desire comfort, we must choose to believe every word of comfort God has spoken. We must refuse to entertain the voices of doubt—whether they come from our circumstances or from our own thoughts. This requires determination. We must set our hearts firmly—like flint—to believe, even when everything around us seems contrary. Being comforted is not passive; it involves the will. We must choose it. When life feels uncertain, we must say: “God has said it. Therefore, it is true. I will believe it, no matter how it appears.” And having chosen to believe, we must refuse to turn back into doubt. Whoever lives this way will, sooner or later, enter into deep and lasting comfort. The psalmist said, “In the multitude of my thoughts within me, Your comforts delight my soul.” Yet often our minds are filled more with our troubles than with God’s comforts. If we want to be comforted, we must intentionally dwell on His promises. It may be helpful to examine our thoughts: How often do we think about God’s comfort compared to our worries? The answer might surprise us. Finally, a word to those who preach the Gospel. What is your message? It is this: “Comfort My people.” Not rebuke them, not burden them—but comfort them. The true Gospel is good news—pure, undiluted good news. Yet often it is mixed with conditions, warnings, and human additions that strip away its comfort. Christ comforts. Man often complicates. The true Gospel is like the angel’s message to the shepherds: “Do not be afraid. I bring you good news of great joy for all people.” (Luke 2:10) These are the words that bring real comfort. If every preacher proclaimed such words clearly, and every listener believed them, there would be no more restless, anxious Christians. Instead, hearts everywhere would be strengthened and filled with peace. And this prayer would be fulfilled: May our Lord Jesus Christ Himself, and God our Father—who has loved us and given us eternal comfort and good hope—comfort your hearts and establish you in every good word and work.

fields.title: The Lord Our Shepherd
fields.body_html:
“The Lord our Shepherd, I shall not want.” Psalm 23:1 I had a vivid experience of this at one time in my Christian life. The Twenty-third Psalm had, of course, always been familiar to me from my nursery days, but it had never seemed to have any special meaning. Then came a critical moment in my life when I was sadly in need of comfort, but could see none anywhere. I could not at the moment lay my hands on my Bible, and I cast about in my mind for some passage of Scripture that would help me. Immediately there flashed into my mind the words, “The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want.” (Psalm 23:1) At first I turned from it almost with scorn.

“Such a common text as that,” I said to myself, “is not likely to do me any good”; and I tried hard to think of a more recherché one, but none would come; and at last it almost seemed as if there were no other text in the whole Bible. And finally I was reduced to saying “Well, if I cannot think of any other text, I must try to get what little good I can out of this one,” and I began to repeat to myself over and over, “The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want.” Suddenly, as I did so, the words were di vinely illuminated, and there poured out upon me such floods of comfort that I felt as if I could never have a trouble again.

The moment I could get hold of a Bible I turned over its leaves with eagerness to see whether it could possibly be true that such untold treasures of comfort were really and actually mine, and whether I might dare to let out my heart into the full enjoyment of them. And I did what I have often found great profit in doing, I built up a pyramid of declarations and promises concerning the Lord being our Shepherd that, once built, presented an immovable and indestructible front to all the winds and storms of doubt or trial that could assail it. And I became convinced, beyond a shadow of doubt, that the Lord really was my Shepherd, and that in giving Himself this name He assumed the duties belonging to the name, and really would be, what He declares Himself to be, a “good shepherd who giveth his life for his sheep.” (John 10:11) He Himself draws a clear contrast between a good shepherd and a bad one. After declaring, “I am the good shepherd,” He continues: “He that is a hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees; and the wolf catches them and scatters the sheep.” (John 10:12) Through His prophets, the Lord speaks with strong condemnation against such unfaithful shepherds. The prophet Zechariah records: “Woe to my worthless shepherd, who deserts the flock! May the sword strike his arm and his right eye! Let his arm be wholly withered, his right eye utterly blinded!” (Zechariah 11:27) And again, through the prophet Ezekiel: “The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought, and with force and harshness you have ruled them.”

Surely no Christian would consciously accuse our divine Shepherd of such faithlessness. And yet, if the hidden thoughts of many hearts were revealed, it might be found that, though unspoken, such suspicions linger beneath the surface.

What else can it mean when believers say the Lord has forsaken them? When they cry for spiritual nourishment and feel unheard? When they are surrounded by trials and believe He does not deliver them? When they feel weak and assume He does not strengthen them, or sick in soul and think He does not heal them?

Are not these thoughts, however unintentional, quiet accusations against the very Shepherd who promises never to abandon His flock?

A dear Christian once shared: “I had always said, ‘The Lord is my Shepherd,’ but it meant nothing to me. In truth, I lived as though I were the shepherd and He the sheep—afraid that if I did not hold tightly to Him, He would wander away. When dark days came, I never expected Him to stand by me. When my soul hungered, I did not believe He would feed me. I see now that I never trusted Him as a faithful Shepherd at all.

But now everything has changed. I am no stronger than before, but I have discovered that I have a good Shepherd—and that is enough. I see now that it is truly real: the Lord is my Shepherd, and I shall not want.”

Dear fellow believer, consider this honestly.

You have said many times, “The Lord is my Shepherd.” But have you truly believed it? Have you lived in the peace and security that such a truth brings? Or have you felt like a lost sheep— uncared for, uncertain, and alone?

Ask yourself plainly: has your spiritual life been marked by comfort or by unease?

If it has been full of struggle and lack, how does that align with the promise, “I shall not want”?

If the Shepherd is perfect, where does the failure lie?

You may answer, “The fault is mine. I am too weak, too foolish, too unworthy.”

But that is precisely the nature of sheep. They are weak, dependent, and unable to care for themselves. That is why they need a shepherd. Their safety does not depend on their strength, but entirely on the shepherd’s care.

And so it is with you.

Imagine two flocks meeting after winter—one strong and healthy, the other weak and starving.

Would the healthy sheep praise themselves? Certainly not. They would speak only of their shepherd: how he protected them, fed them, and guided them through storms. And the weak flock—would they blame themselves? No. They too would speak of their shepherd: “Our shepherd failed us. He did not feed us, did not heal us, did not protect us. In danger, he fled.”

We understand this clearly when speaking of sheep. Yet when we apply it to our spiritual lives, we shift responsibility away from the Shepherd and place it upon ourselves—expecting from ourselves what only He can provide.

And so we fail, and our lives become burdened and restless.

There is, of course, one difference: sheep cannot leave their shepherd, but we can. No sheep would ever say: “Our shepherd offers care, but we are too unworthy to trust him. Others may rest in his provision, but we must fend for ourselves.”

Such thinking would be absurd for sheep. Yet this is exactly how many believers think.

We consider ourselves wiser than sheep—and in doing so, we refuse the very trust that would save us.

The truth is simple: if a sheep in Christ’s flock is weak and starving, only two explanations exist.

Either the Shepherd is unfaithful, or the sheep has not trusted His care. No one would dare say the Lord is unfaithful. Therefore, the issue must be this: either we have not truly believed He is our Shepherd, or we have not allowed Him to care for us.

Face this honestly.

Not only your peace depends on it—but His honor as well.

A shepherd is judged by the condition of his flock. No claim of excellence can stand if the sheep are neglected and broken.

The Lord declares to all creation, “I am the good Shepherd.” And the world looks at His people as the evidence of that claim.

Are we a testimony to His care?

Or do our lives suggest neglect, weakness, and fear?

The apostle Paul writes that through the Church, the wisdom of God is made known—even to heavenly powers. What a profound calling: that our lives would display the goodness and wisdom of our Shepherd.

Should we not, then, trust Him completely? Should we not yield ourselves fully into His care— so that His grace may be seen in us? But if we refuse His care—if we do not feed in His pastures or rest in His fold—then we remain weak and troubled, and our condition not only harms us, but misrepresents Him. The world is watching. And what they see in us will shape what they believe about our Shepherd.

I do not wonder that unbelievers are not drawn into the church when I consider the condition of believers. I do not wonder that in some churches there are no conversions from one end of the year to the other. If I were a poor sheep wandering in the wilderness, and I saw some poor, wretched, sick-looking sheep peering out of a fold and calling me to come in, and I looked into the fold and saw it hard, bare, and uncomfortable, I do not think I would be much tempted to go into such a fold.

Someone once said that some churches were too much like well-ordered graveyards: people were brought in and buried, and that was the end of it. Of course, you cannot expect living people to want to live in graveyards. We must have a fold that shows sheep in good condition if we expect outsiders to come into that fold; and if we want to attract others to the salvation of the Lord Jesus Christ, we must be able to show them that it is a satisfying and comforting salvation. No one wants to add to their earthly discomforts by adopting an uncomfortable religion, and it is useless to expect to win outsiders by the sight of our misery.

Surely, if you do not care for yourselves, you must care about the dishonour you bring upon your divine Shepherd by your poor and wretched condition. You long to serve Him and to bring Him glory; and you can do so if you show the world that He is a Shepherd whom it is safe to trust.

Let me help you to do this. First, face the fact of what a shepherd must be and do in order to be a good shepherd, and then face the fact that the Lord is truly, and in the highest sense, a good Shepherd. Then say these words to yourself with all the determination you can gather: “The Lord is my Shepherd. He is. He is. No matter what I feel, He says He is, and He is. I will believe it, whatever comes.” Then repeat the words with a different emphasis each time: The Lord is my Shepherd.

The Lord is my Shepherd.

The Lord is my Shepherd.

The Lord is my Shepherd.

Realise what your ideal Shepherd would be, all that you would expect from anyone in such a position of trust and responsibility, and then understand that an ideal far beyond yours, and a view of the duties of such a role higher than anything you have imagined, was in the mind of our Lord when He said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11) He, better than anyone, knew the sheep He had undertaken to save, and He knew the Shepherd’s responsibilities. He knew that the Shepherd is responsible for His flock and must, even at the cost of comfort, health, or life itself, care for them and bring them safely home to the Father’s fold. Therefore, He said: “And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.” (John 6:39) And again: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.” (John 10:27–28) Centuries before Jesus came as the Shepherd, the Father said: “I will rescue my flock; they shall no longer be a prey. And I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them: he shall feed them and be their shepherd.” (Ezekiel 34:22–23) It seems that in these words we see the Father’s deep, longing love. He has placed help upon One who is mighty; therefore, none who belong to this flock need fear any evil.

He has taken on His role, fully aware of its responsibilities. He knows He is dealing with very helpless sheep, who have no strength to protect themselves, no wisdom to guide themselves, and nothing to recommend them except their complete weakness and need. Yet none of this confuses Him. His strength and skill are enough for every situation that could arise.

There is only one thing that can hinder Him: if the sheep refuse to trust Him and will not allow Him to care for them. If they stand at a distance, look at the food He has provided, long for it, cry out for it, yet refuse to eat, He cannot satisfy their hunger. If they remain outside the shelter He has made, afraid to enter because they feel unworthy or distrustful, He cannot protect them. No sheep would act like this, but we human beings, who think ourselves wiser, do it continually.

No sheep, if it could speak, would say to the shepherd, “I long for the food you have provided, and for the shelter and peace of your fold, and I wish I could enjoy them; but I feel too unworthy.

I am too weak and foolish. I do not feel grateful enough. I am not sure I desire it strongly enough. I dare not assume that you mean these good things for me.” One can imagine how deeply such words would grieve a good shepherd.

And our Lord has shown us His sorrow over those who refuse to trust Him. When He looked at Jerusalem, He wept and said: “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.” (Luke 19:42) Dear Christians, have you not sometimes grieved your divine Shepherd in this same way? If so, consider for a moment the Shepherd’s perspective. Think about how He feels and what His heart is towards you. If He is your Shepherd, then He desires to care for you in the very best way, because He is a good Shepherd and He cares for His sheep. It does not depend on what you think or feel. You are not the Shepherd—you are the sheep. What matters is what He thinks and how He feels.

Forget yourself for a moment and try to see things from His point of view. Consider your condition as He sees it. See Him coming to find you in your wandering. See His tender love, His deep desire to save you. Believe what He says about Himself, and take Him at His word.

If our faith were simpler, We would take Him at His word; And our lives would be full of joy In the light of our Lord.

Yes, this is the problem. Our faith is not simple enough to take Him at His word. Instead, we add “ifs” and “buts” of our own and cloud the brightness of His love with doubts we create ourselves.

If we truly understood what brings us peace, how quickly we would throw aside every doubt and trust completely in His unfailing love and care.

You may ask, if all this is true of the Shepherd, what is the role of the sheep? It is simply to trust and to follow. There is nothing complicated about obedience when we fully trust the one we are following.

So I urge you to begin trusting and following your Shepherd now. Give yourself fully to His care and guidance, like a sheep under the care of a shepherd, and trust Him completely.

You need not fear following Him wherever He leads, for He always leads His sheep into green pastures and beside still waters. Even if you feel as though you are in a desert, with nothing refreshing around you, the good Shepherd can turn that very place into green pastures. He has the power to make the desert bloom, and He has promised: “Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress; instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle.”

(Isaiah 55:13) “The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus.” (Isaiah 35:1) “And waters break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.” (Isaiah 35:6) Or you may say, “My life is full of storms and troubles. It will take a long time before I can experience peace.” But has not your Shepherd already said: “He awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, ‘Peace! Be still!’ And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.” (Mark 4:39) Can He not do the same again?

Many in Christ’s flock can testify that when they have fully trusted Him, He has calmed their storms and turned their deserts into places of life and beauty. This does not mean that outward troubles disappear, but even in those places, the soul finds peace and nourishment. The Shepherd knows which pastures are best for His sheep, and they must trust Him without doubt. Sometimes the best growth comes in times of difficulty. If He leads you there, you can be sure it is good for you.

Words cannot fully describe what the good Shepherd does for those who trust Him. He fulfils His promise and makes a covenant of peace with them: “I will make with them a covenant of peace and banish wild beasts from the land, so that they may dwell securely in the wilderness and sleep in the woods.” (Ezekiel 34:25) “And I will make them and the places all around my hill a blessing, and I will send down the showers in their season; they shall be showers of blessing.” (Ezekiel 34:26) “And the trees of the field shall yield their fruit, and the earth shall yield its increase… And they shall be no more a prey to the nations, nor shall the beasts of the land devour them. They shall dwell securely, and none shall make them afraid.” (Ezekiel 34:27–28) You may now wonder how you can have the Lord as your Shepherd. The answer is that you do not need to make Him your Shepherd—He already is. You only need to recognise it and yield yourself to His care.

When children are told that a long-awaited baby sister has been born, they do not keep saying, “We wish we had a sister,” or “What must we do to get one?” Instead, they rejoice and say, “We have a sister now!”

In the same way, the announcement has already been made to us: “Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord.” (Luke 2:10–11) We do not need to say, “If only I had a Saviour,” or “What must I do to make Christ my Saviour?” He is already our Saviour. We must simply rejoice and place ourselves in His care. It is not complicated. It is to believe it and live as though it is true. And every person who begins today to trust the good Shepherd will, sooner or later, find themselves feeding in His green pastures and walking beside His still waters.

What else can the Lord, who is our Shepherd, do with His sheep, but just this? He has no folds that are not good folds, no pastures that are not green pastures, and no waters but still waters.

They may not appear so outwardly; but we who have experienced them can testify that, whatever the outward appearance may be, His fold and His pastures are always places of peace and comfort to the inner life of the soul.

If you seem to struggle to understand all this, and if the life of complete trust appears complicated and mysterious, I would advise you not to try to understand it, but simply begin to live it. Just take our nursery psalm and say, “this is my psalm, and I am going to believe it. I have always known it by heart, but it has never meant much to me. But now I have decided to believe that the Lord truly is my Shepherd and that He will care for me as a shepherd cares for his sheep.

I will not doubt or question it again.” And then simply surrender yourself to His care, as the sheep surrender themselves to the care of their shepherd, trusting Him fully, and following wherever He leads.

But we must not forget that while sheep trust unconsciously and by instinct, we need to trust intelligently and intentionally, because our instincts are, unfortunately, all against trusting. We will have to make an effort to trust. We will have to choose to do it. But we can do this, however weak and ignorant we may be. We may not understand all that it means to belong as sheep to such a Shepherd, but He knows. And if our faith will simply embrace Him in this blessed and wonderful relationship, He will care for us according to His love, His wisdom, and His power, and not according to our limited understanding of it.

It really seems to me that we would not need any other passage in the entire Bible besides this nursery psalm to make our spiritual lives full of comfort. I honestly do not see where there is any room left for the believer to worry, if they truly believe this psalm. With the Lord as our Shepherd, how is it possible for anything to go wrong? With Him as our Shepherd, all that this psalm promises must belong to us; and when we have learned to know Him in this way, we will be able to say with triumphant trust: “Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the Lord forever.” (Psalm 23:6) Even the future will lose all its fear for us, and our confidence in our Shepherd will deliver us from all fear of troubling news.

And I can only say, in conclusion, that if each one of you will enter into this relationship with Christ, and truly be a helpless, willing, trusting sheep, and will believe Him to be your Shepherd, caring for you with all the love, care, and tenderness that that name implies, and will follow Him wherever He leads, you will soon lose all your old spiritual unease, and will know the peace of God that surpasses all understanding, guarding your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:7).

“They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father.” (John 8:27)

After declaring, “I am the good shepherd,” He continues: “He that is a hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees; and the wolf catches them and scatters the sheep.” (John 10:12) Through His prophets, the Lord speaks with strong condemnation against such unfaithful shepherds. The prophet Zechariah records: “Woe to my worthless shepherd, who deserts the flock! May the sword strike his arm and his right eye! Let his arm be wholly withered, his right eye utterly blinded!” (Zechariah 11:27) And again, through the prophet Ezekiel: “The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought, and with force and harshness you have ruled them.” Surely no Christian would consciously accuse our divine Shepherd of such faithlessness. And yet, if the hidden thoughts of many hearts were revealed, it might be found that, though unspoken, such suspicions linger beneath the surface. What else can it mean when believers say the Lord has forsaken them? When they cry for spiritual nourishment and feel unheard? When they are surrounded by trials and believe He does not deliver them? When they feel weak and assume He does not strengthen them, or sick in soul and think He does not heal them? Are not these thoughts, however unintentional, quiet accusations against the very Shepherd who promises never to abandon His flock? A dear Christian once shared: “I had always said, ‘The Lord is my Shepherd,’ but it meant nothing to me. In truth, I lived as though I were the shepherd and He the sheep—afraid that if I did not hold tightly to Him, He would wander away. When dark days came, I never expected Him to stand by me. When my soul hungered, I did not believe He would feed me. I see now that I never trusted Him as a faithful Shepherd at all. But now everything has changed. I am no stronger than before, but I have discovered that I have a good Shepherd—and that is enough. I see now that it is truly real: the Lord is my Shepherd, and I shall not want.” Dear fellow believer, consider this honestly. You have said many times, “The Lord is my Shepherd.” But have you truly believed it? Have you lived in the peace and security that such a truth brings? Or have you felt like a lost sheep— uncared for, uncertain, and alone? Ask yourself plainly: has your spiritual life been marked by comfort or by unease? If it has been full of struggle and lack, how does that align with the promise, “I shall not want”? If the Shepherd is perfect, where does the failure lie? You may answer, “The fault is mine. I am too weak, too foolish, too unworthy.” But that is precisely the nature of sheep. They are weak, dependent, and unable to care for themselves. That is why they need a shepherd. Their safety does not depend on their strength, but entirely on the shepherd’s care. And so it is with you. Imagine two flocks meeting after winter—one strong and healthy, the other weak and starving. Would the healthy sheep praise themselves? Certainly not. They would speak only of their shepherd: how he protected them, fed them, and guided them through storms. And the weak flock—would they blame themselves? No. They too would speak of their shepherd: “Our shepherd failed us. He did not feed us, did not heal us, did not protect us. In danger, he fled.” We understand this clearly when speaking of sheep. Yet when we apply it to our spiritual lives, we shift responsibility away from the Shepherd and place it upon ourselves—expecting from ourselves what only He can provide. And so we fail, and our lives become burdened and restless. There is, of course, one difference: sheep cannot leave their shepherd, but we can. No sheep would ever say: “Our shepherd offers care, but we are too unworthy to trust him. Others may rest in his provision, but we must fend for ourselves.” Such thinking would be absurd for sheep. Yet this is exactly how many believers think. We consider ourselves wiser than sheep—and in doing so, we refuse the very trust that would save us. The truth is simple: if a sheep in Christ’s flock is weak and starving, only two explanations exist. Either the Shepherd is unfaithful, or the sheep has not trusted His care. No one would dare say the Lord is unfaithful. Therefore, the issue must be this: either we have not truly believed He is our Shepherd, or we have not allowed Him to care for us. Face this honestly. Not only your peace depends on it—but His honor as well. A shepherd is judged by the condition of his flock. No claim of excellence can stand if the sheep are neglected and broken. The Lord declares to all creation, “I am the good Shepherd.” And the world looks at His people as the evidence of that claim. Are we a testimony to His care? Or do our lives suggest neglect, weakness, and fear? The apostle Paul writes that through the Church, the wisdom of God is made known—even to heavenly powers. What a profound calling: that our lives would display the goodness and wisdom of our Shepherd. Should we not, then, trust Him completely? Should we not yield ourselves fully into His care— so that His grace may be seen in us? But if we refuse His care—if we do not feed in His pastures or rest in His fold—then we remain weak and troubled, and our condition not only harms us, but misrepresents Him. The world is watching. And what they see in us will shape what they believe about our Shepherd. I do not wonder that unbelievers are not drawn into the church when I consider the condition of believers. I do not wonder that in some churches there are no conversions from one end of the year to the other. If I were a poor sheep wandering in the wilderness, and I saw some poor, wretched, sick-looking sheep peering out of a fold and calling me to come in, and I looked into the fold and saw it hard, bare, and uncomfortable, I do not think I would be much tempted to go into such a fold. Someone once said that some churches were too much like well-ordered graveyards: people were brought in and buried, and that was the end of it. Of course, you cannot expect living people to want to live in graveyards. We must have a fold that shows sheep in good condition if we expect outsiders to come into that fold; and if we want to attract others to the salvation of the Lord Jesus Christ, we must be able to show them that it is a satisfying and comforting salvation. No one wants to add to their earthly discomforts by adopting an uncomfortable religion, and it is useless to expect to win outsiders by the sight of our misery. Surely, if you do not care for yourselves, you must care about the dishonour you bring upon your divine Shepherd by your poor and wretched condition. You long to serve Him and to bring Him glory; and you can do so if you show the world that He is a Shepherd whom it is safe to trust. Let me help you to do this. First, face the fact of what a shepherd must be and do in order to be a good shepherd, and then face the fact that the Lord is truly, and in the highest sense, a good Shepherd. Then say these words to yourself with all the determination you can gather: “The Lord is my Shepherd. He is. He is. No matter what I feel, He says He is, and He is. I will believe it, whatever comes.” Then repeat the words with a different emphasis each time: The Lord is my Shepherd. The Lord is my Shepherd. The Lord is my Shepherd. The Lord is my Shepherd. Realise what your ideal Shepherd would be, all that you would expect from anyone in such a position of trust and responsibility, and then understand that an ideal far beyond yours, and a view of the duties of such a role higher than anything you have imagined, was in the mind of our Lord when He said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11) He, better than anyone, knew the sheep He had undertaken to save, and He knew the Shepherd’s responsibilities. He knew that the Shepherd is responsible for His flock and must, even at the cost of comfort, health, or life itself, care for them and bring them safely home to the Father’s fold. Therefore, He said: “And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.” (John 6:39) And again: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.” (John 10:27–28) Centuries before Jesus came as the Shepherd, the Father said: “I will rescue my flock; they shall no longer be a prey. And I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them: he shall feed them and be their shepherd.” (Ezekiel 34:22–23) It seems that in these words we see the Father’s deep, longing love. He has placed help upon One who is mighty; therefore, none who belong to this flock need fear any evil. He has taken on His role, fully aware of its responsibilities. He knows He is dealing with very helpless sheep, who have no strength to protect themselves, no wisdom to guide themselves, and nothing to recommend them except their complete weakness and need. Yet none of this confuses Him. His strength and skill are enough for every situation that could arise. There is only one thing that can hinder Him: if the sheep refuse to trust Him and will not allow Him to care for them. If they stand at a distance, look at the food He has provided, long for it, cry out for it, yet refuse to eat, He cannot satisfy their hunger. If they remain outside the shelter He has made, afraid to enter because they feel unworthy or distrustful, He cannot protect them. No sheep would act like this, but we human beings, who think ourselves wiser, do it continually. No sheep, if it could speak, would say to the shepherd, “I long for the food you have provided, and for the shelter and peace of your fold, and I wish I could enjoy them; but I feel too unworthy. I am too weak and foolish. I do not feel grateful enough. I am not sure I desire it strongly enough. I dare not assume that you mean these good things for me.” One can imagine how deeply such words would grieve a good shepherd. And our Lord has shown us His sorrow over those who refuse to trust Him. When He looked at Jerusalem, He wept and said: “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.” (Luke 19:42) Dear Christians, have you not sometimes grieved your divine Shepherd in this same way? If so, consider for a moment the Shepherd’s perspective. Think about how He feels and what His heart is towards you. If He is your Shepherd, then He desires to care for you in the very best way, because He is a good Shepherd and He cares for His sheep. It does not depend on what you think or feel. You are not the Shepherd—you are the sheep. What matters is what He thinks and how He feels. Forget yourself for a moment and try to see things from His point of view. Consider your condition as He sees it. See Him coming to find you in your wandering. See His tender love, His deep desire to save you. Believe what He says about Himself, and take Him at His word. If our faith were simpler, We would take Him at His word; And our lives would be full of joy In the light of our Lord. Yes, this is the problem. Our faith is not simple enough to take Him at His word. Instead, we add “ifs” and “buts” of our own and cloud the brightness of His love with doubts we create ourselves. If we truly understood what brings us peace, how quickly we would throw aside every doubt and trust completely in His unfailing love and care. You may ask, if all this is true of the Shepherd, what is the role of the sheep? It is simply to trust and to follow. There is nothing complicated about obedience when we fully trust the one we are following. So I urge you to begin trusting and following your Shepherd now. Give yourself fully to His care and guidance, like a sheep under the care of a shepherd, and trust Him completely. You need not fear following Him wherever He leads, for He always leads His sheep into green pastures and beside still waters. Even if you feel as though you are in a desert, with nothing refreshing around you, the good Shepherd can turn that very place into green pastures. He has the power to make the desert bloom, and He has promised: “Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress; instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle.” (Isaiah 55:13) “The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus.” (Isaiah 35:1) “And waters break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.” (Isaiah 35:6) Or you may say, “My life is full of storms and troubles. It will take a long time before I can experience peace.” But has not your Shepherd already said: “He awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, ‘Peace! Be still!’ And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.” (Mark 4:39) Can He not do the same again? Many in Christ’s flock can testify that when they have fully trusted Him, He has calmed their storms and turned their deserts into places of life and beauty. This does not mean that outward troubles disappear, but even in those places, the soul finds peace and nourishment. The Shepherd knows which pastures are best for His sheep, and they must trust Him without doubt. Sometimes the best growth comes in times of difficulty. If He leads you there, you can be sure it is good for you. Words cannot fully describe what the good Shepherd does for those who trust Him. He fulfils His promise and makes a covenant of peace with them: “I will make with them a covenant of peace and banish wild beasts from the land, so that they may dwell securely in the wilderness and sleep in the woods.” (Ezekiel 34:25) “And I will make them and the places all around my hill a blessing, and I will send down the showers in their season; they shall be showers of blessing.” (Ezekiel 34:26) “And the trees of the field shall yield their fruit, and the earth shall yield its increase… And they shall be no more a prey to the nations, nor shall the beasts of the land devour them. They shall dwell securely, and none shall make them afraid.” (Ezekiel 34:27–28) You may now wonder how you can have the Lord as your Shepherd. The answer is that you do not need to make Him your Shepherd—He already is. You only need to recognise it and yield yourself to His care. When children are told that a long-awaited baby sister has been born, they do not keep saying, “We wish we had a sister,” or “What must we do to get one?” Instead, they rejoice and say, “We have a sister now!” In the same way, the announcement has already been made to us: “Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord.” (Luke 2:10–11) We do not need to say, “If only I had a Saviour,” or “What must I do to make Christ my Saviour?” He is already our Saviour. We must simply rejoice and place ourselves in His care. It is not complicated. It is to believe it and live as though it is true. And every person who begins today to trust the good Shepherd will, sooner or later, find themselves feeding in His green pastures and walking beside His still waters. What else can the Lord, who is our Shepherd, do with His sheep, but just this? He has no folds that are not good folds, no pastures that are not green pastures, and no waters but still waters. They may not appear so outwardly; but we who have experienced them can testify that, whatever the outward appearance may be, His fold and His pastures are always places of peace and comfort to the inner life of the soul. If you seem to struggle to understand all this, and if the life of complete trust appears complicated and mysterious, I would advise you not to try to understand it, but simply begin to live it. Just take our nursery psalm and say, “this is my psalm, and I am going to believe it. I have always known it by heart, but it has never meant much to me. But now I have decided to believe that the Lord truly is my Shepherd and that He will care for me as a shepherd cares for his sheep. I will not doubt or question it again.” And then simply surrender yourself to His care, as the sheep surrender themselves to the care of their shepherd, trusting Him fully, and following wherever He leads. But we must not forget that while sheep trust unconsciously and by instinct, we need to trust intelligently and intentionally, because our instincts are, unfortunately, all against trusting. We will have to make an effort to trust. We will have to choose to do it. But we can do this, however weak and ignorant we may be. We may not understand all that it means to belong as sheep to such a Shepherd, but He knows. And if our faith will simply embrace Him in this blessed and wonderful relationship, He will care for us according to His love, His wisdom, and His power, and not according to our limited understanding of it. It really seems to me that we would not need any other passage in the entire Bible besides this nursery psalm to make our spiritual lives full of comfort. I honestly do not see where there is any room left for the believer to worry, if they truly believe this psalm. With the Lord as our Shepherd, how is it possible for anything to go wrong? With Him as our Shepherd, all that this psalm promises must belong to us; and when we have learned to know Him in this way, we will be able to say with triumphant trust: “Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the Lord forever.” (Psalm 23:6) Even the future will lose all its fear for us, and our confidence in our Shepherd will deliver us from all fear of troubling news. And I can only say, in conclusion, that if each one of you will enter into this relationship with Christ, and truly be a helpless, willing, trusting sheep, and will believe Him to be your Shepherd, caring for you with all the love, care, and tenderness that that name implies, and will follow Him wherever He leads, you will soon lose all your old spiritual unease, and will know the peace of God that surpasses all understanding, guarding your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:7). “They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father.” (John 8:27)

fields.title: He Spoke to Them of the Father
fields.body_html:
“They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father.” John 8:27 One of the most illuminating names of God is the one especially revealed by our Lord Jesus Christ, the name of Father. I say especially revealed by Christ, because, while God had been called throughout the ages by many other names expressing other aspects of His character, Christ alone has revealed Him to us under the all-inclusive name of Father—a name that contains within itself all other names of wisdom and power, and above all of love and goodness, a name that provides a complete supply for all our needs. Christ, who was the only begotten Son in the Father’s presence, was the only one who could reveal this name, for He alone knew the Father.

“As the Father knows me and I know the Father.” (John 10:15) “No one has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.” (John 6:46) In the Old Testament, God was not revealed as Father so much as a great warrior fighting for His people, or as a mighty king ruling over them and caring for them. The name of Father is only given to Him a very few times there, six or seven times at most; while in the New Testament it is used about two or three hundred times. Christ, who knew Him, was the only one who could reveal Him. “No one knows who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” (Luke 10:22) The essential question, then, that confronts each one of us is whether we personally understand that Christ speaks to us of the Father. We know He uses the word Father continually, but do we truly understand what that word means? Have we even the slightest understanding of what the Father is? All the discomfort and unrest in the spiritual lives of so many of God’s children comes, I am convinced, from this very issue—that they do not understand that God is truly and personally their Father. They think of Him as a strict Judge, or a harsh Taskmaster, or at best as a distant and unapproachable authority seated far away, issuing demanding laws to a frightened and trembling world; and in their fear that they may fail to meet His requirements, they hardly know which way to turn. But of a God who is a Father, gentle, loving, and full of compassion, a God who, like a father, stands on their side against the entire universe, they have no real understanding.

I am not afraid to say that unrest and inner discomfort are impossible for those who come to know that God is truly their Father.

But before I go further, I must make it clear that I am speaking of a Father such as our highest instincts tell us a good father ought to be. Sometimes earthly fathers are unkind, harsh, selfish, or even cruel, or they may simply be indifferent and neglectful; but none of these can in any true sense be called good fathers. But God, who is good, must be a good Father, or not a Father at all.

We have all known good fathers in this world, or at least can imagine them. I knew one, and he filled my childhood with light through his beautiful fatherhood. I can vividly remember the confidence and joy with which I lived each day, completely secure in the knowledge that I had a father. And I am certain that I have come to understand something of the perfect fatherhood of God through my experience with that earthly father.

But God is not only a Father; He is also described in ways that reflect both fatherly and motherly qualities, and we have all known mothers whose love and tenderness are without limit. It is certain that the God who created them both, and who in Himself embodies the fullness of parental love, could never have created earthly fathers and mothers who are more tender or more loving than He is. Therefore, if we want to understand what sort of Father He is, we must gather together the best qualities of all the fathers and mothers we have ever known or can imagine, and recognise that even this is only a faint reflection of God our Father in heaven.

When our Lord was teaching His disciples how to pray, the name by which He instructed them to address God was, “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.” (Matthew 6:9) This clearly shows that we are to think of Him in this way. Millions upon millions of times throughout the centuries, this name has been spoken by the children of God everywhere; and yet how deeply has it been understood? If all who used this name truly understood its meaning, it would have been impossible for the misrepresentations of His character and the doubts about His love and care, which have troubled the hearts of His children throughout history, to take hold. Tyranny, unkindness, and neglect might perhaps be attributed to a God whose name was only king, judge, or lawgiver; but of a God who is first and foremost a Father, and necessarily, since He is God, a good Father, such ideas cannot rightly be held. Moreover, since He is an “everlasting Father,” He must, by His very nature, always act as a good Father should, under all circumstances, and never otherwise. It is unthinkable that a good father would forget, neglect, or act unjustly toward his children. A wicked or careless father might, but a good father never would. And in calling our God by the blessed name of Father, we must recognise that, if He is a Father at all, He must be the very best of fathers, and His fatherhood must represent the highest ideal of fatherhood we can conceive.

It is a fatherhood that includes the highest ideals of both father and mother combined, encompassing all the love, tenderness, compassion, longing, and self-sacrifice that we rightly associate with parenthood, even though we do not always see these perfectly expressed in earthly parents.

But you may ask about the other names of God—do they not suggest more fearful ideas? They only seem to do so because this blessed name of Father is not understood as underlying them all.

This name must be the foundation of every other name by which He is known. Has He been called a Judge? Yes, but He is a Father-Judge, judging as a loving father would. Is He a King?

Yes, but He is a King who is also the Father of His people, ruling them with a father’s tenderness. Is He a Lawgiver? Yes, but He is a Lawgiver who gives laws as a father would, mindful of the weakness and ignorance of his children. “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the Lord shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust.” (Psalm 103:13–14) We must never, never think of God in any other way than as “our Father.” All other attributes we associate with Him must be grounded in and shaped by this truth of “our Father.” What a good father could not do, God, who is our Father, cannot do either; and what a good father ought to do, God, who is our Father, will certainly do.

In our Lord’s final prayer in John 17, He says that He has made known to us the name of the Father so that we may discover the wonderful truth that the Father loves us as He loved His Son.

Now, which of us truly believes this? We may have read this chapter many times, perhaps more than almost any other in the Bible, and yet do we actually believe that it is literally true that God loves us as much as He loved Christ? If we truly believed this, could we ever again have an anxious or rebellious thought? Would we not be completely and entirely confident in every circumstance that the divine Father, who loves us as much as He loved His only begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, would care for us in the best possible way, and would therefore clearly instruct us not to be anxious or troubled about anything, because He knows His Father and knows that it is completely safe to trust Him entirely?

It is very striking that He so often said, “Your Father in heaven,” not only mine, but yours as well. “Your Father in heaven” cares for the birds of the air and the lilies of the field, and therefore will certainly care for you, who are of far greater value than many birds. How foolish it is, then, for us to be anxious and troubled about things, when Christ has told us that our heavenly Father knows that we need all these things! For being a good Father, He must, by His very nature, provide for us when He knows our needs.

What is the matter with us that we do not understand this?

Again, our Lord compares earthly fathers with our heavenly Father, not to show how much less good and loving our heavenly Father is, but how much more. “Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? ...

how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!”

(Matthew 7:9–11) Can we imagine a good earthly father giving a stone or a serpent to a hungry child instead of bread or fish? Our hearts would recoil at such a thought. Yet many of God’s children seem to believe that their heavenly Father acts in such ways toward them, giving them stones when they ask for bread, or hardship when they ask for blessing. And some of these very people may belong to organisations that exist to protect children from cruelty—yet they have not considered the seriousness of accusing their heavenly Father of the very things they would condemn in earthly fathers.

But our heavenly Father is not only willing to give us good things—He is far more than willing.

Our Lord says, “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.” (Luke 12:32) There is no reluctance in His giving; it is His good pleasure to give. He delights in doing so. He desires to give you the kingdom far more than you desire to receive it.

Those of us who are parents understand how eager we are to give good things to our children, often more eager than they are to receive them; and this helps us understand how it is God’s good pleasure to give us the kingdom. Why then do we approach Him with fear and hesitation, and why do we trouble ourselves with anxiety as though He might fail to provide what we need?

There can only be one answer: we do not truly know the Father.

We are described as being part of the “household of God.” Scripture teaches that if anyone does not provide for his own household, he has “denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.” (1 Timothy 5:8) Since we belong to the household of God, this principle applies to Him; and if He were to fail to provide for us, His own words would stand against Him. I say this with reverence, but also with clarity, because so few seem to have grasped it.

In my own experience, there came a defining moment when I first understood this truth about the responsibility of my Father in heaven. It was as though, in a single instant, the burden of life was lifted from my shoulders and placed upon His, and all my fears, anxieties, and uncertainties were surrendered into the depth of His loving care. I realised that the natural human instinct which expects parents to care for their children is not merely cultural, but divinely implanted. It is meant to teach us that the Creator, who has made human parents responsible for their children, is Himself equally responsible for His children. I could have rejoiced greatly. From that moment, my burdens were turned into rest. For when this understanding comes to a person, that person must, by necessity, enter into rest.

With such a God, who is at the same time a Father, there is no place for anything but rest. And whenever, since that joyful discovery, temptations to doubt, anxiety, or fear have arisen, I have refused to listen to them in light of what I have learned, because I recognise that to do so would be to question the reliability of my Father in heaven.

We may have been used to thinking that our doubts and fears come from our own unworthiness and are a sign of humility. We may even have taken them as evidence of special piety and thought they were in some way pleasing to God. But if children, in their relationship with their earthly parents, allowed doubts about their parents’ love and feared that their care might fail, would those doubts and fears show true love and respect? Would they be pleasing to their parents?

If God is our Father, the only thing we can do with doubts, fears, and anxious thoughts is to cast them behind us completely and refuse to entertain them again. We can do this. We can give up our doubts just as we would urge someone to give up a harmful habit. If we truly see that our doubts are a sin against God and question His trustworthiness, we will be eager to abandon them.

We may have held on to our doubts before because we thought they were part of our faith and a fitting attitude for someone who feels unworthy. But if we now see that God truly is our Father, we will reject every doubt with horror, recognising it as a slander against His love and care.

What more could any soul want than to have a God whose name is “our Father,” and whose character matches that name? As Philip said, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8). And indeed, it is enough—far beyond what words can express.

A friend of mine once went to visit a poor woman living in one of the poorest parts of Philadelphia, whose situation had been reported as one of great need. She found things even worse than expected. The woman was old, crippled with rheumatism, and lived alone in a small, poor room, receiving only occasional help from a kind neighbour. Yet she was cheerful and full of gratitude.

My friend was amazed that such joy could exist under such circumstances and asked, “Do you never feel afraid when you think about what might happen to you, living here alone and in such a condition?”

The woman looked at her with surprise and said, “Afraid? Why, don’t you know I have a Father, and don’t you know He takes care of me all the time?” Then, seeing my friend’s confusion, she added gently, “Surely my Father is your Father too, and you know Him, and you know He always takes care of His children.” It was a lesson my friend never forgot.

“See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1). The love given to us is the love of a father for his child—a tender, protective love that understands our weakness and our needs and cares for us accordingly. He treats us as children, and all He asks in return is that we treat Him as a Father whom we can trust without anxiety.

We must take the place of children—dependent and trusting—and allow Him to take the place of Father—caring and responsible. Because we are the children and He is the Father, we must let Him do the Father’s part. Too often, we take that role upon ourselves and try to care for and provide for our own needs. But no good earthly father would want his children to carry his responsibilities, and certainly our heavenly Father would not want us to carry His.

No wonder we are told, “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Of course He cares for us—it is His role as Father. He would not be a good Father if He did not. All He asks is that we tell Him what we need and then leave the provision to Him. He promises that if we do this, “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7).

Children of a good earthly father are at peace because they trust their father’s care. Yet the children of the heavenly Father often have no peace because they are afraid to trust Him. They may tell Him their needs, but only as a routine. They do not truly believe He will take care of them. And so they continue to carry their burdens as though they had no Father in heaven at all.

What foolishness this is. If any earthly father is worthy of his children’s trust, how much more is our heavenly Father worthy of ours. The reason so few trust Him is either that they have not realised He is truly their Father, or that, although they call Him Father, they have never understood what that really means.

The answer to your unrest is to become truly acquainted with the Father.

“For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). Is this spirit of adoption ruling in your heart, or is it the spirit of fear? Your peace depends entirely on this. No effort, struggle, or prayer can bring you rest while the spirit of adoption is absent.

But you may ask how to receive this spirit. It is not something you obtain by effort. It comes naturally when you discover that God truly is your Father. When you realise this, you cannot help but think and act like a child—and that is what the spirit of adoption means. It is not mysterious; it is simply the natural result of finding a Father where you once thought there was only a Judge.

The great need, therefore, is to make this discovery. To do this, we must listen to what Christ says about the Father and believe it.

“Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony” (John 3:11).

“The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works” (John 14:10).

“Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true” (John 3:33).

If we accept Christ’s testimony, we declare that God is true. If we reject it, we make Him a liar.

“If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him” (John 14:7). We must decide that from now on we will believe His testimony and truly know the Father. For us, there must be “one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist” (1 Corinthians 8:6).
fields.body_text: “They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father.” John 8:27 One of the most illuminating names of God is the one especially revealed by our Lord Jesus Christ, the name of Father. I say especially revealed by Christ, because, while God had been called throughout the ages by many other names expressing other aspects of His character, Christ alone has revealed Him to us under the all-inclusive name of Father—a name that contains within itself all other names of wisdom and power, and above all of love and goodness, a name that provides a complete supply for all our needs. Christ, who was the only begotten Son in the Father’s presence, was the only one who could reveal this name, for He alone knew the Father. “As the Father knows me and I know the Father.” (John 10:15) “No one has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.” (John 6:46) In the Old Testament, God was not revealed as Father so much as a great warrior fighting for His people, or as a mighty king ruling over them and caring for them. The name of Father is only given to Him a very few times there, six or seven times at most; while in the New Testament it is used about two or three hundred times. Christ, who knew Him, was the only one who could reveal Him. “No one knows who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” (Luke 10:22) The essential question, then, that confronts each one of us is whether we personally understand that Christ speaks to us of the Father. We know He uses the word Father continually, but do we truly understand what that word means? Have we even the slightest understanding of what the Father is? All the discomfort and unrest in the spiritual lives of so many of God’s children comes, I am convinced, from this very issue—that they do not understand that God is truly and personally their Father. They think of Him as a strict Judge, or a harsh Taskmaster, or at best as a distant and unapproachable authority seated far away, issuing demanding laws to a frightened and trembling world; and in their fear that they may fail to meet His requirements, they hardly know which way to turn. But of a God who is a Father, gentle, loving, and full of compassion, a God who, like a father, stands on their side against the entire universe, they have no real understanding. I am not afraid to say that unrest and inner discomfort are impossible for those who come to know that God is truly their Father. But before I go further, I must make it clear that I am speaking of a Father such as our highest instincts tell us a good father ought to be. Sometimes earthly fathers are unkind, harsh, selfish, or even cruel, or they may simply be indifferent and neglectful; but none of these can in any true sense be called good fathers. But God, who is good, must be a good Father, or not a Father at all. We have all known good fathers in this world, or at least can imagine them. I knew one, and he filled my childhood with light through his beautiful fatherhood. I can vividly remember the confidence and joy with which I lived each day, completely secure in the knowledge that I had a father. And I am certain that I have come to understand something of the perfect fatherhood of God through my experience with that earthly father. But God is not only a Father; He is also described in ways that reflect both fatherly and motherly qualities, and we have all known mothers whose love and tenderness are without limit. It is certain that the God who created them both, and who in Himself embodies the fullness of parental love, could never have created earthly fathers and mothers who are more tender or more loving than He is. Therefore, if we want to understand what sort of Father He is, we must gather together the best qualities of all the fathers and mothers we have ever known or can imagine, and recognise that even this is only a faint reflection of God our Father in heaven. When our Lord was teaching His disciples how to pray, the name by which He instructed them to address God was, “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.” (Matthew 6:9) This clearly shows that we are to think of Him in this way. Millions upon millions of times throughout the centuries, this name has been spoken by the children of God everywhere; and yet how deeply has it been understood? If all who used this name truly understood its meaning, it would have been impossible for the misrepresentations of His character and the doubts about His love and care, which have troubled the hearts of His children throughout history, to take hold. Tyranny, unkindness, and neglect might perhaps be attributed to a God whose name was only king, judge, or lawgiver; but of a God who is first and foremost a Father, and necessarily, since He is God, a good Father, such ideas cannot rightly be held. Moreover, since He is an “everlasting Father,” He must, by His very nature, always act as a good Father should, under all circumstances, and never otherwise. It is unthinkable that a good father would forget, neglect, or act unjustly toward his children. A wicked or careless father might, but a good father never would. And in calling our God by the blessed name of Father, we must recognise that, if He is a Father at all, He must be the very best of fathers, and His fatherhood must represent the highest ideal of fatherhood we can conceive. It is a fatherhood that includes the highest ideals of both father and mother combined, encompassing all the love, tenderness, compassion, longing, and self-sacrifice that we rightly associate with parenthood, even though we do not always see these perfectly expressed in earthly parents. But you may ask about the other names of God—do they not suggest more fearful ideas? They only seem to do so because this blessed name of Father is not understood as underlying them all. This name must be the foundation of every other name by which He is known. Has He been called a Judge? Yes, but He is a Father-Judge, judging as a loving father would. Is He a King? Yes, but He is a King who is also the Father of His people, ruling them with a father’s tenderness. Is He a Lawgiver? Yes, but He is a Lawgiver who gives laws as a father would, mindful of the weakness and ignorance of his children. “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the Lord shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust.” (Psalm 103:13–14) We must never, never think of God in any other way than as “our Father.” All other attributes we associate with Him must be grounded in and shaped by this truth of “our Father.” What a good father could not do, God, who is our Father, cannot do either; and what a good father ought to do, God, who is our Father, will certainly do. In our Lord’s final prayer in John 17, He says that He has made known to us the name of the Father so that we may discover the wonderful truth that the Father loves us as He loved His Son. Now, which of us truly believes this? We may have read this chapter many times, perhaps more than almost any other in the Bible, and yet do we actually believe that it is literally true that God loves us as much as He loved Christ? If we truly believed this, could we ever again have an anxious or rebellious thought? Would we not be completely and entirely confident in every circumstance that the divine Father, who loves us as much as He loved His only begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, would care for us in the best possible way, and would therefore clearly instruct us not to be anxious or troubled about anything, because He knows His Father and knows that it is completely safe to trust Him entirely? It is very striking that He so often said, “Your Father in heaven,” not only mine, but yours as well. “Your Father in heaven” cares for the birds of the air and the lilies of the field, and therefore will certainly care for you, who are of far greater value than many birds. How foolish it is, then, for us to be anxious and troubled about things, when Christ has told us that our heavenly Father knows that we need all these things! For being a good Father, He must, by His very nature, provide for us when He knows our needs. What is the matter with us that we do not understand this? Again, our Lord compares earthly fathers with our heavenly Father, not to show how much less good and loving our heavenly Father is, but how much more. “Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? ... how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:9–11) Can we imagine a good earthly father giving a stone or a serpent to a hungry child instead of bread or fish? Our hearts would recoil at such a thought. Yet many of God’s children seem to believe that their heavenly Father acts in such ways toward them, giving them stones when they ask for bread, or hardship when they ask for blessing. And some of these very people may belong to organisations that exist to protect children from cruelty—yet they have not considered the seriousness of accusing their heavenly Father of the very things they would condemn in earthly fathers. But our heavenly Father is not only willing to give us good things—He is far more than willing. Our Lord says, “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.” (Luke 12:32) There is no reluctance in His giving; it is His good pleasure to give. He delights in doing so. He desires to give you the kingdom far more than you desire to receive it. Those of us who are parents understand how eager we are to give good things to our children, often more eager than they are to receive them; and this helps us understand how it is God’s good pleasure to give us the kingdom. Why then do we approach Him with fear and hesitation, and why do we trouble ourselves with anxiety as though He might fail to provide what we need? There can only be one answer: we do not truly know the Father. We are described as being part of the “household of God.” Scripture teaches that if anyone does not provide for his own household, he has “denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.” (1 Timothy 5:8) Since we belong to the household of God, this principle applies to Him; and if He were to fail to provide for us, His own words would stand against Him. I say this with reverence, but also with clarity, because so few seem to have grasped it. In my own experience, there came a defining moment when I first understood this truth about the responsibility of my Father in heaven. It was as though, in a single instant, the burden of life was lifted from my shoulders and placed upon His, and all my fears, anxieties, and uncertainties were surrendered into the depth of His loving care. I realised that the natural human instinct which expects parents to care for their children is not merely cultural, but divinely implanted. It is meant to teach us that the Creator, who has made human parents responsible for their children, is Himself equally responsible for His children. I could have rejoiced greatly. From that moment, my burdens were turned into rest. For when this understanding comes to a person, that person must, by necessity, enter into rest. With such a God, who is at the same time a Father, there is no place for anything but rest. And whenever, since that joyful discovery, temptations to doubt, anxiety, or fear have arisen, I have refused to listen to them in light of what I have learned, because I recognise that to do so would be to question the reliability of my Father in heaven. We may have been used to thinking that our doubts and fears come from our own unworthiness and are a sign of humility. We may even have taken them as evidence of special piety and thought they were in some way pleasing to God. But if children, in their relationship with their earthly parents, allowed doubts about their parents’ love and feared that their care might fail, would those doubts and fears show true love and respect? Would they be pleasing to their parents? If God is our Father, the only thing we can do with doubts, fears, and anxious thoughts is to cast them behind us completely and refuse to entertain them again. We can do this.
