We can give up our doubts just as we would urge someone to give up a harmful habit. If we truly see that our doubts are a sin against God and question His trustworthiness, we will be eager to abandon them. We may have held on to our doubts before because we thought they were part of our faith and a fitting attitude for someone who feels unworthy. But if we now see that God truly is our Father, we will reject every doubt with horror, recognising it as a slander against His love and care. What more could any soul want than to have a God whose name is “our Father,” and whose character matches that name? As Philip said, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8). And indeed, it is enough—far beyond what words can express. A friend of mine once went to visit a poor woman living in one of the poorest parts of Philadelphia, whose situation had been reported as one of great need. She found things even worse than expected. The woman was old, crippled with rheumatism, and lived alone in a small, poor room, receiving only occasional help from a kind neighbour. Yet she was cheerful and full of gratitude. My friend was amazed that such joy could exist under such circumstances and asked, “Do you never feel afraid when you think about what might happen to you, living here alone and in such a condition?” The woman looked at her with surprise and said, “Afraid? Why, don’t you know I have a Father, and don’t you know He takes care of me all the time?” Then, seeing my friend’s confusion, she added gently, “Surely my Father is your Father too, and you know Him, and you know He always takes care of His children.” It was a lesson my friend never forgot. “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1). The love given to us is the love of a father for his child—a tender, protective love that understands our weakness and our needs and cares for us accordingly. He treats us as children, and all He asks in return is that we treat Him as a Father whom we can trust without anxiety. We must take the place of children—dependent and trusting—and allow Him to take the place of Father—caring and responsible. Because we are the children and He is the Father, we must let Him do the Father’s part. Too often, we take that role upon ourselves and try to care for and provide for our own needs. But no good earthly father would want his children to carry his responsibilities, and certainly our heavenly Father would not want us to carry His. No wonder we are told, “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Of course He cares for us—it is His role as Father. He would not be a good Father if He did not. All He asks is that we tell Him what we need and then leave the provision to Him. He promises that if we do this, “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7). Children of a good earthly father are at peace because they trust their father’s care. Yet the children of the heavenly Father often have no peace because they are afraid to trust Him. They may tell Him their needs, but only as a routine. They do not truly believe He will take care of them. And so they continue to carry their burdens as though they had no Father in heaven at all. What foolishness this is. If any earthly father is worthy of his children’s trust, how much more is our heavenly Father worthy of ours. The reason so few trust Him is either that they have not realised He is truly their Father, or that, although they call Him Father, they have never understood what that really means. The answer to your unrest is to become truly acquainted with the Father. “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). Is this spirit of adoption ruling in your heart, or is it the spirit of fear? Your peace depends entirely on this. No effort, struggle, or prayer can bring you rest while the spirit of adoption is absent. But you may ask how to receive this spirit. It is not something you obtain by effort. It comes naturally when you discover that God truly is your Father. When you realise this, you cannot help but think and act like a child—and that is what the spirit of adoption means. It is not mysterious; it is simply the natural result of finding a Father where you once thought there was only a Judge. The great need, therefore, is to make this discovery. To do this, we must listen to what Christ says about the Father and believe it. “Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony” (John 3:11). “The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works” (John 14:10). “Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true” (John 3:33). If we accept Christ’s testimony, we declare that God is true. If we reject it, we make Him a liar. “If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him” (John 14:7). We must decide that from now on we will believe His testimony and truly know the Father. For us, there must be “one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist” (1 Corinthians 8:6).

fields.title: Jehovah
fields.body_html:
“That they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth” (Psalm 83:18).

Among all the names of God, perhaps the most complete is Jehovah. This name means the self- existing One, “I AM.” It reveals what God is. At times, additional names are given to show specific aspects of His character: Jehovah-jireh — The Lord will provide.

Jehovah-nissi — The Lord is my banner.

Jehovah-shalom — The Lord is our peace.

Jehovah-tsidkenu — The Lord is our righteousness.

Jehovah-shammah — The Lord is there.

These names were discovered in times of need. When Abraham was about to sacrifice his son and saw no way out, God provided a lamb. Abraham then understood that God provides for His people.

This truth is repeated in the New Testament: “Your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32).

If God sees and knows our needs, He will certainly provide for them.

Over and over our Lord urges us not to be anxious, because God cares for us. “Your heavenly Father knows,” He says, “that you need them all.” (Holy Bible, Matthew 6:32). If the Lord sees and knows our need, it will naturally follow that He will provide for it.

Being our Father, He could not do otherwise. As soon as a good mother sees that her child needs anything, she immediately sets about supplying that need. She does not even wait for the child to ask; the sight of the need is enough. Being a good mother, she could not act differently. When God, therefore, says to us, “I am he who sees your need,” He is in reality also saying, “I am he who provides,” for He cannot see and fail to provide.

“Why do I not have everything I want, then?” you may ask. Only because God sees that what you want is not really what you need, but probably the exact opposite. Often, in order to give us what we need, the Lord must keep from us what we want. “Your heavenly Father knows what you need before you ask him.” (Matthew 6:8). You do not know; and if all your wants were granted, it might be that all your real needs would be left unmet. It ought surely to be enough for us that our God is Jehovah-jireh, the Lord who sees and therefore provides.

But I am afraid that many Christians today have never made Abraham’s discovery, and do not know that the Lord is truly Jehovah-jireh. They may trust Him to save their souls in the future, but they never imagine that He wants to carry their cares for them here and now. They are like a man I have heard of, with a heavy load on his back, who was given a lift by a friend and gladly accepted it. He climbed into the carriage but kept his burden on his back, sitting there bent under its weight. “Why do you not put your burden down on the floor of the carriage?” his friend asked.

“Oh,” replied the man, “it is already a great deal for you to carry me, and I could not ask you to carry my burden as well.” You may wonder how anyone could be so foolish, and yet are you not doing the same? Are you not trusting the Lord to take care of you, while still carrying your burdens yourself? Which is more foolish—that man or you?

Jehovah-nissi, that is, “The Lord my banner,” was a discovery made by Moses when Amalek came to fight against Israel at Rephidim, and the Lord gave Israel a great victory. Moses realised that the Lord was fighting for them, and he built an altar and called its name, “The Lord Is My Banner” (Exodus 17:15). The Bible is full of expressions of this truth. “The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name.” (Exodus 15:3). “The LORD your God who goes before you will himself fight for you.” (Deuteronomy 1:30). “The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.” (Exodus 14:14). “Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God’s.” (2 Chronicles 20:15). “God himself has been with us as our head.”

(2 Chronicles 13:12).

Nothing is more clearly shown in the Bible than this: the Lord will fight for us if we will only let Him. He knows that we have no strength against our spiritual enemies; and, like a tender mother when her helpless children are attacked, He fights for us. All He asks is that we remain still and allow Him to act. This is the only kind of spiritual conflict that ever succeeds. But we are slow to learn this. When temptations come, instead of handing the battle over to the Lord, we gather all our strength to fight them ourselves. We may believe that the Lord is nearby and will help if things become desperate; but for the most part, we feel that we must do all the fighting ourselves.

Our way of fighting usually consists of repeated repentance, making resolutions and promises, struggling hard for victory, and then failing again; followed by more repentance, more resolutions, more promises, and renewed struggle—over and over again. Each time we tell ourselves that now we will surely succeed, and each time we fail, often worse than before. This may continue for weeks, months, or even years, without any real or lasting deliverance.

But you may ask, “Are we not to fight at all?” Of course we are to fight, but not in this way. We are to fight “the good fight of the faith” (1 Timothy 6:12), and the fight of faith is not a struggle of effort, but a struggle of trust. It is like the fight of King Hezekiah, when he and his people faced their enemy and found that “when they began to sing and praise, the LORD set an ambush… so that they were routed” (2 Chronicles 20:22). Our part is to hand the battle over to the Lord and trust Him for the victory.

There is nothing here about promises or resolutions; nothing about hours or days of agonising struggles or bitter remorse. “In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Holy Bible, Ephesians 6:16). Above all, faith.

Faith is the one essential thing, without which everything else is useless. It means that we must not only hand the battle over to the Lord, but also leave it with Him, and have complete confidence that He will win.

This is where the real struggle lies. It feels unsafe to be still and simply trust the Lord, and the temptation to take the battle back into our own hands is often very strong. Keeping our hands off in spiritual matters is as difficult for us as it is for a drowning person to stop struggling against the one trying to rescue them. We all know how impossible it is to save someone who is drowning if they fight their rescuer, and it is just as impossible for the Lord to fight our battles for us when we insist on trying to fight them ourselves. It is not that He is unwilling, but that He cannot. Our interference hinders His work. Spiritual forces cannot operate while earthly efforts are taking over.

Our Lord tells us, “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and we have read and repeated these words many times; but does anyone truly believe them? If we were honest about our hidden thoughts, would we not find something like this: “When Christ said those words, He surely meant that we cannot do much on our own, or at least nothing great. But nothing at all— that cannot be right. We are not helpless children, and we are surely meant to use all the strength we have to fight our enemies; and when that strength fails, then we can ask the Lord for help.”

Despite all our failures, we still tend to think that if we just tried harder and persevered more, we could succeed in any situation. But we completely overlook the crucial truth that our natural abilities are of no use in spiritual matters or against spiritual enemies.

The grub of a dragonfly, living at the bottom of a pond, may be strong and well developed for its environment; but when it becomes a dragonfly, the abilities that helped it crawl through the mud are useless for flying in the open air. In the same way, just as our ability to walk on the ground would be useless if we needed to fly, our natural abilities are of no use in spiritual warfare. In fact, if we rely on them, they become real obstacles—just as trying to walk would hinder us if we were meant to float or fly.

We can see, then, that trusting in ourselves when facing spiritual enemies has serious consequences. It not only leads to failure, but ultimately leads to rebellion. Much of what is called “spiritual conflict” would be more accurately described as “spiritual rebellion”. God has told us to stop relying on our own efforts and to hand our battles over to Him, yet we refuse to obey. We do fight, but it is not a fight of faith; it is a fight of unbelief. The “wrestling” we are often proud of is not wrestling for God against His enemies, but wrestling against Him alongside His enemies. We allow doubts and fears to grow, and as a result we fall into darkness, turmoil, and inner struggle. Then we label this “spiritual conflict” and consider ourselves a special or unusual case. But the single word that explains this condition is unbelief, and the simple cure is faith.

You may ask about Jacob’s wrestling—did he not gain victory through struggle? In fact, he gained victory by becoming too weak to struggle any longer. It was not Jacob wrestling with the angel, but the angel wrestling with Jacob. Jacob was the one who needed to be overcome. When the angel saw that Jacob’s resistance was too strong to overcome, he touched his hip and put it out of joint; and then the victory was achieved. As soon as Jacob was too weak to resist, he prevailed with God. He gained strength when he lost it. He overcame when he could no longer fight.

Jacob’s experience reflects our own. The Lord wrestles with us to bring us to complete dependence on Him. We resist as long as we have strength, until at last He brings us to a place of helplessness where we must yield; and then we conquer through that very surrender. Our victory is always a victory of weakness. Paul understood this when he wrote: “But he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me… For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:9–10).

Who could ask for a more glorious victory than this?

And this victory will be ours if we take the Lord as our Banner and commit all our battles to Him. The name Jehovah-shalom, meaning “The Lord is peace,” was discovered by Gideon when the Lord called him to a task for which he felt completely unqualified. He said, “Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house” (Judges 6:15). And the Lord said to him, “But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man” (Judges 6:16)… “Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die” (Judges 6:23). Then Gideon believed the Lord; and although the battle had not yet been fought and no victory had yet been seen, by faith he saw peace already secured. He built an altar to the Lord and called it “The LORD Is Peace” (Judges 6:24).

Of all the needs of the human heart, none is greater than the need for peace, and none is more fully promised in the gospel. “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you… Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John 14:27). And again, “I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

We often think peace must come from outward calm—that all enemies must disappear and all troubles must end. But the Lord speaks of an inner peace that can exist even in the middle of turmoil and rise above it. The foundation of this peace is not that we have overcome the world, or ever could, but that Christ has overcome it. Only the conqueror can declare peace, and those for whom He has fought can only enter into it. They cannot create it or destroy it. But they can refuse to believe it, and so fail to let it rule in their hearts. You may hesitate to believe that Christ has made peace for you, and so continue in a restless state of conflict; yet He has already done it, and your continued struggle is unnecessary.

The Bible tells us that Christ Himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). Therefore, whether I feel peaceful or not, peace is already mine in Him, and I must take hold of it by faith. Faith simply believes and declares what God has said. If He says there is peace, faith affirms it and enters into it. If He has declared peace in Scripture, I must declare it in my own heart, regardless of appearances. “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17), and anyone who has not entered into peace has not yet fully entered into this kingdom.

In practice, we can always enter into peace by simply obeying Philippians 4:6–7: “do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus”. The steps are very clear, and there are only two: first, give up all anxiety; second, hand your cares over to God. Then remain firmly there— peace must come. It must, because nothing else can take its place.

The name Jehovah-tsidkenu, meaning “The Lord our righteousness,” was revealed by the Lord through the prophet Jeremiah when he spoke of the coming of Christ: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch… And this is the name by which he will be called: ‘The LORD is our righteousness’” (Jeremiah 23:5–6).

Greater than any other need is our need for righteousness. Most of the struggles and conflicts in our Christian life come from our battles with sin and our efforts to become righteous. And it hardly needs to be said how often we fail. As long as we try to overcome sin or gain righteousness by our own efforts, we are bound to fail. But if we discover that the Lord is our righteousness, we will have found the secret of victory.

In the Lord Jesus Christ we have a fuller revelation of this wonderful name of God. The apostle Paul, speaking as an ambassador for Christ, declares that “for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (Holy Bible, 2 Corinthians 5:21). And again he says, “And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

I am afraid that very few Christians truly understand what this means. We repeat these words as part of our religious language, and in a vague way think of them as belonging to Christ’s salvation; but what they really mean, or how they apply in daily life, we scarcely understand.

To me, this name of God—“The Lord our righteousness”—is of such practical importance that I want, if possible, to make it clear. It is not easy, and I cannot explain it theologically. But in experience, it seems to be like this: we are not meant to store up righteousness within ourselves, as if we could draw from it when needed. Instead, we are to receive a continual fresh supply as we need it from the righteousness that is stored up for us in Christ.

In other words, if we need any kind of righteousness—patience, humility, love—it is useless to look within ourselves, hoping to find it there, for we never will. Instead, we must simply take it by faith, as something already given to us in Christ, who is our righteousness. I may not be able to explain exactly how this works, but I know from experience that it does, and that the results are real and powerful. I have seen gentleness and kindness poured like sunlight into hearts that were once bitter and dark, when faith reached out to take them as a present possession in Christ. I have seen harsh words become gentle, anxious hearts become calm, and restless spirits become quiet through this simple act of faith—taking the righteousness that is ours in Christ.

The apostle, after showing in Romans chapter 3 that it is impossible for us to gain righteousness through the law—that is, through our own efforts—goes on to say: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law… the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction” (Romans 3:21–22).

It is faith, and faith alone, that receives this righteousness that is ours in Christ. Just as we receive forgiveness by faith, so we must also receive patience, gentleness, meekness, long- suffering, or any other virtue we need—by faith. Our own efforts cannot produce righteousness any more than they can produce forgiveness. And yet, how many Christians still try!

Paul describes such people when he says: “For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:2–4).

If only all such earnest souls could discover this wonderful name of God—“The Lord our righteousness”—and would stop trying to establish their own righteousness, and instead submit to the righteousness of God. The prophet tells us that even our best righteousness is like “a polluted garment” (Isaiah 64:6). And Paul expresses his desire to “be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith” (Philippians 3:9).

Do we truly understand what this means? And are we ready to embrace it with all our hearts? If so, our struggle to become righteous will come to an end. Jehovah-tsidkenu will meet every need.

The name Jehovah-shammah, meaning “The Lord is there,” was revealed to the prophet Ezekiel when he was shown in a vision, in the twenty-fifth year of the captivity, what would be the future home of the children of Israel. He described the land and the city of Jerusalem, and ended by saying: “And the name of the city from that time on shall be, The LORD Is There” (Ezekiel 48:35).

To me, this name includes all the others. Wherever the Lord is, everything must be right for His children. Where a good mother is, things go well for her children, as far as she is able to provide.

How much more is this true of God. His presence alone is enough.

We can all remember how, as children, the simple presence of our mother was enough for us. All the comfort, rest, and help we needed seemed assured just by her being there—sitting in her usual place with her work or her book—while we came to her with our troubles. If we could only realise that God’s presence gives the same assurance—only infinitely greater—a deep well of joy would open in our spiritual lives, driving out every trace of fear and distress.

All through the Old Testament, the Lord’s answer to the fears and anxieties of Israel was simply this: “I will be with you” (Exodus 3:12). Nothing more needed to be said. His presence was a complete guarantee that all their needs would be met; and once they were sure of it, they were no longer afraid to face even the fiercest enemy. You may say, “Ah, yes, if the Lord would only say the same thing to me, I should not be afraid either.” Well, He has said it, and He has said it in unmistakable terms. When the “angel of the Lord” announced to Joseph the coming birth of Christ, he said: “‘Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel’ (which means, God with us)” (Matthew 1:23). In this short sentence is revealed to us the grandest fact the world can ever know—that God, the Almighty God, the Creator of Heaven and earth, is not a far-off God, dwelling in a Heaven of unapproachable glory, but has come down in Christ to dwell with us right here in this world, in the midst of our poor, ignorant, helpless lives, as close to us as we are to ourselves. If we believe in Christ at all, we are forced to believe this, for this is His name, “God with us.”

Both these names then, Jehovah-shammah and Emmanuel, mean the same thing. They mean that God is everywhere present in His universe, surrounding everything, and sustaining everything, and holding all of us in His safe and blessed keeping. They mean that we can find no place in all His universe of which it cannot be said, “The Lord is there.” The psalmist says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me” (Psalm 139:7-10).

We cannot drift from the love and care of an ever-present God. And those Christians who think He has abandoned them, and who cry out for His presence, are crying out in ignorance of the fact that He is always and everywhere present with them. In truth, they cannot get out of His presence, even if they tried. Oh, that they knew this wonderful and satisfying name of God!

Speak to Him, for He hears; and spirit may meet with spirit; He is closer than breathing, and nearer than hands and feet.

Let us sum up, once more, the teaching of these five names of God. What is it they say to us?

Jehovah-jireh, i.e., “I am he who sees your need, and therefore provides for it.”

Jehovah-nissi, i.e., “I am the captain, and your banner, and he who will fight your battles for you.”

Jehovah-shalom, i.e., “I am your peace. I have made peace for you, and my peace I give to you.”

Jehovah-tsidkenu, i.e., “I am your righteousness. In me you will find all you need of wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption.”

Jehovah-shammah, i.e., “I am with you. I am your ever-present, all-encompassing God and Saviour. I will never leave you nor forsake you. Wherever you go, I am there, and there shall my hand hold you, and my right hand lead you.”

All this is true, whether we know it and recognise it or not. We may never have dreamed that God was such a God as this, and we may have gone through our lives until now starved, and weary, and wretched. But all the time we have been starving in the midst of plenty. The fullness of God’s salvation has awaited our faith; and “the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness” (Romans 5:17) have awaited our receiving.

I wish I could believe that for some of my readers all this was ended, and that from now on they would see that these all-embracing names of God leave no tiny corner of their need unsupplied.

Then they would be able to testify with the prophet to everyone around them: “Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the Lord God is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation. With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation” (Isaiah 12:2-3).
fields.body_text: “That they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth” (Psalm 83:18). Among all the names of God, perhaps the most complete is Jehovah. This name means the self- existing One, “I AM.” It reveals what God is. At times, additional names are given to show specific aspects of His character: Jehovah-jireh — The Lord will provide. Jehovah-nissi — The Lord is my banner. Jehovah-shalom — The Lord is our peace. Jehovah-tsidkenu — The Lord is our righteousness. Jehovah-shammah — The Lord is there. These names were discovered in times of need. When Abraham was about to sacrifice his son and saw no way out, God provided a lamb. Abraham then understood that God provides for His people. This truth is repeated in the New Testament: “Your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32). If God sees and knows our needs, He will certainly provide for them. Over and over our Lord urges us not to be anxious, because God cares for us. “Your heavenly Father knows,” He says, “that you need them all.” (Holy Bible, Matthew 6:32). If the Lord sees and knows our need, it will naturally follow that He will provide for it. Being our Father, He could not do otherwise. As soon as a good mother sees that her child needs anything, she immediately sets about supplying that need. She does not even wait for the child to ask; the sight of the need is enough. Being a good mother, she could not act differently. When God, therefore, says to us, “I am he who sees your need,” He is in reality also saying, “I am he who provides,” for He cannot see and fail to provide. “Why do I not have everything I want, then?” you may ask. Only because God sees that what you want is not really what you need, but probably the exact opposite. Often, in order to give us what we need, the Lord must keep from us what we want. “Your heavenly Father knows what you need before you ask him.” (Matthew 6:8). You do not know; and if all your wants were granted, it might be that all your real needs would be left unmet. It ought surely to be enough for us that our God is Jehovah-jireh, the Lord who sees and therefore provides. But I am afraid that many Christians today have never made Abraham’s discovery, and do not know that the Lord is truly Jehovah-jireh. They may trust Him to save their souls in the future, but they never imagine that He wants to carry their cares for them here and now. They are like a man I have heard of, with a heavy load on his back, who was given a lift by a friend and gladly accepted it. He climbed into the carriage but kept his burden on his back, sitting there bent under its weight. “Why do you not put your burden down on the floor of the carriage?” his friend asked. “Oh,” replied the man, “it is already a great deal for you to carry me, and I could not ask you to carry my burden as well.” You may wonder how anyone could be so foolish, and yet are you not doing the same? Are you not trusting the Lord to take care of you, while still carrying your burdens yourself? Which is more foolish—that man or you? Jehovah-nissi, that is, “The Lord my banner,” was a discovery made by Moses when Amalek came to fight against Israel at Rephidim, and the Lord gave Israel a great victory. Moses realised that the Lord was fighting for them, and he built an altar and called its name, “The Lord Is My Banner” (Exodus 17:15). The Bible is full of expressions of this truth. “The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name.” (Exodus 15:3). “The LORD your God who goes before you will himself fight for you.” (Deuteronomy 1:30). “The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.” (Exodus 14:14). “Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God’s.” (2 Chronicles 20:15). “God himself has been with us as our head.” (2 Chronicles 13:12). Nothing is more clearly shown in the Bible than this: the Lord will fight for us if we will only let Him. He knows that we have no strength against our spiritual enemies; and, like a tender mother when her helpless children are attacked, He fights for us. All He asks is that we remain still and allow Him to act. This is the only kind of spiritual conflict that ever succeeds. But we are slow to learn this. When temptations come, instead of handing the battle over to the Lord, we gather all our strength to fight them ourselves. We may believe that the Lord is nearby and will help if things become desperate; but for the most part, we feel that we must do all the fighting ourselves. Our way of fighting usually consists of repeated repentance, making resolutions and promises, struggling hard for victory, and then failing again; followed by more repentance, more resolutions, more promises, and renewed struggle—over and over again. Each time we tell ourselves that now we will surely succeed, and each time we fail, often worse than before. This may continue for weeks, months, or even years, without any real or lasting deliverance. But you may ask, “Are we not to fight at all?” Of course we are to fight, but not in this way. We are to fight “the good fight of the faith” (1 Timothy 6:12), and the fight of faith is not a struggle of effort, but a struggle of trust. It is like the fight of King Hezekiah, when he and his people faced their enemy and found that “when they began to sing and praise, the LORD set an ambush… so that they were routed” (2 Chronicles 20:22). Our part is to hand the battle over to the Lord and trust Him for the victory. There is nothing here about promises or resolutions; nothing about hours or days of agonising struggles or bitter remorse. “In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Holy Bible, Ephesians 6:16). We all know how impossible it is to save someone who is drowning if they fight their rescuer, and it is just as impossible for the Lord to fight our battles for us when we insist on trying to fight them ourselves. fields.title: The Lord is Good
fields.body_html:
“Oh, taste and see that the Lord is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!” (Psalm 34:8).

Have you ever asked yourself what you honestly think of God at the bottom of your heart— whether you believe Him to be a good God or a bad God? I expect the question will shock you, and you will be horrified at the suggestion that you could by any possibility think that God is a bad God. But before you have finished this chapter, I suspect some of you will be forced to acknowledge that, perhaps unconsciously but nonetheless truly, you have, by your doubts and your complaints, attributed to Him a character that you would be horrified to have attributed to yourself.

I shall never forget the hour when I first discovered that God was really good. I had, of course, always known that the Bible said He was good, but I had thought it only meant He was religiously good; and it had never dawned on me that it meant He was actually and practically good, with the same kind of goodness He has commanded us to have. The expression, “The goodness of God,” had seemed to me nothing more than a sort of heavenly statement, which I could not be expected to understand. And then one day I came across the words in my Bible reading, “Oh, taste and see that the Lord is good,” and suddenly they meant something.

The Lord is good, I repeated to myself. What does it mean to be good? What but this: living up to the best and highest that one knows. To be good is exactly the opposite of being bad. To be bad is to know the right thing and not do it, but to be good is to do the best we know. And I saw that, since God knows everything, He must know what is the best and highest good of all, and that therefore His goodness must necessarily be beyond question. I can never express what this meant to me. I had such a view of the real, actual goodness of God that I saw nothing could possibly go wrong under His care, and it seemed to me that no one could ever be anxious again.

And over and over, when appearances have been against Him, and when I have been tempted to question whether He had been unkind, or neglectful, or indifferent, I have been stopped in my tracks by the words, “The Lord is good”; and I have seen that it was simply unthinkable that a God who was good could have done the bad things I had imagined.

You shrink with horror, perhaps, from the suggestion that you could under any circumstances, even in the secret depths of your heart, attribute to God what was bad. And yet you do not hesitate to accuse Him of doing things which, if one of your friends did them, you would look upon as most dishonourable and unkind. For instance, Christians get into trouble; everything looks dark, and they have no sense of the Lord’s presence. They begin to question whether the Lord has abandoned them, and sometimes even accuse Him of indifference and neglect. They never realise that these accusations are the same as saying that the Lord does not keep His promises, and does not treat them as kindly and honourably as they expect all their human friends to treat them. If one of our human friends should abandon us because we were in trouble, we would consider such a friend to be very far from being good. How is it, then, that we can even for one moment accuse our Lord of such actions? No, dear friend, if the Lord is good—not just pious, but really good—it must be because He always, under every circumstance, acts up to the highest ideal of that which He Himself has taught us is goodness. Goodness in Him must mean, just as it does with us, living up to the best and highest He knows.

Practically, then, it means that He will not neglect any of His duties toward us, and that He will always treat us in the best possible way. This may sound like a cliché, and you may exclaim, “Why tell us this, for it is what we all believe?” But do you? If you did, would it be possible for you ever to think He was neglectful, or indifferent, or unkind, or self-absorbed, or inconsiderate?

Do not put on a righteous air and say, “Oh, but I never do accuse Him of any such things. I would not dare to.” Do you not? Have you never blamed Him for things you would be ashamed to do yourselves? How was it when that last painful disappointment came? Did you not feel as if the Lord had been unkind in permitting such a thing to happen to you, when you were trying so hard to serve Him? Do you never look upon His will as a tyrannical and bossy will that must be submitted to, of course, but that could not by any possibility be loved? Does it never seem to you a hard thing to say, “Your will be done”? But could it seem hard if you really believed that the Lord is good, and that He always does that which is good?

The Lord Jesus took great care to tell us that He was a good Shepherd, because He knew how often appearances would be against Him, and how tempted we would be to question His goodness. “I am the good shepherd,” He says in effect, “not a bad one. Bad shepherds neglect and abandon their sheep, but I am a good Shepherd, and never neglect nor abandon My sheep. I lay down My life for the sheep.” His ideal of goodness in a shepherd was that the shepherd must protect the sheep entrusted to his care, even at the cost of his own life; and He lived up to His own ideal. Now, can we not see that if we really believe that He is good—not in some mysterious, religious way, but in this common-sense, human way—we shall be brought into a place of great peace and comfort at once. If I am a sheep, and the Lord is a good Shepherd in the ordinary, common-sense definition of good, how utterly secure I am! How sure I may be of the best care in every respect! How safe I am for time and for eternity!

Let us be honest with ourselves. Have we never in our secret hearts accused the Lord of the characteristics that He has told us in Ezekiel are the marks of a bad shepherd? Have we not thought that He cared for His own comfort or glory more than He cared for ours? Have we not complained that He has not strengthened us when we were weak, or bound up our broken hearts, or searched for us when we were lost?

Have we not even actually looked upon our diseased, and helpless, and lost condition, as a reason why He would not any longer have anything to do with us? In what does this differ from if we should say out plump and plain, the Lord is a bad shepherd, and does not fulfill His duties to His sheep. You shrink in horror, perhaps, at this translation of your inward murmurings and complainings, but what else, I ask you, can they in all honesty mean? It is of vital importance now and then to drag out our secret thoughts and feelings about the Lord into the full light of the Holy Spirit, that we may see what our attitude about Him really is. It is fatally easy to get into a habit of wrong thoughts about God, thoughts which will insensibly separate us from Him by a wide gulf of doubt and unbelief.

More than anything else, more even than sin, wrong thoughts about God sap the foundations of our spiritual life, and grieve His heart of love. We can understand this from ourselves. Nothing grieves us so much as to have our friends misjudge and misunderstand us, and attribute to us motives we scorn. And nothing, I believe, so grieves the Lord. It is, in fact, idolatry. For what is idolatry but creating and worshipping a false God, and what are we doing but this very thing, when we allow ourselves to misjudge Him, and attribute to Him actions and feelings that are unkind and untrustworthy.

It is called in the Bible a speaking against God. “They spoke against God, saying, “Can God spread a table in the wilderness?” This seemed a very innocent question to ask. But God had promised to supply all their needs in the wilderness; and to ask this question implied a secret want of confidence in His ability to do as He had promised; and it was therefore, in spite of its innocent appearance, a real “speaking against” Him. A good God could not have led His people into the wilderness, and then have failed to “spread a table” for them; and to question whether He was able to do it was to imply that He was not good.

In the same way we are sometimes sorely tempted to ask a similar question. Circumstances often seem to make it so impossible for God to supply our needs, that we find ourselves tempted over and over to “speak against” Him by asking if He can. Often as He has done it before, we seem unable to believe He can do it again, and in our hearts we “limit” Him, because we do not believe His Word or trust in His goodness.

If our faith were what it ought to be, no circumstances, however untoward, could make us “limit” the power of God to supply our needs. The God who can make circumstances can surely control circumstances, and can, even in the wilderness, “furnish a table” for all who trust in Him.

There are many similar questions to be found in the Bible, each one throwing doubts upon the goodness of God, and each one, I am afraid, is a duplicate of questions asked by God’s children now.

“Is God among us or not?”

“Has God forgotten to be gracious?”

“Is God’s mercy clean gone forever?”

“Has God in anger shut up his tender mercies?”

“Do God’s promises fail forevermore?”

“O God, why hast thou cast us off forever?”

“Why have you made me this way?”

Let us consider these questions for a little, and see whether we can find any counterparts to them in our own secret questionings.

“Is God among us or not?”

He has declared to us in unmistakable terms, as He did to the children of Israel, that He is always with us, and will never forsake us; and yet when trouble comes, we begin, as they did, to doubt His Word and to question whether He really can be there. Moses called this, when the Israelites did it, “tempting the Lord,” and it deserves the same condemnation when we do it. No one can ask such a question without casting a doubt upon the truthfulness and trustworthiness of the Lord; and to ask it is, if we only knew it, to insult Him, and to libel His character. I know that it is, alas! a common question even among God’s own children, and I know also that many of them think it is only true humility to ask it, and that, for such unworthy creatures as they feel themselves to be, it would be the height of presumption to be sure of His presence with them.

But what about His own Word in the matter? He has declared to us in every possible way that He is with us, and will never leave us nor forsake us, and dare we “make him a liar” by questioning the truth of His Word? A good God cannot lie, and we must give up forever asking such a question as this. The Lord is with us as truly as we are with ourselves, and we have simply just got to believe that He is, no matter what the seeming may be.

“Has God forgotten to be gracious?”

To ask this question is to “speak against” Him as grievously as it would be to ask a good mother if she had forgotten her child. And yet the Lord Himself says: “Can a woman forget her sucking child? Yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.” Those of us who are mothers know very well how grieved and insulted we should feel if anyone should suggest the possibility of our forgetting our children; and we mothers at least, if no one else does, should be able to understand how such questioning must grieve the Lord.

“Is God’s mercy clean gone forever?” “Has God in anger shut up his tender mercies?”

To ask these two questions of a good God is to insult Him. It would be as impossible for His tender mercies to be shut up toward us, or for His mercy to go from us forever, as it would be for the tender mercies of a mother come to an end. The psalmist says: “The Lord is good to all, and his tender mercies are over all his works.” In the very nature of things this must be, because He is a good God, and cannot do otherwise.

“Do God’s promises fail forevermore?”

There come times in every Christian’s life when we are tempted to ask this question. Everything seems to be going wrong, and all God’s promises seem to have failed. But if we remember that the Lord is good, we shall see that He would cease to be good if such a thing could be. A man who breaks his promises is looked upon as a dishonorable and untrustworthy man; and a God who could break His, if one could imagine such a thing, would be dishonorable and untrustworthy also. And to ask such a question is to cast a stigma on His goodness, that may well be characterised as “speaking against God.” No matter how affairs may look, we may be sure of this, that because God is good no promise of His has ever failed, or can ever fail.

Heaven and earth may pass away, but His Word never.

“O God, why have you cast us off forever?”

It will be impossible for a good God to cast us off as it would be for a good mother to cast off her child. We may be in trouble and darkness, and may feel as if we were cast off and forsaken, but our feelings have nothing to do with the facts, and the fact is that God is good, and could not do it. The good Shepherd does not cast off the sheep that is lost, and take no further care of it, but He goes out to seek for it, and He seeks until He finds it. To suspect Him of casting us off forever is to wound and grieve His faithful love, just as it would wound a good mother’s heart is she should be supposed capable of casting off her child, let that child have wandered as far as it may. The thing is impossible in either case, but far more impossible in the case of God than even in the case of the best mother that ever lived.

“Why have you made me this way?”

This is a question we are very apt to ask. There is, I imagine, hardly one of us who has not been tempted at one time or another to “reply against God” in reference to the matter of our own personal make-up. We do not like our peculiar temperaments or our especial characteristics, and we long to be like someone else who has, we think, greater gifts of appearance or of talent. We are discontented with our make-up, both inward and outward, and we feel sure that all our failures are because of our unfortunate temperaments; and we are inclined to blame our Creator for having “made us this way.”

I remember vividly a time in my life when I was tempted to be very rebellious about my own make-up. I was a plain-spoken, energetic sort of an individual, trying to be a good Christian, but with no especial air of piety about me. But I had a sister who was so saintly in her looks, and had such a pious manner, that she seemed to be the embodiment of piety; and I felt sure I could be a great deal better Christian if only I could get her saintly looks and manner. But all my struggles to get them were useless.

My natural temperament was far too energetic and outspoken for any appearance of saintliness, and many a time I said upbraidingly in my heart to God, “Why hast thou made me thus?” But one day I came across a sentence in an old mystic book that seemed to open my eyes. It was as follows: “Be content to be what thy God has made thee”; and it flashed on me that it really was a fact that God had made me, and that He must know the sort of creature He wanted me to be; and that if He had made me a potato vine, I must be satisfied to grow potatoes, and must not want to be a rosebush and grow roses; and if He had fashioned me for humble tasks, I must be content to let others do the grander work. We are “God’s workmanship,” and God is good, therefore His workmanship must be good also; and we may securely trust that before He is done with us, He will make out of us something that will be to His glory, no matter how unlike this we may as yet feel ourselves to be.

The psalmist seemed to delight in repeating over and over again this blessed refrain, “for the Lord is good.” It would be worthwhile for you to take your concordances and see how often he says it. And he exhorted everyone to join him in saying it. “Let the redeemed of the Lord say so,” was his earnest cry. We must join our voices to his—The Lord is good—The Lord is good. But we must not say it with our lips only, and then by our actions give the lie to our words. We must “say” it with our whole being, with thought, word, and action, so that people will see we really mean it, and will be convinced that it is a tremendous fact.

A great many things in God’s divine providences do not look like goodness to the eye of sense, and in reading the Psalms we wonder perhaps how the psalmist could say, after some of the things he records, “for his mercy endureth forever.” But faith sits down before mysteries such as these, and says, “The Lord is good, therefore all that He does must be good, no matter how it looks, and I can wait for His explanations.”

A housekeeping illustration has often helped me here. If I have a friend whom I know to be a good housekeeper, I do not trouble over the fact that at housecleaning time things in her house may seem to be more or less upset, carpets up, and furniture shrouded in coverings, and even perhaps painting and decorating making some rooms uninhabitable. I say to myself, “My friend is a good housekeeper, and although things look so uncomfortable now, all this upset is only because she means in the end to make it far more comfortable than ever it was before.”

This world is God’s housekeeping; and although things at present look grievously upset, yet, since we know that He is good, and therefore must be a good Housekeeper, we may be perfectly sure that all this present upset is only to bring about in the end a far better state of things than could have been without it. I dare say we have all felt at times as though we could have done God’s housekeeping better than He does it Himself, but, when we realize that God is good, we can feel this no longer. And it comforts me enormously, when the world seems to me to be going all wrong, just to say to myself, “It is not my housekeeping, but it is the Lord’s; and the Lord is good, therefore His housekeeping must be good too; and it is foolish for me to trouble.”

A deeply taught Christian was asked by a despairing child of God, “Does not the world look to you like a wreck?

“Yes,” was the reply, in a tone of cheerful confidence; “yes, like the wreck of a bursting seed.”

Any of us who have watched the first sproutings of an oak tree from the heart of a decaying acorn will understand what this means. Before the acorn can bring forth the oak, it must become itself a wreck. No plant ever came from any but a wrecked seed.

Our Lord uses this fact to teach us the meaning of His processes with us. “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” John 12:24.

The whole explanation of the apparent wreckage of the world at large, or of our own personal lives in particular, is here set forth. And, looked at in this light, we can understand how it is that the Lord can be good, and yet can permit the existence of sorrow and wrong in the world He has created, and in the lives of the human beings He loves. It is His very goodness that compels Him to permit it. For He knows that, only through such apparent wreckage, can the fruition of His glorious purposes for us be brought to pass. And we whose hearts also long for that fruition will, if we understand His ways, be able to praise Him for all His goodness, even when things seem hardest and most mysterious.

The apostle tells us that the will of God is “good and acceptable, and perfect.” The will of a good God cannot help being “good”—in fact, it must be perfect’; and, when we come to know this, we always find it “acceptable”; that is we come to love it. I am convinced that all trouble about submitting to the will of God would disappear, if once we could see clearly that His will is good.

We struggle and struggle in vain to submit to a will that we do not believe to be good, but when we see that it is really good, we submit to it with delight. We want it to be accomplished. Our hearts spring out to meet it.

I worship thee, sweet Will of God!

And all thy ways adore; And, every day I live, I seem To love thee more and more.

I love to kiss each print where thou Hast set thine unseen feet: I cannot fear thee, blessed Will!

Your empire is so sweet.

Space fails me to tell all that I might of the infinite goodness of the Lord. Each one must “taste and see” for himself. And if he will but do it honestly and faithfully, the words of the psalmist will become true of him: “They shall pour forth the fame of your abundant goodness and shall sing aloud of your righteousness.” Psalm 145:7
