fields.title: Is God In Everything?
fields.body_html:
Recognizing God's presence in all aspects of life, including human actions and trials, is essential. Everything, even suffering caused by others, is part of God's plan and must be accepted as His will. By trusting in His sovereignty, believers can face difficulties with peace, knowing that God oversees all and uses even challenges for spiritual growth and triumph.

Amajor obstacle to living a life of total surrender is the difficulty of seeing God in everything.

People say, "I can submit to things from God. But, I cannot submit to man. "Most of my trials come through humans." Or, "It's fine to talk of trusting. But, when I commit a matter to God, man is sure to come in and mess it up. I can trust God, but I see serious problems with trusting men."”

This is no imaginary trouble. It is of vital importance. If it cannot be met, it makes faith an impossible, visionary theory. Nearly everything in life comes to us through human means. Most of our trials result from someone's failure, ignorance, carelessness, or sin. We know God cannot be the author of these things. Yet, unless He is the agent, how can we say to Him, "Your will be done"? Besides, what good is it to trust our affairs to God, if man can come in and disrupt them? And, how can we live by faith if we can't trust humans? They will have too much influence on our lives.

Moreover, things in which we can see God’s hand always have a sweetness in them which consoles while it wounds. But, man's trials are full of bitterness. So, we must see God in everything. We must accept all things as His direct gifts, with no second causes. We must be brought to this. Only then can we know a lasting experience of total abandonment and perfect trust. Our abandonment must be to God, not to man, and our trust must be in Him, not in any arm of flesh, or we shall fail at the first trial.

The question is, "Is God in everything? “Do we have scripture to accept everything from Him? It was caused by other factors."" I answer, unhesitatingly, yes. To the children of God, all comes from their Fath er's hand. It matters not who the apparent agents were. There are no “second causes” for them. The whole teaching of the Bible asserts and implies this. “Not a sparrow falls to the ground without our Father.” The very hairs of our head are all numbered. We are not to be careful about anything, because our Father cares for us. We are not to avenge ourselves, because our Father has charged Himself with our defence.

We are not to fear, for the Lord is on our side. No one can be against us, because He is for us. We shall not want, for He is our Shepherd. When we pass through the rivers, they shall not overflow us. When we walk through the fire, we shall not be burned. He will be with us. He shuts the mouths of lions, that they cannot hurt us. He delivers and rescues. He changes the times and the seasons; He removes kings and sets up kings. A man’s heart is in His hand, and, as the river of water, He turns it whithersoever He will.” "He rules over all the heathen kingdoms. In His hand is power and might. None can withstand Him."

He rules the raging of the sea; when the waves thereof arise, He stills them. He brings the advice of the unruly to mischief; He makes the devices of the people of no effect. Whatsoever the Lord pleases that does Him in heaven, and in earth, in the seas, and all deep places. If you see the poor oppressed and justice perverted, don't marvel. For there is one higher than the highest. He sees all. These are a part of His ways, but how little a portion is heard of Him? But the thunder of His power, who can understand?”

"Have you not known, have you not heard? The everlasting God, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, does not grow faint or weary. There is no searching of His understanding.

And this God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear. The earth may be removed. The mountains may be carried into the sea. The waters may roar and be troubled.

The mountains may shake with their swelling. I will say of the Lord, He is my refuge and my fortress, my God, in Him will I trust. Surely He shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noise of some pestilence. He shall cover me with His feathers, and under His wings shall I trust. His truth shall be thy shield and buckler. Do not be afraid of the terror by night, or the arrow that flies by day. Do not fear the pestilence that walks in darkness, or the destruction that wastes at noon.

“A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not c ome near you. You will only look with your eyes and see the recompense of the wicked. Because you have made the Lord your dwelling place, the Most High, who is my refuge, no evil shall be allowed to befall you, no plague come near your tent. For he will co mmand his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways.”

Psalms 91:7-11 These Scriptures, and others like them, settle, once and for all, the question of second causes in the lives of God's children. They are all under the control of our Father. Nothing can touch us except with His knowledge and by His permission. Man's sin may cause the action. So, it can't be called God's will. But by the time it reaches us, it is God's will. We must accept it as directly from His hands.

No man or group, no power on earth or in heaven, can touch the soul that abides in Christ. They must first pass through Him and get His permission. If God be for us, it matters not who may be against us; nothing can disturb or harm us, except He shall see that it is best for us, and shall stand aside to let it pass. An earthly parent’s care for his helpless child is a feeble illustration of this. If the child is in its father’s arms, nothing can touch it without that father’s consent, unless he is too weak to prevent it.

And even if this should be the case, he suffers the harm first in his own person, before he allows it to reach his child. If an earthly parent would thus care for his helpless child, how much more will our Heavenly Father! His love is infinite. His strength and wisdom are unfailing.

Some, even of God's children, doubt His love and care. They secretly blame Him for neglect they would not tolerate. But His care is far beyond human care. He counts the hairs on our heads and knows when a sparrow falls. He watches every small thing that affects His children's lives. He controls them all according to His will, no matter their origin.

The instances of this are numberless. Take Joseph. What could seem more a result of sin than his being sold into slavery? It was u tterly against God's will. And yet Joseph, in speaking of it, said, “ As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. ” Genesis 50:20.Now, do not be grieved or angry with yourselves for selling me. “ God sent me here to preserve life." To the eye of sense, it was surely Joseph's wicked brethren who had sent him into Egypt.

Yet, with faith, Joseph could say, "God sent me." His brothers had sinned. But by the time it reached Joseph, it was God's will. It was, though it didn't seem so at first, the greatest blessing of his life. So we see how the Lord can turn even man's anger to praise Him. And, how all things, even others' sins, shall work for good to those who love Him.

I learned this lesson, practically and experimentally, long before I knew the scripture. I was at a prayer meeting for scriptural holiness. A strange lady rose to speak. I wondered who she was, not knowing she would teach me a grand lesson. She said she had great difficulty in living a life of faith. The second cause that seemed to control everything about her caused it. Her confusion grew. She began to ask God to teach her the truth. Was he really in everything, or not?

After praying this for a few days, she had what she described as a vision. She thought she was in a dark place. Then, a body of light advanced towards her from a distance. It gradually surrounded and enveloped her and everything around her. As it approached, a voice seemed to say, “This is the presence of God; this is the presence of God.” This presence showed her all the great and awful things in life.

She saw fighting armies, wicked men, raging beasts, storms, and plagues. She saw every kind of sin and suffering. At first, she shrank back in terror. But, she soon saw that God's presence surrounded and enveloped each one of these. Not a lion could reach out its paw, nor a bullet fly through the air, except as His presence moved to permit it.

She knew that, if there were the thinnest of sheets of this glorious presence between her and the terrible violence, nothing could touch her. Not a hair on her head could be ruffled.

But, the presence must divide to let the evil through. Then, all the small annoyances of life flashed before her. She saw they were so wrapped in God's presence that nothing could touch her. Not a cross look, harsh word, or petty trial could reach her unless He let them through.

Her difficulty vanished. Her question was answered forever. God was in everything, and to her henceforth there were no second causes. She saw that her life came to her, day by day, and hour by hour, from His hand. It did not matter what seemed to control it. And, she never again found it hard to trust in His care. But if we focus on the seen things, we won't understand this secret. The children of God must "not look at the things which are seen: for the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal." If we could see His unseen forces around us, we'd feel safe. We would walk through this world in an unbreakable fortress. For "the angel of the Lord encamped round about them that fear Him, and delivered them."

We have a striking illustration of this in the history of Elisha. The king of Syria was at war with Israel.

His evil plans were foiled by a prophet. So, he sent his army to the prophet's city to capture him. We read, “He sent their horses and chariots and a great host; and they came by night and compassed the city about.” This was the seen thing. A nd the servant of the prophet, whose eyes had not yet been opened to see the unseen things, was alarmed. We read, "And when the man, God's servant, rose early and went forth, a host encompassed the city, with horses and chariots." His servant said, "Alas, my master, how shall we do?” But his master could see the unseen things, and he replied, “Fear not; for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.” And then he prayed, saying, “Lord, I pray thee, open his eyes that he may see.

The Lord opened the young man's eyes, and he saw. The mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha. The presence of God is the fortress of His people. Nothing can withstand it. At His presence, the wicked perish. The earth trembles. The hills melt like wax. The cities crumble. "The heavens also dropped, and Sinai itself was moved at the presence of God." Unless, of course, your God, in whom you trust, allows it. “He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. We long for some victory over sin and self, and we ask God to grant it to us.

His answer comes in the form of a trial, which He means shall be the chariot to bear us to the longed for triumph. We may either let it roll over us and crush us like an unstoppable force. If we accept the trial as from God and submit, it will be the best discipline. It will give us the patience we seek.

If the will of God is our will, and if He always has His way, then we always have our way also, and we reign in a perpetual kingdom. He who sides with God will win every time. Whatever the outcome, we can join the ap ostle's victory shout: “ But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains uplifted , because only through Christ is it taken away.”

(2Corinthians 2:14)
fields.body_text: Recognizing God's presence in all aspects of life, including human actions and trials, is essential. Everything, even suffering caused by others, is part of God's plan and must be accepted as His will. By trusting in His sovereignty, believers can face difficulties with peace, knowing that God oversees all and uses even challenges for spiritual growth and triumph. Amajor obstacle to living a life of total surrender is the difficulty of seeing God in everything. People say, "I can submit to things from God. But, I cannot submit to man. "Most of my trials come through humans." Or, "It's fine to talk of trusting. But, when I commit a matter to God, man is sure to come in and mess it up. I can trust God, but I see serious problems with trusting men."” This is no imaginary trouble. It is of vital importance. If it cannot be met, it makes faith an impossible, visionary theory. Nearly everything in life comes to us through human means. Most of our trials result from someone's failure, ignorance, carelessness, or sin. We know God cannot be the author of these things. Yet, unless He is the agent, how can we say to Him, "Your will be done"? Besides, what good is it to trust our affairs to God, if man can come in and disrupt them? And, how can we live by faith if we can't trust humans? They will have too much influence on our lives. Moreover, things in which we can see God’s hand always have a sweetness in them which consoles while it wounds. But, man's trials are full of bitterness. So, we must see God in everything. We must accept all things as His direct gifts, with no second causes. We must be brought to this. Only then can we know a lasting experience of total abandonment and perfect trust. Our abandonment must be to God, not to man, and our trust must be in Him, not in any arm of flesh, or we shall fail at the first trial. To the children of God, all comes from their Fath er's hand. It matters not who the apparent agents were. There are no “second causes” for them. The whole teaching of the Bible asserts and implies this. “Not a sparrow falls to the ground without our Father.” The very hairs of our head are all numbered. We are not to be careful about anything, because our Father cares for us. We are not to avenge ourselves, because our Father has charged Himself with our defence. When we pass through the rivers, they shall not overflow us. When we walk through the fire, we shall not be burned. He will be with us. He shuts the mouths of lions, that they cannot hurt us. fields.title: Growth
fields.body_html:
Believers' spiritual journey begins with surrender and trust, but true growth in grace continues beyond that. Scripture calls for ongoing development, as seen in 2 Peter 3:18, which encourages growth in grace and knowledge. Growth happens when believers are rooted in God's grace, allowing the Divine Husbandman to nurture them.

By abiding in God's presence and trusting His guidance, without relying on self-effort, believers will mature spiritually, becoming fruitful and strong, just like a tree planted by waters.

After a believer fully surrenders and trusts, they find a life of happy communion and peace. This raises the question, "Is this the end? “I answer emphatically “No, it is only the beginning.” But, this is so little understood that many oppose the faith advocates. They claim the advocates do not believe in growth in grace. They are to teach that the soul can reach a perfect state. There is no further advance beyond it. This teaching voids all the Scriptural calls for growth and development.

Since the opposite is true, I must, next, consider this subject. I want to, if possible, fully answer such objections. I also want to show the scriptural place and way for the soul to grow. The most quoted text is 2 Pet 3:18. It says, " But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen. " This text expresses our belief in God's will for us. It also reflects our belief that He has made it possible for us to experience it. We accept, in their fullest meaning, all commands and promises. They concern our growth into Christ in all things, until we are perfect, and measure up to His fullness.

We are glad that we don't always have to be like babies, needing milk. We may, by use and growth, become skilled in the word of righteousness. We should then be able to discern good from evil and need strong meat. And none would grieve more than we at the thought of an end to the Christian life.

There could be no advance beyond it. But, we believe in a growth that produces maturity. We believe in a development that, in fact, bears ripe fruit. We expect to reach the aim set before us, and if we do not, we feel sure there must be some fault in our growing. No parent would be satisfied if, year after year, their child remained a helpless babe. And no farmer would be pleased if his grain grew only to the blade, but never produced the ear or the full corn in the ear.

Growth, to be real, must be progressive. The days, weeks, and months must bring a maturity in the thing growing. But is this the case with a large part of that which is called growth in grace?

Doesn't the very Christian who longs for it, too often find that, at year's end, he is not as far in his Christian experience as at the beginning? His zeal, devotion, and separation from the world are not as complete as when his Christian life began.

I was urging a group of Christians to take an immediate, definite step into the Promised Land. A very intelligent lady interrupted me. She thought her words would completely rebut my argument. She exclaimed, "Ah! But, my dear friend, I believe in growing in grace.” “How long have you been growing?” I asked. “About twenty - five years,” was her answer. “And how much more unworldly and devoted to the Lord are you now than w hen you began your Christian life?” I continued, “Sadly!” was the answer. "I fear I am not nearly so much so." Her eyes opened to see that, at least, her growth had failed. It had done the opposite.

The trouble with her, and every other such case, is simply this, they are trying to grow into grace, instead of in it. They are like a rosebush. The gardener should plant it in the hard, stony path to grow into the flower-bed. But, it would reduce and wither instead of flourishing. The children of Israel wandering in the wilderness are a perfect picture of this sort of growing. They had traveled for forty years. They took many weary steps. They found little rest from their wanderings. Yet, at the end, they were no nearer the Promised Land than at the start. At Kadesh Barnea, they were at the land's borders.

A few steps would have taken them into it.

Upon ending their wanderings in the plains of Moab, they were at its borders. But now there was a river to cross, which there hadn't been at first. Their wanderings and fights in the wilderness had not won them an inch of the Promised Land. To possess this land, one must first be in it. To grow in grace, one must first be planted in it. But, once in the land, their conquest was very rapid. Once planted in grace, the soul will grow in one month more than in years in any other soil. For grace is a most fruitful soil, and the plants that grow therein are plants of a marvelous growth.

A Divine Gardener takes care of them. The Sun of Righteousness warms them. The dew from Heaven waters them. Surely, it is no wonder they bear fruit. "Some a hundred-fold, some sixty-fold, some thirty-fold." But, what does "growing in grace" mean? Few people understand what the grace of God is. So, it is hard to answer this question. To say that it is free, unmerited favor, only expresses a little of its meaning. It is God's wondrous, boundless love, poured out upon us without measure. It is not based on our worthiness, but on His infinite, unfathomable love. Its heights and depths surpass all knowledge. I sometimes think we change the meaning of "love" with God. We understand it well in its human use.

But, if ever human love was tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted; if it could bear and forbear; if it could gladly suffer for its loved ones; if it would pour itself out for their comfort and pleasure, then Divine love is far more so. It is infinitely more tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted. It is glad to bear and forbear, to suffer, and to lavish its best gifts on those it loves.

Take all the tenderness and love you know of, dear reader. Add the deepest love you have ever felt.

Then add the strongest love ever given to you. Next, pile on the love of all the world's loving hearts.

Now multiply it by infinity. You might then faintly glimpse the love of God in Christ Jesus. And this is grace. To be planted in grace is to live in love. It means to envelop yourself in it, steep yourself in it, and revel in it. It means to know nothing but love, and to grow in knowledge and faith in it. It means to trust it completely and have no doubt that it will order all things well.

To grow in grace is opposed to all self-dependence, to all self-effort, to all legality of every kind. It is to put our growing, as well as everything else, into the hands of the Lord and leave it with Him. We should trust our Husbandman. His skill and wisdom are perfect. So, we won't question His methods or His cultivation plan. It is to grow as the lilies or babes grow. To grow, without a care or anxiety. To grow by a life force that must grow. To grow because we live and must grow. To grow because He who planted us made us to grow.

Surely, this is what our Lord meant. He said, “And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?" Or, when He says again, “And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?" There is no effort in the growing of a child or of a lily. They do not toil or spin. They do not stretch or strain.

They make no effort to grow. They are not even aware that they are growing. But, by an inner life force, they grow. God's providence, a gardener, the sun, and the rain nurture them.

And the result is sure. Even Solomon, our Lord, says, in all his glory, was not arrayed like one of these.

Solomon's array cost much toil and gold, but the lily's cost none of these. We may toil to make ourselves beautiful spiritual garments. We may strain for spiritual growth. But we will achieve nothing. No man can add a cubit to his stature by thinking. Our efforts can't match the beautiful dress the great Husbandman gives His garden's plants. They grow under His care.

If I could make my readers see how helpless we are in growing, I believe it would relieve many lives.

Imagine a child obsessed with growing. He would not grow unless he tried to. He insisted on a combination of rope and pulleys to stretch himself to the desired height. He might, it's true, waste his days in a weary strain. But, there would be no change in the fact, "No man can add to his stature by thinking." His years of labor would be wasted if they did not hinder the longed-for end.

Imagine a lily trying to clothe itself in beauty. It stretched its leaves and stems to grow. It tried to manage the clouds and sunshine, to meet its needs. Yet, these two pictures show a truth. Many Christians want to grow. They know they should. They feel a deep instinct to grow. But, they try to do it by toiling and spinning. They wear themselves out with endless self-effort.

It is wear ying to watch. Grow, dear friends. But, please, grow in God’s way, the only true way. Be sure to be rooted in grace. Then, let the Divine gardener cultivate you in His own way.

Expose yourselves to His presence in the sunshine. Let the dew of heaven fall on you. Then, see what will happen. Leaves, flowers, and fruit must come in their season. Your Husbandman is a skilled one.

He never fails in His harvesting. Just don't hinder the shining of the Sun of Righteousness or the falling of the dew from Heaven. A very thin covering may block the heat or moisture. The plant may wither even in their midst. A slight barrier between your soul and Christ may cause you to fade like a plant in a cellar or under a bushel. Keep the sky clear. Open every part of you to receive the blessings our Divine Husbandman may bring.

Bask in the sunshine of His love. Drink in the waters of His goodness. Keep your face upturned to Him.

The gardener who tends the vine will care for its branches too. He will prune, purge, water, and tend them. They will grow and bear fruit that will last.

He controls the elements to ensure our rapid growth. Let me entreat of you, then, to give up all your efforts after growing, and simply to let yourselves grow. Leave it all to the Gardener, whose responsibility it is, and who alone can manage it. No difficulties in your case can baffle Him.

Nothing in your past can mar His perfect work. Not the limiting of your growth, the dryness of your life, or any deformity. If you will, put yourselves completely in His hands and let Him have His way with you. His own gracious promise to His backsliding children a ssures you of this. “ I will heal their apostasy ,” He says: “I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them.

I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily; he shall take root like the trees of Lebanon.

But, you know what your Lord meant when He said, “And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin"(Mathew 6:28 ).

Scripture calls for ongoing development, as seen in 2 Peter 3:18, which encourages growth in grace and knowledge. Growth happens when believers are rooted in God's grace, allowing the Divine Husbandman to nurture them. By abiding in God's presence and trusting His guidance, without relying on self-effort, believers will mature spiritually, becoming fruitful and strong, just like a tree planted by waters. After a believer fully surrenders and trusts, they find a life of happy communion and peace. This raises the question, "Is this the end? “I answer emphatically “No, it is only the beginning.” But, this is so little understood that many oppose the faith advocates. They claim the advocates do not believe in growth in grace. They are to teach that the soul can reach a perfect state. There is no further advance beyond it. This teaching voids all the Scriptural calls for growth and development. Since the opposite is true, I must, next, consider this subject. I want to, if possible, fully answer such objections. I also want to show the scriptural place and way for the soul to grow. The most quoted text is 2 Pet 3:18. It says, " But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen. " This text expresses our belief in God's will for us. It also reflects our belief that He has made it possible for us to experience it. We accept, in their fullest meaning, all commands and promises. They concern our growth into Christ in all things, until we are perfect, and measure up to His fullness. We are glad that we don't always have to be like babies, needing milk. We may, by use and growth, become skilled in the word of righteousness. We should then be able to discern good from evil and need strong meat. And none would grieve more than we at the thought of an end to the Christian life. There could be no advance beyond it. But, we believe in a growth that produces maturity. We believe in a development that, in fact, bears ripe fruit. We expect to reach the aim set before us, and if we do not, we feel sure there must be some fault in our growing. No parent would be satisfied if, year after year, their child remained a helpless babe. And no farmer would be pleased if his grain grew only to the blade, but never produced the ear or the full corn in the ear. Growth, to be real, must be progressive. The days, weeks, and months must bring a maturity in the thing growing. But is this the case with a large part of that which is called growth in grace? Doesn't the very Christian who longs for it, too often find that, at year's end, he is not as far in his Christian experience as at the beginning? His zeal, devotion, and separation from the world are not as complete as when his Christian life began. I was urging a group of Christians to take an immediate, definite step into the Promised Land. A very intelligent lady interrupted me. She thought her words would completely rebut my argument. She exclaimed, "Ah! But, my dear friend, I believe in growing in grace.” “How long have you been growing?” I asked. “About twenty - five years,” was her answer. “And how much more unworldly and devoted to the Lord are you now than w hen you began your Christian life?” I continued, “Sadly!” was the answer. The trouble with her, and every other such case, is simply this, they are trying to grow into grace, instead of in it. They are like a rosebush. The gardener should plant it in the hard, stony path to grow into the flower-bed. But, it would reduce and wither instead of flourishing. The children of Israel wandering in the wilderness are a perfect picture of this sort of growing. They had traveled for forty years. They took many weary steps. They found little rest from their wanderings. Yet, at the end, they were no nearer the Promised Land than at the start. At Kadesh Barnea, they were at the land's borders. A few steps would have taken them into it. Upon ending their wanderings in the plains of Moab, they were at its borders. But now there was a river to cross, which there hadn't been at first. Their wanderings and fights in the wilderness had not won them an inch of the Promised Land. To possess this land, one must first be in it. To grow in grace, one must first be planted in it. fields.title: Service
fields.body_html:
Christian service often starts as a burden, but through trust ing God’s will, it becomes a joy. As believers surrender their will to God, they find freedom and strength in serving Him. True service comes from yielding to God’s guidance, trusting Him for the results, and letting go of self-reflection. This life of faith brings rest, freedom, and power, as believers rely on God’s strength rather than their own.

Perhaps, no part of Christian experience knows a greater change than in service. This is upon entering into the life hid with Christ in God. In lower forms of Christian life, service can feel binding. It is often a duty, and a trial and a cross. At first, some things may bring joy. But, they become weary tasks. They are done faithfully, but with secret disinclination. There are many wishes, both confessed and unconfessed, that they need not be done, or at least, not so often. The soul finds itself saying, instead of the “May I” of love, the “Must I” of duty. The yoke, which was at first easy, begins to gall, and the burden feels heavy instead of light.

One dear Christian expressed it once to me in this way. "After my conversion," she said, "I was full of joy and love. I was so glad and thankful to do anything for my Lord. So, I eagerly entered every open door." But, as my early joy faded and my love cooled, I began to regret my eagerness. I found myself in services that were becoming very distasteful and burdensome. I could not give them up, since I had begun them. It would excite great remark. Yet, I increasingly longed to do so. I was expected to visit the sick, and pray beside their beds.

I was expected to attend prayer-meetings, and speak at them. I was expected to be always ready for every effort in Christian work. The weight of these expectations bowed me down continually. At last, it became unbearable to live the Christian life I had begun, and that everyone expected of me. I would have infinitely preferred to scrub all day on my hands and knees rather than endure my daily Christian work. I envied,” she said, “the servants in the kitchen, and the w omen at the wash- tubs.”

This may seem a strong statement. But, does it not evoke some of your own experiences, dear Christian?

Have you never gone to your work as a slave to his daily task, knowing it was your duty? You must do it. But, like a rubber ball, you bounced back to your real interests and pleasures the moment your work was done.

You know this was the wrong way to feel. You are ashamed of it, but you can't help it. You have not loved your work. If you could have, you would have gladly given it up. Or, if this does not describe your case, perhaps another picture will. You love your work in the abstract. But, in doing it, you find many cares and responsibilities. You have doubts about your ability. This makes it a heavy burden.

You go to it, weary and bowed down, before the work has even begun.

You also distress yourself about your work. You are troubled if the results are not what you want. This, too, is a constant burden. Now, the soul is entirely delivered from all these forms of bondage. It enters fully into the blessed life of faith. First, it delights in any service. It has surrendered its will to the Lord.

He works in it to desire and do His pleasure. The soul now wants to do what God wants. It is always nice to do what we want, no matter how hard or tiring it is. If a man is truly set on a thing, he will. He'll ignore the obstacles in his way. He'll laugh at the idea of any opposition or difficulties hindering him.

How many men have, gladly and thankfully, searched the earth for wealth or to fulfill their ambitions?

They scorned any thoughts of the cross connected with it! How many mothers have congratulated themselves on their sons' promotions to powerful government jobs? They have rejoiced. But, it may have meant years of separation and hardship for their dear ones. Yet, these men and their mothers would have called it an unbearable cross if Christ's service had required the same sacrifice of home, friends, and ease.

It is altogether the way we look at things, whether we think they are crosses or not. I am ashamed to think that any Christian would mourn for doing a thing for Christ, which a worldly man would do for money.

What we need in the Christian life is to get believers to want to do God’s will, as much as other people want to do their own will. And this is the idea of the Gospel. It is what God intended for us; and it is what He has promised. In describing the new covenant in Heb. 8:6- 13 “ But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises. Putting it into our minds is the same as God working in us to “For it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. ” (Philippians 2:13)It means we will want what God wills. We will obey His commands, not out of duty, but because we want to do what He wants. Nothing could possibly be conceived more effectual than this. We, a stiff-necked people by nature, always rebel against an outside law. But we embrace a law that springs up within us.

God's plan is to possess a man's inner self. He wants to control and manage his will, and work it for him. Then, obedience is easy and a delight. Service becomes perfect freedom. The Christian must exclaim, "This happy service!" Who could dream earth had such liberty?” Then, dear Christian, if you are in bondage, you must surrender your will to your Lord. Give Him complete control of it. Say, “Yes, Lord, YES !” To everything. Trust Him to work in you to will. To bring your wishes and affections into harmony with His lovely will. You, who find daily Christian living hard, will find that your Master will transform your bondage into the most delicious liberty!

Or, if you love His will in theory, but find it hard to do, there is deliverance in the wonderful life of faith. For in this life no burdens are carried, nor anxieties felt. The Lord is our burden-bearer, and upon Him we must lay off every care. He says, in effect, be careful for nothing, but just make your requests known to me, and I will attend to them all. Be anxious for nothing, He says, not even your service.

Above all, I should think, our service. We are utterly helpless in this. So, even if we were careful, it would not matter. What have we to do with thinking whether we are fit or not!

And in truth, if we only knew it, our chief fitness is in our utter helplessness. His strength can only be made perfect in our weakness. I can give you a convincing illustration of this.

They are usually strong, but they lack the skill to use that strength. So, they can’t do much. In the dumbbell exercises, this problem was very clear. They made all sorts of awkward movements.

Occasionally, they would move in time with the music and the teacher’s instructions, but most of the time, it was all out of sync .

And the reason was, not that she had more strength than the others, but that she had no strength at all. She could not close her hands over the dumb-bells, nor lift her arms. The master had to stand behind her and do it all. She yielded up her members as instruments to him, and his strength was made perfect in her weakness. He knew how to do those exercises. He had planned them. So, when he did them, they were done right. She did nothing but yield herself up utterly into his hands, and he did it all.

The yielding was her part, the responsibility was all his. It was not her skill that was needed to make harmonious movements, but only his. The question was not of her capacity, but of his. Her utter weakness was her greatest strength. If this shows our Christian life, it's no wonder. Then, too, if the work is His, the responsibility is His, and we have no room left for worrying about it.

Everything in reference to it is known to Him, and He can manage it all. Why not leave it all with Him then, and consent to be treated like a child and guided where to go. They ask Him to guide them and trust Him for the wisdom and strength they need, moment by moment.

You will wonder how any of God's workers can dare to bear burdens or responsibilities that He alone can bear.

There are one or two other bonds of service from which this life of trust delivers us. We find out that we are not responsible for all the work in the world. The commands cease to be general, and become personal and individual.

The Master does not map out a general course of action for us and leave us to get along through it by our own wisdom and skill as best we may. He leads us step by step, giving us each hour the special guidance needed for that hour.

His blessed Spirit in us brings to mind, when needed, the command. So, we need not think ahead. We should simply take each step as it is revealed to us, following our Lord wherever He leads. “The steps of a good man are ordered of the Lord, ” not his way only, but each separate step in that way. They think, because He tells them to give a tract to one person on a train, that they must always give tracts to everyone. They burden themselves with an impossible command.

Once, a young Christian met a soul on a walk. The Lord had sent her to deliver a message. She took it as a command to speak to everyone she met about their souls. This was, of course, impossible, and as a consequence, she was soon in hopeless bondage about it. She was terrified to go outside. She lived in constant shame.

At last, she told her distress to a friend. This friend, a servant of God, said she was mistaken. The Lord has a special work for each worker. In a well-run household, each servant must not try to do the others' work. The same goes for the Lord's servants. They are not obliged to do everything. He told her to seek the Lord's guidance on her work. She should trust Him to show her whom to speak to. He assured her that He guides His own sheep. He goes before them and makes a way for them.

She followed this advice. She laid her work on the Lord. The result was a happy path of daily guidance.

She was led into much blessed work for her Master. She did it all without a care, for He prepared the way before her. Trusting God is like connecting the machinery to the steam engine. The power is not in the machinery, but in the steam. The machinery is useless, disconnected from the engine. But if you connect them, the machinery will run easily. It has great power behind it. So, the Christian life becomes easy and natural. It develops the divine work within.

Most Christians are tense. Their wills clash with God's. The connection is not perfect. It takes effort to move the machinery. But when the connection is made, the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus can work in us with all its power. We are then free from the law of sin and death. We shall know the glorious liberty of the children of God. We shall lead frictionless lives.

One of these is sure to come. Of the two, I dread the first more. The last causes greater suffering at the time. But in the life of trust, neither will trouble us. We have committed ourselves and our work to the Lord. We will be satisfied to leave it to Him and not think about ourselves at all.

Years ago, I found this sentence in an old book: "Never indulge, at the end of an action, in any self- reflection, whether of self-congratulation or despair." Forget the things that are behind, the moment they are past. Leave them with God.” It has been of unspeakable value to me. When the temptation comes, as it always does, to indulge in these reflections, I turn from them at once. I refuse to think about my work at all. I leave it to the Lord to overrule the mistakes and bless it as He chooses.

In short, for happy and effective service, just trust your work to the Lord and leave it there. Do not pray, "Lord, guide me; give me wisdom; arrange for me." Then, rise from your knees and take back the burden. Don't try to guide and arrange for yourself. Leave it with the Lord, and remember that what you trust to Him, you must not worry over nor feel anxious about. Trust and worry cannot go together.

If your work is a burden, it is because you are not trusting it to Him. If you trust it to Him, you will find the yoke He puts on you is easy. The burden He gives you is light. Even amid a life of ceaseless activity, you will find rest for your soul.

But some may say that this teaching would make us into mere puppets. I answer, No, it would simply make us into servants. A servant must not plan, arrange, decide, or supply materials. He must only obey. It is for the Master to do all the rest. The servant is not responsible, either, for results. The Master alone knows what results he wished to have produced, and so he alone can judge of them. Intelligent service must, of course, sympathize with the Master's plans. But, there cannot be a full understanding.

The Master cannot shift his responsibility to the servant. With our limited view and great ignorance, we can do little but accept God's will. We shouldn't expect to fully understand it. We must leave all results to Him.

What seems like failure on the surface is often, on the unseen side, a great success. If we allow ourselves to lament and worry, we will be foolish. We should be singing and rejoicing, not weeping. It is far better to avoid all self-reflection. We should not think about ourselves at all, whether for good or ill.

We are not our own property, nor our own business. We belong to God. We are His instruments and His business. He always attends to His own business. So, He will, of course, attend to us.

I once heard of a slave on a ship during a violent storm. While everyone else was scared, he whistled happily. Finally, someone asked if he was afraid of drowning. He smiled and said, "Well, maybe I am.

May God quickly raise such an army! And may you, my dear reader, enroll in this army today. Yield yourself to God as one alive from the dead. May every part of you be His instrument of righteousness, to be used by Him as He wishes.

fields.title: Difficulties Concerning Guidance
fields.body_html:
Believers are encouraged to trust in God's promised guidance, despite struggles with doubts about His will. God speaks through Scripture, the Holy Spirit's impressions, personal judgment, and providential circumstances. These must align to confirm His will. The chapter warns against self-deception and stresses testing impressions with Scripture and common sense. Ultimately, believers are urged to trust God’s wisdom and act promptly on His guidance while avoiding doubt.

You have now begun, dear reader, the life of faith. You have given yourself to the Lord, to be His wholly. He has taken you and begun to mold you into a vessel of His honor. Your deepest desire is to be very flexible in His hands. You want to follow Him wherever He may lead you.

You trust Him to work in you to will and to do of His good pleasure. But you find a great difficulty here. You do not know the voice of the Good Shepherd. So, you are in doubt about His will for you.

God is calling you to certain paths. Your friends express strong disapproval. And, these friends may be older than you in the Christian life. They seem much more advanced, too. You can hardly bear to differ from or distress them. You also feel very unsure about yielding to any duty they might disapprove of.

Yet, you cannot shake these impressions. You plunge into doubt and unease. There is a way out of all these difficulties, to the fully surrendered soul. I would repeat, fully surrendered. Any will to resist makes it hard to know God's mind on that point. So, first, ensure you truly want to obey the Lord in all respects. If this is the case, your soul only needs to know God's will to consent to it.

Then, you cannot doubt His desire to make it known and to guide you.

There are many very clear promises in reference to this. Take, for instance, John 10:3- 4 “To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, when he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. ” John 14:26: But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you." Also, James 1:56: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. ” With such passages as these, and many more like them, we must believe that Divine guidance is promised to us, and our faith must confidently look for and expect it.

This is essential; for in James 1:6- 7, we are told, “ But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord .

First, settle this point. Divine guidance has been promised. You will surely have it if you ask for it.

Let no doubt turn you from this.

Next, remember that our God has all knowledge and wisdom. Therefore, He may guide you to paths where great blessings await you. But, to the short-sighted human eyes around you, those paths may seem to lead to confusion and loss.

You must accept that God's thoughts and ways differ from man’s . Only He, who knows the end from the beginning, can judge the results of any action. You must realize that His love for you may lead you to go against your dearest friends' wishes.

You must learn from Luke 14 and similar passages, “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’ Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.” ( Luke 14:26-33.)

To be a disciple of your Lord, you may need to forsake all you have. You may have to turn your back on your family, or even your own life. If this is not clearly recognized, the soul may suffer. Often, a child's path of obedience will displease those he loves most. If he cannot trust the Lord through this, he will be lost.

Of course, this is in harmony with our duties of honor and love to one another in our various life relationships. The closer we are to Christ, the more we will show His meekness and gentleness. We will also be tender to our natural guardians and counselors. The Master's guidance will always show itself by the Master's Spirit. If, in obeying Him, we act against our friends' wishes, our love and patience will prove our motive. But, this point settled, we now ask how God's guidance will come to us. How shall we know His voice?

There are four special ways God speaks: 1. the voice of Scripture, 2. the inward impressions of the Holy Spirit, 3. our higher judgment, and 4. providential circumstances. If these four align, it is safe to say that God speaks. I lay it down as a principle, which none can dispute. His voice will always be in harmony with itself, no matter how many ways He may speak.

The voices may be many, the message can be but one. If God tells me in one voice to do or to leave undone anything, He cannot possibly tell me the opposite in another voice. If there is a contradiction in the voices, the speaker cannot be the same.

My rule for distinguishing the voice of God is to test it against this harmony. If I have an impression, I must check if it aligns with Scripture. I must also see if my higher judgment approves it, and, as we Quakers say, if "way opens" to carry it out. If either test fails, it is not safe to proceed. I must wait in quiet trust until the Lord shows me the point of harmony. He will, if it is His voice that has spoken. For we must not overlook the fact that there are other voices that speak to the soul. There is the loud and clamoring voice of self that is always seeking to be heard. And there are the voices of evil, deceiving spirits. They lie in wait to entrap every traveler who enters these higher regions of the spiritual life.

In the same epistle which tells us that we are seated in “ and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus , ” (Eph. 2:6) , we are also told that we shall have to fight there with spiritual enemies. “ For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.” (Eph. 6:12). These spiritual enemies, whoever they are, must communicate with us through our spiritual faculties. Their voices, therefore, will be, like God's, an inward impression on our spirits.

So, just as the Holy Spirit may tell us, by impressions, the will of God, so will these spiritual enemies.

They will, by impressions, tell us their will, though not giving their name. It is plain, therefore, that we need a test. We must try these inner impressions. It is to know whose voice is speaking. And that test will always be the harmony to which I have referred. In a misguided attempt to honor the Divine Spirit, some earnest Christians have ignored and even violated the Bible. They have disregarded clear signs from Providence and outraged their own better judgment. God, who sees their sincere hearts, can and does forgive. But, the consequences in this life are often very sad.

We must first test any voice claiming to be divine. It must align morally with God's mind and will, as revealed in the Gospel of Christ. Whatever is contrary to this, cannot be Divine, because God cannot contradict Himself. We cannot expect a direct revelation until we seek and obey God's will, as revealed in the Bible. A great many fatal mistakes are made in this matter of guidance, by the overlooking of this simple rule. If our Father has given us clear directions, He won't reveal anything more. No man needs or could expect a direct revelation to tell him not to steal. God has already, in the Scriptures, plainly declared His will about it. It seems so obvious that I would not mention it. But, I have met Christians who overlooked it and became fanatical.

For the Scriptures are far more explicit even about details than most people think. And there are not many important affairs in life for which a clear direction may not be found in God’s book.

Take the matter of dress, and we have 1 Pet. 3:3- 4 “ Do not let your adorning be external — the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear — but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is very precious .” and 1 Tim. 2:9 - 10 “ likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness —with good works.”

Take the matter of conversation, and we have Eph. 4:29 “ Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear . ” , and 5:4 “ Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving .” Take the matter of avenging injuries and standing up for your rights, and we have (Romans.12:19- 21) “ Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.” To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will hear burning coals on his head.” Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good ,” and (Matthew. 5:38 - 48) “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also.

And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you. You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

“ For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God. For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps .”(1Peter.

2:19-21) Take the matter of forgiving one another, and we have (Ephesians.4:32) “ Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.”

Mark 11:25- 26 “And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses .” Take the matter of conformity to the world, and we have (Romans 12:20) “ Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. ” and (1 John 2:15- 17) “ Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world — the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life — is not from the Father but is from the world. And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.

“ You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God?

Therefore, whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.”(James 4:4) Take the matter of anxieties of all kinds, and we have (Matthew 6:25- 34) “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Isn't life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? And which of you, by being anxious, can add a single hour to his span of life?

And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore, do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’

or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. “Therefore , do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.

“ Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.”( Philippians 4:6-7) I only give these as examples to show how very full and practical the Bible guidance is. If you are confused, first, check if the Bible addresses your question. Ask God to reveal His will to you through the Scriptures. And whatever shall seem to you to be plainly taught there, that you must obey. Reading and meditating on this record of God's mind and will enlightens us. The inspiring Spirit will do so. Our obedience will then be, as if, a present, living word. It will be as if our Lord spoke it to us today from Heaven. The Bible is an ancient message from God, sent to us long ago. It is also a present message, sent to us now each time we read it.

"My words are spirit and life. You must obey them. It's a command, personal and present." But we must remember, the Bible is a book of principles. It is not a group of unrelated sayings . Isolated texts may be used to sanction things. These are opposed by Scripture's principles.

I recently heard of a Christian woman at a Western meeting. The text, "For we walk by faith, and not by sight," brought it to mind. She felt it was a command to be literally obeyed. So, she blindfolded herself and insisted on walking up and down the aisle to illustrate the walk of faith. She soon stumbled and fell against the stove, burning herself. Then, she wondered at the mysterious dispensation.

Applying Scripture and her common sense would have saved her from the delusion.

The second test, therefore, is our own higher judgment, or common sense. It is as true now as in Solomon's time. A "man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels." His exhortation still binds us: "Get wisdom, the principal thing. “Wi th all you're getting, get understanding." The Scriptures say it is vital for God's children to use all their abilities on their journey through this world. They are to use their outward faculties for their outward walk, and their inward faculties for their inward walk. They might as well expect to be "kept" from stubbing their toes if they walk blindfolded. It's the same as expecting to be "kept" from spiritual stumbling if they ignore their judgment and common sense.

I asked a "sound mind" Christian how she told false spirits from the Holy Spirit. She replied, "I rap them over the head and see if they have any common sense." Some may say, "But we should not depend on our human understanding in divine things." I answer that we should not depend on our unenlightened understanding. We should rely on our judgment and common sense, which the Spirit of God has enlightened. That is, God will speak to us through the faculties He has Himself given us, and not independently of them. We must use our eyes when we walk, no matter how faithful we are.

Similarly, we must use our minds in our inner lives.

The third and last test is that of providential circumstances. If a “leading” is of God, a way will always open for it. Our Lord assures us of this in John 10:4. It says, “When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. ” Notice here the expressions “goes before,” and “ follows .” He goes before to open a way, and we are to follow in the way thus opened. A Christian should not force his way and trample opposition. That is never a sign of a Divine leading. If the Lord “goes before” us, He will open all doors for us, and we shall not need ourselves to hammer them down.

The fourth point is this: We must test our impressions by the other three voices. We must also test those voices by our inward impressions. If we feel a "stop in our minds" about anything, we must wait until it is removed before acting. A Christian, who had quickly advanced in the Divine life, gave me this secret: "I always mind the checks." We must not ignore our inner voice, nor ride roughshod over it, any more than we must the other three voices of which I have spoken.

These four voices, then, will always be found to agree in any truly Divine leading. The voice of our impressions, the voice of Scripture, the voice of our own sanctified judgment. The voice of providential circumstances. If these four do not agree at first, we must wait until they do.

A divine sense of “oughtness,” derived from the harmony of all God’s various voices, is the only safe foundation for any action. I have guarded the points of danger. So, please let me out. I long for the joy of this direct communication of God's will to us. It seems to me to be the grandest of privileges. In the first place, that God should love me enough to care about the details of my life is perfectly wonderful.

And that He would tell me all about it. And, to know how to live and walk to perfectly please Him, seems almost too good to be true.

We never care about the little details of people’s lives unless we love them. We don't care what most people do or how they spend their time. But when we love someone, we start to care. God's care for us proves His love. It's a great blessing that He speaks to us about everything in our lives. This includes our duties, pleasures, friendships, and all we do, think, or say.

You must know this in your own experience, dear reader. Only then will you find the joy and privilege of a life hid with Christ in God. It is one of its most precious gifts. God promises to work in us to will and to do of His good pleasure.

This means He will take control of our will and work it for us. His suggestions will come to us as desires, not commands. They will originate in our will; we shall feel as though we wanted to do so and so, not as though we must. This makes it a service of perfect liberty. For it is always easy to do what we desire, no matter how difficult the circumstances. Every mother knows she could get perfect obedience from her child. She just needs to control his will, making him want to do what she wants.

And this is what our Father does for His children in the new dispensation.

He writes His laws on our hearts and minds. We love them. Our affections and judgment, not our fears, draw us to obey. The Holy Spirit usually guides by impressing a desire to do or avoid certain things.

In prayer, the soul feels a sudden suggestion about a duty. “I would like to do this or the other,” it thinks, “I wish I could.” Or the suggestion may come as a question, “I wonder whether I had not better do so and so?” Or it may be only at first in the way of a conviction that such is the right and best thing to be done. The matter should be committed to the Lord. We must instantly choose to obey Him. If the suggestion agrees with the Scriptures, a holy judgment, and the circumstances, we should obey it.

Immediate obedience is the safest and easiest course. When the Spirit speaks, it is easy to obey. But if the soul hesitates and reasons, it becomes harder to obey.

The first convictions are usually right in a fully surrendered heart. God is faithful and will make His voice heard above all others. Such convictions, therefore, should never be met by reasoning. Prayer and trust are the only safe attitudes of the soul. But even these should be brief.

We must act before the time passes and we miss the blessing.

If the suggestion is unclear and doubt arises, we should wait for further insight. This is especially true if our friends disagree. The Scripture rule is, “Whatsoever is not of faith is sin” which means plainly that we must never act in doubt. A clear conviction of right is the only safe guide. But we must wait in faith. We must fully surrender, saying, "Yes," to our Lord's will, whatever it may be.

Our troubles stem from a lack of will. Next, many doubt any real Divine guidance. God's children are very skeptical here. They read the promises and feel the need. But, they cannot believe that someone will guide them.

It's as if God wants us to obey His voice, but didn't know how to make us hear and understand Him. It is, thus, very possible for God to speak, but for the soul not to hear, because it does not believe He is speaking. No earthly parent or master could guide his children or servants if they did not believe him or accept his voice as his true will. God, who spoke to the fathers in many ways, still speaks. He wants to see if any souls will obey His will.

Every moment of our lives our Father is seeking to reveal Himself to us. “ Jesus said to her, “I who speak to you am he.”(John 4:26) I that speak in your heart, in your circumstances, in your losses, in your gains, in your sorrows, and in your joys, am He. "I speak everywhere and in everything." So, we must have perfect faith that the Lord's voice is speaking to us. It will teach and lead us. He will give us wisdom for our guidance. After asking for guidance, we must follow our strongest sense of what we should do. A few rules can help us with this.

I. We must believe that God will guide us.

II. We must surrender our own will to His guidance.

III. We must hearken for the Divine voice.

IV. We must wait for the divine harmony.

When we are certain of God’s guidance, we must follow it without hesitation. He is our t rue home. The path may be difficult and narrow, but nothing else can satisfy a heart that longs for Him. How little of that path you have walked, my soul! Take courage, and let the thought of God draw you further. The perfect way may be hard for the flesh, but it is not hard for love. If you were desperate for God, how quickly you would move toward Him.

Do not give your duties to God reluctantly — let your hands be open and free. Fix your eyes on Jesus and consider how freely He gave His love to you. True perfection requires only a heart that remains at peace throughout the day, listening for the Spirit’s voice moment by moment. Keep your conscience sensitive — do not ignore His quiet nudges. And go wherever His grace leads you.
