They were one with Him, their very indwelling Life. Henceforth, He was to them Christ within. He worked in them to will and to do of His good pleasure. He, by the law of the Spirit of His life, delivered them from the bondage to the law of sin and death, under which they had been held. No longer was it between themselves and Him, a war of wills and a clashing of interests. One will alone animated them, and that was His will. One interest alone was dear to them, and that was His. They were made ONE with Him. Surely, all can recognize this picture. But the final stage may not be fully reached. You may have left much to follow Christ, dear reader. You may have believed in, worked for, and loved Him. Yet, you may not be like Him. Allegiance, you know, and confidence you know, but not yet union. There are two wills, two interests, two lives. You have not yet lost your own life that you may live only in His. Once it was I and not Christ. Then it was I and Christ. Perhaps now it is even Christ and me. But has it come to be Christ only, and not I at all? Perhaps you do not understand what this oneness means. Some believe it is a great emotion or a feeling of oneness. They turn inward, examining their emotions. They hope to find, in these, their union with God. But nowhere is the mistake of trusting to feelings greater than here. Oneness with Christ must, by nature, mean a Christ-like life and character. It is not what we feel, but what we are that settles the question. No matter how strong our feelings, there can be no oneness without a likeness of character with Christ. We must share a unity of aim, purpose, and thought. Our actions must be similar, too. This is common sense, and it is Scriptural too. We say two people are one. We mean their purposes, actions, thoughts, and desires are alike. A friend may express great love and unity. But if their aims, actions, and views are the opposite of ours, we can't feel any real oneness. This is true despite our affection for each other. To be truly one with another, we must share everything. Our likes and dislikes, joys and sorrows, hopes and fears, must all be the same. As someone says, we must look through one another’s eyes, and think with one another’s bra ins. This is, as I said above, only plain common sense. And oneness with Christ can be judged by no other rule. It is out of the question to be one with Him in any other way than in the way of nature, character, and life. Unless we are Christ-like in our thoughts and our ways, we are not one with Him, no matter how we feel. I have seen Christians with few Christ- like traits. They were so emotional and ecstatic in their love for Christ that they believed they were justified in claiming a close oneness with Him. I scarcely know a sadder sight. Surely our Lord meant to reach such cases when He said, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.” (Mathew 7:21.) He w as not making here any arbitrary statement of God’s will, but a simple announcement of the nature of things. Of course it must be so. It is like saying, “No man can enter the ranks of astronomers who is not an astronomer.” Emotions will not make a man an a stronomer, but life and action. He must be one, not merely feel that he is one. There is no escape from this inexorable nature of things, and especially here. We must be one with Christ in character, life, and action. If not, we cannot be one with Him in any other way. There is no other way. We must be "partakers of His nature" to share His life. His life and His nature are one. But emotional souls do not always see this. They feel so near to Christ and so united to Him that they think it must be real. They overlook the need for a Christ-like character and walk. So, they build their hopes on their delightful emotions and exalted feelings. They believe they must be one with Him to have such rich, holy experiences. It is a fact that other causes can produce these emotions. They are not solely due to a divine influence. The emotions depend largely on temperament and physical conditions. It is most dangerous, therefore, to make them a test of our spiritual union with Christ. It may result in just such a grievous self-deception as our Lord warns against in (Luke 6:46-49): “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you? Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, it immediately fell, and the ruin of that house was great.” Our soul delights in calling Him, "Lord, Lord." But, are we doing what He said? He tells us this is the important point, after all. If, led by our feelings, we claim to abide in Him in meetings, among friends, or in our hearts before the Lord, let us consider these words of the Holy Ghost: "He that says he abides in Him, ought himself so to walk, even as He walked." Unless we are walking as He did, we cannot be abiding in Him, no matter how much we may feel we are. If you are one with Christ, you will be sweet to those who are cross with you. You will bear everything and make no complaints. When reviled, you will not revile again. You will consent to be trampled on, as Christ was, and feel only love in return. You will seek others' honor rather than your own. You will take the lowest place and serve all, as Christ did. You will truly love your enemies and do well to those who spitefully use you. In short, you will live a Christ-like life. You will show and feel, a Christ-like spirit and walk among men as He did. This, dear friends, is what it is to be one with Christ. If this is not your life, you are not one with Him. Your feelings, no matter how ecstatic, do not matter. To be one with Christ is too wonderful and solemn a thing. It is too mighty an experience to be reached by mere feelings. He was holy, and those who are one with Him will be holy also. There is no escape from this simple and obvious Fact. When our Lord tried to show His oneness with God, He said, “And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him.”(Joshua 8:29) “So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel. For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Fat her. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John 5:19-23) The test of oneness, then, was the doing of the same works, and it is the test of oneness now. If our Lord could say that, so must His disciples. He said to believe in Him only if He did the works of His Father. He asked for no belief based on His claims. It is forever true that "So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseas ed tree bear good fruit” (Mathew 7:17 -18 ). It is not that they will not, but they cannot. A soul united with Christ will, for sure, bear a Christ-like life. A grapevine bears grapes, not thistles. I don't object to emotions, though. On the contrary, I believe they are very precious gifts when they are from God, and are to be greatly rejoiced in. I object to using them to test spiritual states, in ourselves or others. I don't want to base our faith on them. Let them come or let them go, just as God pleases, and make no account of them either way. But, we must have the vital marks of oneness with Christ. We must share a likeness in character, life, and walk. If we do, all will be well. For “ Whoever says 'I know him' but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him: whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.” (1John 2:4 -6) It may be, my dear reader, that the grief of your life has been the fact that you have so few good feelings. You try your hardest to get up the feelings that you hear others talking about, but they will not come. You pray for them fervently and are often tempted to upbraid God because He does not grant them to you. You are filled with unbearable anguish. You think your lack of emotion means your soul is not united with Christ. You judge altogether by your feelings, and think there is no other way to judge. Now my advice to you is to let your feelings go, and pay no regard to them whatever. They really have nothing to do with the matter. They do not reflect your spiritual state. They only show your temperament or current physical condition. People in very low states of grace often feel intense emotions. We all know this from the scenes we have heard of or witnessed at camp-meetings and revivals. I once had a servant who was deeply involved in her church's revival meetings. Sometimes, she would become so overwhelmed by the experience that she fainted. However, at other times, she showed little evidence of spiritual commitment and did not live a moral life. The Bible teaches, if nothing else, this: A Christ-like life must accompany any true experience of His spirit. It could not be otherwise in the very nature of things. But I fear some Christians have separated the two things so much that they now value their experiences over their walk. They care more about their feelings than their character. A certain colored congregation in one of the Southern States was a plague to the whole neighborhood. They openly disregarded even the ordinary rules of morality. They stole, lied, and cheated, without a single prick of conscience. And yet their nightly meetings were times of the gre atest emotion and “power.” Someone finally spoke to the preacher about it. They begged him to preach a sermon on morality to make his people see their sins. "Ah, misses," he replied, "I know the day is bad. But, it always brings a coldness over the meetings when I preach about these things." You are helpless as to your emotions, but you can have character if you will. You can be so filled with Christ as to be Christ-like. If you are Christ-like, then you are one with Him in the only vital, essential way. Your feelings may say it's impossible, but they are wrong. Now that we've defined oneness with Christ, we must find how to achieve it. We must first of all find out what the facts in the case are, and what our own relation to these facts is. If you read such passages as ( 1 Corinthians 3:16), “ Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you ?” Then, look at the chapter's opening. It shows to whom these wonderful words are spoken. They are for babies in Christ, who were yet carnal and walked according to man. This soulunion, this glorious mystery of an indwelling God, is the possession of even the weakest and most failing believer in Christ. So that it is not a new thing you are to ask for, but only to realize that which you already have. It is absolutely true for every believer in the Lord Jesus. His "body is the temple of the Holy Ghost, who is in him, who is of God.” It seems to me just in this way. It is as though Christ lived in a house, shut in a closet. The house's dwellers don't know or notice Him. He longs to be known to them, to share their daily lives and interests. But, He won't force Himself upon them. Only a voluntary companionship could satisfy His love. The days pass over that favored household. They remain unaware of their great privilege. They come and go about all their daily affairs with no thought of their wonderful Guest. Their plans are laid without reference to Him. His wisdom to guide, and His strength to protect, are all lost to them. Lonely days and weeks are spent in sadness, which might have been full of the sweetness of His presence. But suddenly, the announcement is made, “The Lord is in the house!” How will its owner receive the intelligence? Will he call out a thankful greeting and open every door for his glorious Guest? Or will he shrink, afraid of His presence, and seek a private corner to hide from His all-seeing eye? Dear friend, I am glad to announce that the Lord is in your heart. Since your conversion, He has been there. But you have lived in ignorance of it. Every moment might have been spent in the sunshine of His sweet presence. Every step might have been taken under His advice. But because you did not know it, and have never looked for Him, your life has been lonely and full of failure. But now that I announce to you, how will you receive it? Are you glad to have Him? Will you throw wide open every door to welcome Him in? Will you joyfully and thankfully give up the governance of your life into His hands? Will you consult Him about everything, and let Him decide each of your steps, and mark out every path? Will you invite Him to your innermost chambers, and make Him the sharer in your most hidden life? Will you say, YES to all His longing for union with you, and with a glad and eager abandonment, will you, then, hand yourself and all that concerns you over into His hands? If you will, then shall your soul begin to know something of the joy of union with Christ. And yet, after all, this is but a faint picture of the blessed reality. For it is far more glorious than to have Christ in the heart or the house. It is to be united with Him as to be one with Him, one will, one purpose, one interest, and one life. Human words cannot express such glory as this. And yet I want to express it. I want to make your souls so unutterably hungry to realize it, that day or night, you cannot rest without it. Do you understand the words, one with Christ? Do you catch the slightest glimpse of their marvellous meaning? Does not your whole soul begin to exult over such a wondrous destiny? For it is a reality. It means to have no life but His. To have no will but His. To have no interests but His. To share His riches. To enter into His joys. To partake of His sorrows. To manifest His life. To have His mind. To think, feel, act, and walk as He did. Oh, who could have dreamed that such a destiny could have been ours! Will you have it, dear soul? Your Lord will not force it on you. He wants you as His friend. A forced union would ruin this. It must be yo ur choice. The bride must say a willing “Yes,” to her bridegroom, or the joy of their union is utterly wanting. Can’t you say a willing “Yes,” to your Lord? It is such a simple transaction, and yet so real! The steps are three. First, be sure that the Scriptures teach this glorious indwelling of your God. Then, surrender your whole being to Him to be possessed by Him. Finally, believe that He has taken possession and is dwelling in you. Begin to reckon yourself dead, and to reckon Christ as your only life. Maintain this attitude of soul unwaveringly. Repeat, "I am crucified with Christ, nevertheless I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me," day and night. Do this until it becomes your soul's breath. Put off thy self-life by faith and in fact continually, and put on practically the life of Christ. Let this act become, by its constant repetition, the attitude of your whole being. And, as surely as you do this daily, you will find your body continually bearing the dying of the Lord Jesus. Then, the life of Jesus will be made manifest in your mortal flesh. You must learn what salvation means. You will see, with amazement, the Lord's secrets, of which you have hardly dreamed. How have I made a mistake! God is my home. God Himself is here. Why have I looked so far for Him, who is nowhere but near? Yet, God is never so far off as even to be near; He is within, our spirit is the home He holds most dear. I thought myself Homeless, forlorn, and weary. I missed my joy. I walked the earth, a weary soul, in God's sanctuary.

fields.title: A Lesson In The Interior Life
fields.body_html:
True spiritual joy comes from trusting in God's unchanging nature, not from external circumstances. Like the caterpillar that must die to become a butterfly, the soul must let go of the self-life to embrace divine life. Through trials and loss, the soul learns to find peace and joy in God alone. The key lesson is captured in the prophet’s words: “Although... yet,” showing the triumph of rejoicing in Go d despite challenges.

At Christmas, many of our store windows show a significant picture. It is a dreary, desolate winter scene. There is a dark, stormy sky, bare trees, and brown grass and dead weeds, with patches of snow over them. On a leafless tree at one side of the picture is an empty and snow-covered nest, and on a branch near sits a little bird. It is cold, dark, and desolate enough to daunt any bird, and drive it to some fairer clime. But, this bird sits there, content. Its little head is bravely lifted to the sky, and a winter song is about to burst from its tiny throat.

This picture, which always stands on my shelf, has preached me many a sermon. And the test is always the same. It is in the two words at the head of this article, "Although" and "Yet."

“ Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive fail and the fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls,” (Habakkuk3:17). There come times in many lives when, like this winter bird, the soul finds itself without comfort. All seems dark and wrong. Everything we trusted fails us. Promises seem unfulfilled, and our prayers go unanswered. We find nothing left to rely on in earth or Heaven. And it is at such times as these that the brave little bird with its message is needed. Although all is wrong everywhere, yet there is one thing to rejoice in: God. He is the God of our salvation. He does not change. He is the same good, loving, tender God yesterday, today, and forever.

We can rejoice in Him always, whether we have anything else to rejoice in or not. By rejoicing in Him, I do not mean rejoicing in ourselves. I fear most people think this is what is meant. Their feelings, revelations, and experiences form the basis of their joy. If none are satisfactory, they see no chance of joy at all. But the lesson the Lord is trying to teach us all the time is the lesson of humility.

He commands us to look away from the self and its experiences. We must crucify the self and count it dead. We must cease to care about the self. We should know and want nothing but God.

The reason for this is that God has destined us for a higher life than the self-life. That, just as He has destined the caterpillar to be a butterfly, He has appointed its life to die. So, the butterfly may take its place. Likewise, He has appointed our self-life to die so that the divine life may be ours instead. The caterpillar destroys its grub form to become a butterfly. It dies that it may live. And just so must we.

So, the most essential thing now is to die to self and be reborn to a life in God. And it is for this reason that the lesson of joy in the Lord, and not in self, must be learned. Every advancing soul must, sooner or later, trust God. The bare God, if I may. It must trust Him for what He is, not for His promises or gifts. It must learn to have its joy in Him alone, and to rejoice in Him when all else in Heaven and earth shall seem to fail.

I believe the only way to reach this place is by the soul. It must face, in its own experience, the loss of all things, both inward and outward. I don't mean that all one's friends must die, or all one's money be lost. I mean that the soul shall find itself, from either inward or outward causes, abandoned, lost, and empty of all consolation. It must come to the end of everything that is not God, and must have nothing else left to rest on within or without. It must experience just what the prophet meant when he wrote that “Although.”

It must go through the mud, fall off the edge, and be covered by the water . It must, at last, find, among and below them, the present, living, loving, omnipotent God! Only then will it understand the prophet's exulting shout of triumph. It will be able to join it : " yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation.”(Habakkuk 3:10) Then, and not until then, will it know the full meaning of the verse that follows: “ GOD, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the deer’s; he makes me tread on my high places .”(Habakkuk3:19) The soul often walks on what seem high places. They are, however, largely self-made and emotional, with little of God in them. In moments of loss and failure, these high places become edges. But the high places to which the Lord brings the soul that rejoices only in Him can be touched by no darkness or loss. Their very foundations are laid in the midst of an utter loss and death of all that is not God.

To find an unwavering experience, we must seek it only in the Lord. We must seek it apart from all else, His gifts, and His blessings. We must seek it apart from all that can change with our earthly life.

Today's answered prayer may seem unanswered tomorrow. The once-fulfilled promises may no longer feel real. The spiritual blessing that once brought joy may be lost. All we may have left is a hungry, longing memory of it all. But when all else is gone, God is still left. Nothing changes Him. He is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and in Him is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.

And the soul that finds its joy in Him alone can suffer no wavering. It is grand to trust in the promises, but it is grander still to trust in the Promiser. The promises may be misunderstood or misapplied. When we rely on them, they may seem to fail us. But no one ever trusted in the Promiser and was confounded.

The God behind His promises is infinitely greater than them. He can never fail us in any emergency.

The soul that trusts in Him knows perfect peace.

The little child does not always understand its mother's promises. But it knows its mother. Its trust is based not on her word, but on herself. And just so it is with those of us who have learned the lesson of this “Although” and “Yet.” There may not be a prayer answered or a prom ise fulfilled to our own consciousness, but what of that? Behind the prayers and behind the promises, there is God, and He is enough. And to such a soul the simple words, “God is”, answer every question and solve every doubt.

To the little trusting child, the simple fact of the mother’s existence is the answer to all its needs. The mother may not make one single promise or detail any plan, but she is, and that is enough for the child.

The child rejoices in the mother, not in her promises, but in herself. To the child, as to us, there is joy.

It is the one unchangeable thing behind all that changes and can change. It is the mother's existence.

The child must be cared for while the mother lives. The child, instinctively if not intelligently, knows this and rejoices in it. And while God lives, His children must be cared for. They should know this and rejoice in it more than a human child would.

For what else can God do, being what He is? Neglect, indifference, forgetfulness, and ignorance are all impossible to Him. He knows everything. He cares about everything. He can manage everything. He loves us. What more could we ask? So, come what may, we will lift our faces to our God, like our brave little bird teacher. In our darkest "Althoughs," we will sing our glad and triumphant "Yet."

All of God’s saints in all ages have done this. Job said, out of the depths of sorrow and trial which few can equal, “ Though he slay me I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face .”(Job 13:15). In his deepest ang uish, David could say, “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.” (Psalm 23:4) And again, "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble."(Psalm 46:1). Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling. Selah there is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High. God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns.

In his sorrows, Paul could say, "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies.

For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus ’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh. So death is at work in us, but life in you.” (2Corinthianss 4:812).The soul that learned to rejoice in God alone can say all this and more.

Spiritual joy is not a thing, not a lump of joy, so to speak, stored away in one’s heart to be looked at and rejoiced over. Joy is the gladness from having something good or knowing something pleasant.

And the Christian’s joy is simply his gladness in knowing Christ, and in his possession o f such a God and Saviour. We do not on an earthly plane rejoice in our joy, but in the thing that causes our joy. And on the heavenly plane, it is the same. We must " yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation. "(Habakkuk 3:18.) No man or devil can take this joy from us. No earthly sorrows can touch it.

A writer on the interior life says, in effect, that our spiritual journey has three very different regions.

Each is a necessary stage in our progress. First, there is the region of beginnings. It is a time of simple joys and delights, strong hopes, and deep feelings. Many secrets reveal God. Next is a vast wilderness, full of temptations and trials. It brings a loss of reason, dryness, and inner and outer darkness. If, after a long trial, you endure the desert, a region of mountain heights awaits. There, you will find a union with God, a detachment from earthly things, and a perfect contentment with His will. You will be transformed into the image of Christ.

I cannot discuss if this order is true. But, I am sure of one thing. Many souls, who found joy in the "Region of beginnings" here, later faced a desert experience that left them amazed and perplexed. And I cannot but think such might, perhaps, in this explanation, find the answer to their trouble. They are learning to detach from all that is not God. This is to unite their souls with Him, as shown in a picture of the third and highest region of bliss.

The soul’s pathway is always through death to life. The caterpillar must die to become a butterfly. It can only do so by giving up one life to live another. And neither can we. So, we may have to pass through this desolate, deadly region to reach the calm mountain heights beyond. If we know this, we can walk through the darkest times, sure that all is well, since God is God. Many who read this paper have at least one of these desert "Althoughs." Some have many.

Dear friends, is the “Yet” there also? Have you learned the prophet’s lesson? Is God enough for you?

Can you sing and mean it, "You, O Christ, are all I want, more than all in you I find" If not, you need the little bird to speak to you.

His song, as he sits on that bare, leafless tree in the howling winter storm, must become your song too.

Though the rain may fall and the wind blow, And the chill is the wintry blast; Though the cloudier sky is still clouding, And the dead leaves tell that summer is passed; Yet my face I hold to the stormy heaven, My heart is as calm as a summer sea; Glad to receive what my God has given, Whatever it may be.

When I feel the cold, I can say, 'He sends it.' And His wind blows blessing, I surely know. For I've never wanted but that He attends it. My heart beats warm, though the winds may blow. The soft, sweet summer was warm and glowing. Bright were the blossoms on every bough. I trusted Him when the roses were blowing. I trust Him now.

My faith would be small and weak if it wavered just because the roses have stopped blooming . Frail was the trust that now should alter, doubting His love when the storm-clouds grow. If I trust Him once, I must trust Him ever. His way is best, though I stand or fall. Through wind or storm, He will leave me never, for He sends all."
