Every advancing soul must, sooner or later, trust God. The bare God, if I may. It must trust Him for what He is, not for His promises or gifts. It must learn to have its joy in Him alone, and to rejoice in Him when all else in Heaven and earth shall seem to fail. I believe the only way to reach this place is by the soul. It must face, in its own experience, the loss of all things, both inward and outward. I don't mean that all one's friends must die, or all one's money be lost. I mean that the soul shall find itself, from either inward or outward causes, abandoned, lost, and empty of all consolation. It must come to the end of everything that is not God, and must have nothing else left to rest on within or without. It must experience just what the prophet meant when he wrote that “Although.” It must go through the mud, fall off the edge, and be covered by the water . It must, at last, find, among and below them, the present, living, loving, omnipotent God! Only then will it understand the prophet's exulting shout of triumph. It will be able to join it : " yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation.”(Habakkuk 3:10) Then, and not until then, will it know the full meaning of the verse that follows: “ GOD, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the deer’s; he makes me tread on my high places .”(Habakkuk3:19) The soul often walks on what seem high places. They are, however, largely self-made and emotional, with little of God in them. In moments of loss and failure, these high places become edges. But the high places to which the Lord brings the soul that rejoices only in Him can be touched by no darkness or loss. Their very foundations are laid in the midst of an utter loss and death of all that is not God. To find an unwavering experience, we must seek it only in the Lord. We must seek it apart from all else, His gifts, and His blessings. We must seek it apart from all that can change with our earthly life. Today's answered prayer may seem unanswered tomorrow. The once-fulfilled promises may no longer feel real. The spiritual blessing that once brought joy may be lost. All we may have left is a hungry, longing memory of it all. But when all else is gone, God is still left. Nothing changes Him. He is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and in Him is no variableness, neither shadow of turning. And the soul that finds its joy in Him alone can suffer no wavering. It is grand to trust in the promises, but it is grander still to trust in the Promiser. The promises may be misunderstood or misapplied. When we rely on them, they may seem to fail us. But no one ever trusted in the Promiser and was confounded. The God behind His promises is infinitely greater than them. He can never fail us in any emergency. The soul that trusts in Him knows perfect peace. The little child does not always understand its mother's promises. But it knows its mother. Its trust is based not on her word, but on herself. And just so it is with those of us who have learned the lesson of this “Although” and “Yet.” There may not be a prayer answered or a prom ise fulfilled to our own consciousness, but what of that? Behind the prayers and behind the promises, there is God, and He is enough. And to such a soul the simple words, “God is”, answer every question and solve every doubt. To the little trusting child, the simple fact of the mother’s existence is the answer to all its needs. The mother may not make one single promise or detail any plan, but she is, and that is enough for the child. The child rejoices in the mother, not in her promises, but in herself. To the child, as to us, there is joy. It is the one unchangeable thing behind all that changes and can change. It is the mother's existence. The child must be cared for while the mother lives. The child, instinctively if not intelligently, knows this and rejoices in it. And while God lives, His children must be cared for. They should know this and rejoice in it more than a human child would. For what else can God do, being what He is? Neglect, indifference, forgetfulness, and ignorance are all impossible to Him. He knows everything. He cares about everything. He can manage everything. He loves us. What more could we ask? So, come what may, we will lift our faces to our God, like our brave little bird teacher. In our darkest "Althoughs," we will sing our glad and triumphant "Yet." All of God’s saints in all ages have done this. Job said, out of the depths of sorrow and trial which few can equal, “ Though he slay me I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face .”(Job 13:15). In his deepest ang uish, David could say, “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.” (Psalm 23:4) And again, "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble."(Psalm 46:1). Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling. Selah there is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High. God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns. In his sorrows, Paul could say, "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus ’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh. So death is at work in us, but life in you.” (2Corinthianss 4:812).The soul that learned to rejoice in God alone can say all this and more. Spiritual joy is not a thing, not a lump of joy, so to speak, stored away in one’s heart to be looked at and rejoiced over. Joy is the gladness from having something good or knowing something pleasant. And the Christian’s joy is simply his gladness in knowing Christ, and in his possession o f such a God and Saviour. We do not on an earthly plane rejoice in our joy, but in the thing that causes our joy. And on the heavenly plane, it is the same. We must " yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation. "(Habakkuk 3:18.) No man or devil can take this joy from us. No earthly sorrows can touch it. A writer on the interior life says, in effect, that our spiritual journey has three very different regions. Each is a necessary stage in our progress. First, there is the region of beginnings. It is a time of simple joys and delights, strong hopes, and deep feelings. Many secrets reveal God. Next is a vast wilderness, full of temptations and trials. It brings a loss of reason, dryness, and inner and outer darkness. If, after a long trial, you endure the desert, a region of mountain heights awaits. There, you will find a union with God, a detachment from earthly things, and a perfect contentment with His will. You will be transformed into the image of Christ. I cannot discuss if this order is true. But, I am sure of one thing. Many souls, who found joy in the "Region of beginnings" here, later faced a desert experience that left them amazed and perplexed. And I cannot but think such might, perhaps, in this explanation, find the answer to their trouble. They are learning to detach from all that is not God. This is to unite their souls with Him, as shown in a picture of the third and highest region of bliss. The soul’s pathway is always through death to life. The caterpillar must die to become a butterfly. It can only do so by giving up one life to live another. And neither can we. So, we may have to pass through this desolate, deadly region to reach the calm mountain heights beyond. If we know this, we can walk through the darkest times, sure that all is well, since God is God. Many who read this paper have at least one of these desert "Althoughs." Some have many. Dear friends, is the “Yet” there also? Have you learned the prophet’s lesson? Is God enough for you? Can you sing and mean it, "You, O Christ, are all I want, more than all in you I find" If not, you need the little bird to speak to you. His song, as he sits on that bare, leafless tree in the howling winter storm, must become your song too. Though the rain may fall and the wind blow, And the chill is the wintry blast; Though the cloudier sky is still clouding, And the dead leaves tell that summer is passed; Yet my face I hold to the stormy heaven, My heart is as calm as a summer sea; Glad to receive what my God has given, Whatever it may be. When I feel the cold, I can say, 'He sends it.' And His wind blows blessing, I surely know. For I've never wanted but that He attends it. My heart beats warm, though the winds may blow. The soft, sweet summer was warm and glowing. Bright were the blossoms on every bough. I trusted Him when the roses were blowing. I trust Him now. My faith would be small and weak if it wavered just because the roses have stopped blooming . Frail was the trust that now should alter, doubting His love when the storm-clouds grow. If I trust Him once, I must trust Him ever. His way is best, though I stand or fall. Through wind or storm, He will leave me never, for He sends all."

fields.title: How To Reign In The Interior Life
fields.body_html:
The kingdom of God is an inner, spiritual realm, not an external, physical one. Jesus teaches that it is not a place to observe, but exists within those who live according to God’s will. In this kingdom, individuals find freedom from external pre ssures and sin, with Christ as the sovereign who bears all burdens. The true power of this kingdom lies in inner peace and triumph over worldly struggles.

When the Pharisees asked him when the kingdom of God would come, he answered, "It does not come with observation."" Neither shall they say, 'Look, here!'" or, look there! For, Behold, the kingdom of God is within you." The phrases "kingdom of God" and "kingdom of Heaven" refer to the divine life in the soul. They are in Scripture. They mean simply the place or condition where God rules, and where His will is done. It is an interior kingdom, not an exterior one. Its thrones are not for human pomp and glory. They are for dominion over the things of time and sense. Its kings wear not royal robes of purple and fine linen. They wear instead the inner garments of purity and truth. And its reign is not in outward show, but in inward power.

Neither is it in one place rather than another, nor in one form of things above another. We should not seek Christ in this mountain or at Jerusalem. That is not where to find Him and enter His kingdom. It is not a matter of place at all, but one of condition. In every place, under every name, and in every form, all who seek God and do good will find His kingdom within them. But this is very little understood. Our childish literalism has led us to believe that a kingdom must be in a specific place. We expected the kingdom of heaven to mean an outward victory of heaven over earth in some particular location. We thought that to sit on a throne with Christ would mean to be publicly uplifted in power and glory.

But, as Scripture's inner sense unfolds, we see that this would be a poor, superficial fulfillment of the real meaning of these symbols. And the vision of their true significance grows before the "eyes that see." At last, we know our Lord's words were truer than we had ever dreamed. The "kingdom of God comes not with observation; neither shall they say, lord here! or, lord there!" for, behold, the kingdom of God is wi thin you.”

Daniel 2:44 “And in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, nor shall the kingdom be left to another people. It shall break in pieces all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, and it shall stand forever,” announces the kingdom. Isaiah 9:6-7 announces the King: -- “ For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace, there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this.”

This kingdom has the right to destroy all others. The law says the inward must rule the outward. If there is peace within, no turmoil can affect the soul. But outward peace can't calm an inner storm. A happy heart can walk, indifferent, through a sea of trouble. But internal anguish can't find joy in the best surroundings. A man's inner self makes or unmakes his joy, not his possessions. Someone told Diogenes, "The king has degraded you." “Yes , ” replied Diogenes triump hantly, “but I am not degraded!” No act of kings or emperors can degrade a soul that retains its own dignity; no tyrant can enslave an inwardly free man.

So, to have this divine kingdom within means all other powers to conquer or enslave are broken. The soul reigns triumphant over them all. Men and devils may try to enslave one. But they are powerless before the might of this interior kingdom. No longer will fashion, convention, or fear of man rule a soul raised to a throne in this inward kingdom. Nor will the love of ease. Christians cringe and bow to many tyrants. No sin or temptation can overcome, no sorrow can crush, no discouragement can hinder.

Let a man or woman have been bound in ever so tyrannical chains of sinful habits, this kingdom will set them free. Circumstances may make men kings in the outside world. But, in the hidden life, men become kings over circumstances. And, the soul that was once a slave to a thousand things, now finds itself completely independent of them.

For the King in this kingdom is one whom nothing can affect or baffle. He it is who makes circumstances. Since the government is on His shoulders, we cannot doubt that He will rule with perfect justice. His subjects will want for nothing. The phrase "the government shall be upon His shoulder" holds the secret of this wonderful kingdom. Upon His shoulder, not upon ours. The care is His. The burdens are His. The responsibility is His. The protection is His. The planning, providing, controlling, and guiding are all in His hands. No one can question as to His perfect fulfilment of every requirement of His kingship. So, those in His kingdom are free from anxiety, burden, and trouble.

And by this deliverance they become kings. The government is not upon their shoulders, and they have no business to interfere with it. Their King has assumed all responsibility. If He sees His subjects happy and prosperous, He is content to bear all the weight and care of kingship. We often speak of the duties of earthly kings. We pity them for the burdens of kingship. We recognize, even on an earthly plane, that to be a king means, or ought to mean, the bearing of the burdens of even the meanest of his subject.

Even now, as I write, many hearts ache for the new Czar. He has taken on the heavy burden of the vast Russian Empire.

We can learn, from every human heart, of kingship's duties. It means to be in a kingdom where God is King. He has declared that all things shall be ordered with judgment and justice, forever. Surely no care or anxiety can ever enter here, if the heart but knows its kingdom and its King! In John 18:36, our King tells us the tactics of His kingdom: “ Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.”

Earthly kings and kingdoms gain supremacy through war. God's kingdom conquers by inward power.

Earthly kings subdue enemies; God subdues enmity. His victories must be interior before they can be exterior. He does not subjugate, but he conquers. Even we, on our earthly plane, know this principle.

We do not value any victory over another that only reaches the body and has not subdued the heart. No true mother cares for an outward obedience merely; nothing will satisfy her but the inward surrender.

Unless the center of the heart is conquered, the conquest seem worthless. And with God how much more so? We are told, “But the LORD said to Samuel, “Do not look on his appearan ce or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.” (1samuel 16:7) We speak of "subduing hearts." We do not mean to force a surrender. We mean that they are won and willingly given to another. And it is after this fashion and no other that God subdues. So that to read that “His kingdom rules over all” means that all hearts are won to His service in a glad and willing surrender.

For again I repeat, His reign must be inward before it can be outward. And in truth, it is no reign at all, unless it is within. If we think for a moment, we will see this must be so. It is impossible to imagine God reigning in a kingdom where His subjects' actions are not controlled beyond their outward actions.

His kingdom is not of this world. It is a spiritual realm. Its power is over souls, not bodies.

So, it can only be set up once the soul is conquered.

Seen this way, all those declarations and prophecies become full of love and blessing. They say that God will subdue His enemies and will rule them in righteousness and power! And how glorious with hope does the voice of that great multitude heard by John sound out, saying, “Alleluia! For the Lord God omnipotent reigns” In confirmation of all this we have two passages descriptive of this kingdom, in (Romans.14:17) “ For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.” , and (1 Corinthian s 4:20): “ For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power.”

Not outward things, but inward. Not what a man eats or drinks. Not where he lives. Not his nationality or the customs of his race. Not even his thoughts or words. But what are the inward traits of his nature?

What is the power of his spirit? For these alone constitute this kingdom of God.

Not what I do, but what I am, is to decide whether I belong to it or not. This kingdom can be set up only when we have and experience, inward righteousness, peace, joy, and power. So, no external domination can achieve such results. Only the inner work of God's all-subduing spirit can.

I have learned a lot from the story of Odysseus and his journey, when he was sailing past the islands of the sirens. These sirens could charm anyone who listened to their songs. They lured them to leap into the sea. To avert this danger, Odysseus filled his crew's ears with wax. He did this so they would not hear the fatal music. He then bound himself to the mast with knotted cords. They passed the isle in safety. But, when Orpheus had to sail by the same island, he won a better victory. He made sweeter music than the sirens and enchanted his crew with more alluring songs. So, they passed the dangerous charmers, not only safely but with disdain. Wax and knotted cords kept Odysseus and his crew from a fatal leap. But, inward delights let Orpheus and his crew triumph over temptation itself. And just so is it with the kingdom of which we speak. It needs no outward law to bind it, but reigns by right of its inward life.

So that it is said of those who have entered it, “Against such there is no law. “For it is a kingdom of kings. The song we shall one day sing, nay, that we ought to be singing even now and here in this life, declares this: " and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth. To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen (Revelation.1:5- 6.)

We who have entered this kingdom, or, rather, in whom this kingdom is set up, sit upon the throne with our King and share His dominion. The world was His footstool, and it becomes our footstool also. He reigned above the things of time and sense. A life lived in a higher, superior plane gave him that power.

So may we. We all know the saying that someone "rises above his surroundings." It means there is a hidden power in that person. It controls his surroundings instead of being controlled by them. Our King rose above His surroundings. We, who reign with Him, can do the same.

But, just as He was not a king in outward appearance, but only in inward power, so shall we be. He reigned, not in that He had all the world's riches. But that He had none, and could do without them.

And so shall our reigning be. We shall not have all men bow to us, nor do all things bend to our will.

With all men opposing us and all things adverse, we shall walk in a royal triumph of soul through them.

We shall suffer the loss of all things, and by that loss be set forever free from their power to bind. We shall hide in the King's will, an impregnable fortress. There, we shall reign in a perpetual Kingdom.

All this is contrary to man’s thought of kingship. The human heart can only grasp one idea. It is this: that outward circumstances must bend to the soul that is on a throne with Christ. Friends must approve, enemies must be silenced, and obstacles must be overcome. Affairs must prosper, or there can be no reigning. If man had ordered Daniel's business, or the three Hebrews in the fiery furnace, he would have said to win, they must change the kings' minds. Daniel should not have been cast into the lion's den, and the Hebrew children should have been kept out of the furnace.

But God’s way was infinitely grander. He allowed Daniel to be cast among the lions. He wanted to reign triumphant over them in their midst. He allowed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to be cast into a burning furnace. He wanted them to walk through it without even the smell of fire on them. He tells us, not to walk in paths without dragons and adders. But, we shall walk through the midst of them, and "tread them under our feet."”

And how much more glorious a kingdom is this than any outward rule or control could be! To be a king inside, but a slave outside, is a great triumph. It is the best our hearts can conceive. To be destitute, afflicted, and tormented. To be stoned, torn apart, and slain with the sword. To wander in sheepskins and goatskins, and in deserts, mountains, dens, and caves. Yet, through it all, to be kings in a kingdom of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. This is a kingdom that none but God could give, and none but God-like souls could receive.

We have seen or heard of a few such kings. All hearts have acknowledged their unconscious effect. I read about one of the members of the St. Cyr monastery. Their devotion made the monasteries and their superiors hate them. They were cast out as evil from their community. One was sent as a prisoner to a monastery where his enemies dwelt. There, he suffered cruel and degrading treatment. Although he came from a noble background and was a former leader, he had to do the simplest tasks . He was forced to carry a heavy burden on his back and made to beg with a sign on his chest saying he was the worst of the worst. But, through it all, the saint's spirit triumphed. Nothing disturbed his calm or soured his Christ-like sweetness.

For his persecutors, he never had anything but words of kindness and smiles of love. At last, by the divine kingdom's great power, he won all hearts. He became the trusted friend and adviser, and the beloved ruler of his former enemies who had once delighted in persecuting him. “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Mathew 5:5) . By his meekness, he conquered and became king. At one time, a dangerous criminal was sent to the monastery for imprisonment. He was so violent that no bonds sufficed to bind him, and no strength could control him. At last, he was taken to the cell of a brother from St. Cyr. They were shut up together. Even the stolid monks recognized that divine meekness. It had a power to conquer that surpassed all they knew. The saint received the violent man as a beloved brother and smiled upon him with heavenly kindness.

But the criminal returned it with abuse and violence. He broke the monk’s furniture and destroyed his bed, he kicked him, beat him, and tore his hair, and spat upon him. He exhausted himself in his violence against him. Through it all, the monk resisted nothing.

He spoke only words of love. Finally, the criminal, worn out with fury, paused to catch his breath. The beaten and outraged man then smiled at his persecutor with deep love and compassion. It was as if he wanted to comfort him for his misery. It was more than the criminal could bear. Hatred, revenge, and anger he could repay in kind. But, he had no weapons against such love and meekness. His heart was conquered. He fell at the feet of the saint and washed them with his tears, as he entreated forgiveness for his cruelty, and vowed a lifelong loyalty to his service.

And from that moment all trouble with that criminal was over. He followed the saint about like a loving and faithful dog, eager to do or to be anything the other might desire. When his prison term ended, the gates opened. He could not be induced to leave, for he could not bear to leave the man who had saved him by love. Of such a nature is kingship in this kingdom of heaven. Each soul can make the application for itself, without need of comment from me.

In ( Mathew 5: 6-7), we have the King of this kingdom describing the characteristics of His kingdom and giving the laws for Hi s subjects. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy. “Not the rich, or great, or wise, or learned. But the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, those who mourn, and those who hunger and thirst. Also, the persecuted, reviled, and slandered. All such belong to this kingdom. These kings are gentle, yielding, meek, and charitable. They reign with that power.

One Christian asked anoth er, “How can I make people respect me?” “I would command their respect,” was the reply. This meant, not that he should demand, "Respect me!" But, he should act, live, and be, so that all would respect him. Men can win a show of respect by being tyrannical. But, to rule their hearts, they must try other methods.

Our Lord developed this thought to some who wished to share His throne. He called them to Him, and said, “But Jesus called them to him and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it o ver them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.”(Mathew 20:25). But it shall not be so among you. Whoever wants to be great must be your minister. Whoever wants to be first must be the servant of all. For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”

From a human view, only one man reigns. He is the one who can be lord over those around him.

From the divine standpoint the soul that serves is the soul that reigns.

Not he who demands most, receives this inward crowning, but he who gives up most. What greater leadership can be imagined than Christ's in the Sermon on the Mount? “But I say to you, do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also . ” If someone sues you and takes your shirt, give them your coat too . And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. (Mathew 5:39) Surely only a soul that is in harmony with God can mount such a throne of dominion as this! But this is our destiny. We are made for this purpose. We are born of a kingly race, and are heirs to this Inexpressible kingdom; “ and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him .”(Romans 8:17) With that we could realize this, and, see in every act of service or surrender, an upward step. It would lead us to our kingdom and throne! I mean this in a very practical sense. I mean that our daily, humble tasks and small sacrifices, if done well, will be steps up a ladder to our thrones. If we are faithful over the "few things" of our earthly kingdom, we shall be made rulers over the "many things" of the heavenly kingdom.

He who serves and suffers for Christ will reign with Him. He will be the "chiefest" in His kingdom of love. Knowing this, who would hesitate to turn the other cheek? A kingdom and a throne are to be won.

Joseph was a type of all this. In slavery and in prison he reigned as king, as truly as when seated on Pharaoh’s throne or riding in Pharaoh’s chariot. (See Gen. 39:6) “So he left all that he had in Joseph’s charge, and because of him he had no concern about anything but the food he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance.”

(Genesis 39:22- 23.) “ And the keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever was done there, he was the one who did it. The keeper of the prison paid no attention to anything that was in Joseph’s charge, beca use the LORD was with him. And whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed.” He became the greatest by being the least, the chiefest by being servant of all.

Dear reader, are you ruling in this way, in this kind of kingdom? Are you the greatest in your small world — at home, church, or in your social circle? Then be the least. Be the servant of everyone. If not, your kingdom is not Christ’s kingdom, and your throne is not shared with Him. Accessing the secrets and power of this inner kingdom is not a fantasy . It’s not just an imagined victory. It’s a real and true way of reigning. It will make you rise above the world and its concerns. You will move through it, unaffected by its praise or criticism. You will live in a place of peace and victory that the world can neither give nor take away.

“For the kingdom of God is not in word but in power.” It is not a talk but a fact , and those who are in it recognize their kingship and prove it by reigning. But perhaps thou will say, “How can I enter into this kingdom , if I am not already in?” Let our Lord himself answer you: “At that time the disciples came to Jesus, saying, 'Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven? ” (Mathew 18:1) “And calling to him a child, he put him in the midst of them and said , 'Truly, I say to you, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.”(Mathew 18:2 -3) It is a kingdom of childlike hearts, and only such can en ter it. To be a “little child” means simply to be one. I cannot describe it better than this. We all know little children.

We delight in their simplicity, trust, and carelessness. We admire their unquestioning obedience to authority. To be the greatest in this divine kingdom, one must have the most of this child's trusting, tender, and obedient heart. It is guileless and self-forgetting.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Fa ther who is in heaven.”( Matthew 7:21 ) .It is not saying, but doing, that will avail us here. We must be a child, or we cannot sit on the child’s throne. And to be a child means to do the Father’s will, since the very essence of true childhood is the spirit of obedience united to the spirit of trust.

Become a little child. Set aside your greatness, self-assertion, and wisdom. Give up your strength and self-dependence. Consent to die to your old self. Be born again into the kingdom of God. The only way out of one life into another is by a death to one and a new birth into the other. It is the old story, therefore, reiterated so often and in so many different ways, of through death to life. Die, then, that you my live. Lose your own life that you may find Christ’s life.

They can only enter the butterfly's kingdom by dying to its caterpillar life, and then becoming a butterfly. Likewise, we can only enter God's kingdom by dying to the kingdom of self, and then rising to life in Christ. Let go of everything natural. This includes your ideas, plans, and thoughts. Instead, accept God's plans, ways, and thoughts. Do this faithfully and persistently. You shall, at last, sit on His throne and reign with Him in an eternal kingdom. It will break and consume all other kingdoms, and stand forever.

There is no other way. This kingdom can't be entered through pride, appearance, or power . It can only be entered by littleness, helplessness, childlikeness, babyhood, and death. Only he who humbles himself shall be exalted. To share Christ's throne, we must first follow Him in suffering, loss, and crucifixion. If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with Him.

Not as an arbitrary reward for our suffering, but as the result that will follow in the very nature of things. Christ's loss must bring Christ's gain. His death must bring His resurrection. To follow Him in the regeneration will, without fail, bring the soul that follows to His crown and throne. In a volume of sermons for children, I have found a vivid illustration of this royal kingdom: – A young boy from one of the refuges in England had risked his life to save his friend. The Queen of England had sent him a medal through one of her earls. His friends pushed him forward to receive it, as he was shy and nervous and tried to step away.

Look at the honorable chairman. He had come from the House of Lords, where earls, dukes, and distinguished men like lawyers, judges, statesmen, and warriors were gathered. Royal princes were also there. Yet, all peer though he was, he was moved. He murmured, "I have the honor," and pinned the lifesaving medal on the child's jacket. His heart was full. He paused to swallow down something that would rise in his throat before he could go on.

There is the 'glory and honor' of statesmen, warriors, and lawyers. But the glory of selfless lifesaving excels all. That was the wondrous glory won by this boy." He had plunged into the stream and shared a drowning boy's risk. That little hand, look at it there, steadying him by holding the table, had come out holding the saved.

“Why has self -forgetfulness such mighty power? How was it that a twelve-year old boy could bow down an audience of grown men before him? What gave to that brow, that it’s stubby crown of carroty hair, a glory and honor more than the luster of gold and jewels?

Why did that small body in its little breeches and jacket, wiping its tears on the rough little sleeve, grip thousands of hearts? Why did it make them, for a time, loyal subjects of its kingdom?

Why was all this so? It was so because that little boy had been like Christ, in his spirit of selfless sacrifice for others." He had some of the beauty we are meant to worship. It is the glory that makes angels shout. All of heaven falls and adores. They say, " saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!”( Revelations 5:12) .The Lamb that was slain is the mightiest King ever. All who share His spirit are in His kingdom. This kingdom is not a place, but a character. So, those without that character cannot be in it.

We pray daily, “Your kingdom come.” Do we know what we are praying for? Do we comprehend the change it will make in us if it comes in us? Are we willing to be so changed? What is the kingdom of God but the rule of God? And what is the rule of God but the will of God? Therefore, when we pray, “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven,” we have touched the secret of it all. A group of savages might take over a kingdom by force, but to truly control its civilization, they must follow its rules. The same is true for the kingdom of heaven. It only grants its power to those who obey its laws. “ The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne . ”( Revelation 3:21 ) “He always reigns who sides with God,” says an old writer. And again, “He who perfectly accepts the will of God, dwells in a perpetual kingdom.”

Are you reigning after this fashion and in this sort of a kingdom? Are you the most important by being the servant of all? Are you a king over your circumstances, or do your circumstances reign over you?

Do you triumph over your temptations, or do your temptations triumph over you? Can you sit on an inward throne in the midst of outward defeat and loss?

Can you conquer by yielding, and become the greatest by being the least? If you can’t answer yes to all these questions, then you can’t come into his kingdom. "Whatever yo ur lot or men's opinions, you are among those whom our Lord calls 'the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.'"
fields.body_text: The kingdom of God is an inner, spiritual realm, not an external, physical one. Jesus teaches that it is not a place to observe, but exists within those who live according to God’s will. In this kingdom, individuals find freedom from external pre ssures and sin, with Christ as the sovereign who bears all burdens. The true power of this kingdom lies in inner peace and triumph over worldly struggles. When the Pharisees asked him when the kingdom of God would come, he answered, "It does not come with observation."" Neither shall they say, 'Look, here!'" or, look there! For, Behold, the kingdom of God is within you." The phrases "kingdom of God" and "kingdom of Heaven" refer to the divine life in the soul. They are in Scripture. They mean simply the place or condition where God rules, and where His will is done. It is an interior kingdom, not an exterior one. Its thrones are not for human pomp and glory. They are for dominion over the things of time and sense. Its kings wear not royal robes of purple and fine linen. They wear instead the inner garments of purity and truth. And its reign is not in outward show, but in inward power. Neither is it in one place rather than another, nor in one form of things above another. We should not seek Christ in this mountain or at Jerusalem. That is not where to find Him and enter His kingdom. It is not a matter of place at all, but one of condition. In every place, under every name, and in every form, all who seek God and do good will find His kingdom within them. But this is very little understood. Our childish literalism has led us to believe that a kingdom must be in a specific place. We expected the kingdom of heaven to mean an outward victory of heaven over earth in some particular location. We thought that to sit on a throne with Christ would mean to be publicly uplifted in power and glory. But, as Scripture's inner sense unfolds, we see that this would be a poor, superficial fulfillment of the real meaning of these symbols. And the vision of their true significance grows before the "eyes that see." At last, we know our Lord's words were truer than we had ever dreamed. The "kingdom of God comes not with observation; neither shall they say, lord here! or, lord there!" for, behold, the kingdom of God is wi thin you.” Daniel 2:44 “And in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, nor shall the kingdom be left to another people. It shall break in pieces all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, and it shall stand forever,” announces the kingdom. Isaiah 9:6-7 announces the King: -- “ For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace, there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this.” This kingdom has the right to destroy all others. The law says the inward must rule the outward. If there is peace within, no turmoil can affect the soul. But outward peace can't calm an inner storm. A happy heart can walk, indifferent, through a sea of trouble. But internal anguish can't find joy in the best surroundings. A man's inner self makes or unmakes his joy, not his possessions. Someone told Diogenes, "The king has degraded you." “Yes , ” replied Diogenes triump hantly, “but I am not degraded!” No act of kings or emperors can degrade a soul that retains its own dignity; no tyrant can enslave an inwardly free man. So, to have this divine kingdom within means all other powers to conquer or enslave are broken. The soul reigns triumphant over them all. Men and devils may try to enslave one. But they are powerless before the might of this interior kingdom. No longer will fashion, convention, or fear of man rule a soul raised to a throne in this inward kingdom. Nor will the love of ease. Christians cringe and bow to many tyrants. No sin or temptation can overcome, no sorrow can crush, no discouragement can hinder. Let a man or woman have been bound in ever so tyrannical chains of sinful habits, this kingdom will set them free. Circumstances may make men kings in the outside world. But, in the hidden life, men become kings over circumstances. And, the soul that was once a slave to a thousand things, now finds itself completely independent of them. For the King in this kingdom is one whom nothing can affect or baffle. He it is who makes circumstances. Since the government is on His shoulders, we cannot doubt that He will rule with perfect justice. His subjects will want for nothing. The phrase "the government shall be upon His shoulder" holds the secret of this wonderful kingdom. Upon His shoulder, not upon ours. The care is His. The burdens are His. The responsibility is His. The protection is His. The planning, providing, controlling, and guiding are all in His hands. No one can question as to His perfect fulfilment of every requirement of His kingship. So, those in His kingdom are free from anxiety, burden, and trouble. And by this deliverance they become kings. The government is not upon their shoulders, and they have no business to interfere with it. Their King has assumed all responsibility. If He sees His subjects happy and prosperous, He is content to bear all the weight and care of kingship. We often speak of the duties of earthly kings. We pity them for the burdens of kingship. We recognize, even on an earthly plane, that to be a king means, or ought to mean, the bearing of the burdens of even the meanest of his subject. Even now, as I write, many hearts ache for the new Czar. He has taken on the heavy burden of the vast Russian Empire. We can learn, from every human heart, of kingship's duties. It means to be in a kingdom where God is King. He has declared that all things shall be ordered with judgment and justice, forever. Surely no care or anxiety can ever enter here, if the heart but knows its kingdom and its King! In John 18:36, our King tells us the tactics of His kingdom: “ Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.” Earthly kings and kingdoms gain supremacy through war. God's kingdom conquers by inward power. Earthly kings subdue enemies; God subdues enmity. His victories must be interior before they can be exterior. He does not subjugate, but he conquers. Even we, on our earthly plane, know this principle. We do not value any victory over another that only reaches the body and has not subdued the heart. No true mother cares for an outward obedience merely; nothing will satisfy her but the inward surrender. Unless the center of the heart is conquered, the conquest seem worthless. And with God how much more so? We are told, “But the LORD said to Samuel, “Do not look on his appearan ce or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.” (1samuel 16:7) We speak of "subduing hearts." We do not mean to force a surrender. We mean that they are won and willingly given to another. And it is after this fashion and no other that God subdues. So that to read that “His kingdom rules over all” means that all hearts are won to His service in a glad and willing surrender. For again I repeat, His reign must be inward before it can be outward. And in truth, it is no reign at all, unless it is within. If we think for a moment, we will see this must be so. It is impossible to imagine God reigning in a kingdom where His subjects' actions are not controlled beyond their outward actions. His kingdom is not of this world. It is a spiritual realm. Its power is over souls, not bodies. So, it can only be set up once the soul is conquered. Seen this way, all those declarations and prophecies become full of love and blessing. They say that God will subdue His enemies and will rule them in righteousness and power! And how glorious with hope does the voice of that great multitude heard by John sound out, saying, “Alleluia! For the Lord God omnipotent reigns” In confirmation of all this we have two passages descriptive of this kingdom, in (Romans.14:17) “ For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.” , and (1 Corinthian s 4:20): “ For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power.” Not outward things, but inward. Not what a man eats or drinks. Not where he lives. Not his nationality or the customs of his race. Not even his thoughts or words. But what are the inward traits of his nature? What is the power of his spirit? For these alone constitute this kingdom of God. Not what I do, but what I am, is to decide whether I belong to it or not. This kingdom can be set up only when we have and experience, inward righteousness, peace, joy, and power. So, no external domination can achieve such results. Only the inner work of God's all-subduing spirit can. I have learned a lot from the story of Odysseus and his journey, when he was sailing past the islands of the sirens. These sirens could charm anyone who listened to their songs. They lured them to leap into the sea. To avert this danger, Odysseus filled his crew's ears with wax. He did this so they would not hear the fatal music. He then bound himself to the mast with knotted cords. They passed the isle in safety. But, when Orpheus had to sail by the same island, he won a better victory. He made sweeter music than the sirens and enchanted his crew with more alluring songs. So, they passed the dangerous charmers, not only safely but with disdain. Wax and knotted cords kept Odysseus and his crew from a fatal leap. But, inward delights let Orpheus and his crew triumph over temptation itself. And just so is it with the kingdom of which we speak. It needs no outward law to bind it, but reigns by right of its inward life. So that it is said of those who have entered it, “Against such there is no law. “For it is a kingdom of kings. The song we shall one day sing, nay, that we ought to be singing even now and here in this life, declares this: " and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth. To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen (Revelation.1:5- 6.) We who have entered this kingdom, or, rather, in whom this kingdom is set up, sit upon the throne with our King and share His dominion. The world was His footstool, and it becomes our footstool also. He reigned above the things of time and sense. A life lived in a higher, superior plane gave him that power. So may we. We all know the saying that someone "rises above his surroundings." It means there is a hidden power in that person. It controls his surroundings instead of being controlled by them. Our King rose above His surroundings. We, who reign with Him, can do the same. But, just as He was not a king in outward appearance, but only in inward power, so shall we be. He reigned, not in that He had all the world's riches. But that He had none, and could do without them. And so shall our reigning be. We shall not have all men bow to us, nor do all things bend to our will. With all men opposing us and all things adverse, we shall walk in a royal triumph of soul through them. We shall suffer the loss of all things, and by that loss be set forever free from their power to bind. We shall hide in the King's will, an impregnable fortress. There, we shall reign in a perpetual Kingdom. All this is contrary to man’s thought of kingship. The human heart can only grasp one idea. It is this: that outward circumstances must bend to the soul that is on a throne with Christ. Friends must approve, enemies must be silenced, and obstacles must be overcome. Affairs must prosper, or there can be no reigning. If man had ordered Daniel's business, or the three Hebrews in the fiery furnace, he would have said to win, they must change the kings' minds. Daniel should not have been cast into the lion's den, and the Hebrew children should have been kept out of the furnace. But God’s way was infinitely grander. He allowed Daniel to be cast among the lions. He wanted to reign triumphant over them in their midst. He allowed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to be cast into a burning furnace. He wanted them to walk through it without even the smell of fire on them. He tells us, not to walk in paths without dragons and adders. But, we shall walk through the midst of them, and "tread them under our feet."” And how much more glorious a kingdom is this than any outward rule or control could be! To be a king inside, but a slave outside, is a great triumph. It is the best our hearts can conceive. To be destitute, afflicted, and tormented. To be stoned, torn apart, and slain with the sword. To wander in sheepskins and goatskins, and in deserts, mountains, dens, and caves. Yet, through it all, to be kings in a kingdom of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. This is a kingdom that none but God could give, and none but God-like souls could receive. We have seen or heard of a few such kings. All hearts have acknowledged their unconscious effect. I read about one of the members of the St. Cyr monastery. Their devotion made the monasteries and their superiors hate them. They were cast out as evil from their community. One was sent as a prisoner to a monastery where his enemies dwelt. There, he suffered cruel and degrading treatment. Although he came from a noble background and was a former leader, he had to do the simplest tasks . He was forced to carry a heavy burden on his back and made to beg with a sign on his chest saying he was the worst of the worst. But, through it all, the saint's spirit triumphed. Nothing disturbed his calm or soured his Christ-like sweetness. For his persecutors, he never had anything but words of kindness and smiles of love. At last, by the divine kingdom's great power, he won all hearts. He became the trusted friend and adviser, and the beloved ruler of his former enemies who had once delighted in persecuting him. “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Mathew 5:5) . By his meekness, he conquered and became king. At one time, a dangerous criminal was sent to the monastery for imprisonment. He was so violent that no bonds sufficed to bind him, and no strength could control him. At last, he was taken to the cell of a brother from St. Cyr. They were shut up together. Even the stolid monks recognized that divine meekness. It had a power to conquer that surpassed all they knew. The saint received the violent man as a beloved brother and smiled upon him with heavenly kindness. But the criminal returned it with abuse and violence. He broke the monk’s furniture and destroyed his bed, he kicked him, beat him, and tore his hair, and spat upon him. He exhausted himself in his violence against him. Through it all, the monk resisted nothing. He spoke only words of love. Finally, the criminal, worn out with fury, paused to catch his breath. The beaten and outraged man then smiled at his persecutor with deep love and compassion. It was as if he wanted to comfort him for his misery. It was more than the criminal could bear. Hatred, revenge, and anger he could repay in kind. But, he had no weapons against such love and meekness. His heart was conquered. He fell at the feet of the saint and washed them with his tears, as he entreated forgiveness for his cruelty, and vowed a lifelong loyalty to his service. And from that moment all trouble with that criminal was over. He followed the saint about like a loving and faithful dog, eager to do or to be anything the other might desire. We are made for this purpose. We are born of a kingly race, and are heirs to this Inexpressible kingdom; “ and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him .”(Romans 8:17) With that we could realize this, and, see in every act of service or surrender, an upward step. It would lead us to our kingdom and throne! I mean this in a very practical sense. I mean that our daily, humble tasks and small sacrifices, if done well, will be steps up a ladder to our thrones. If we are faithful over the "few things" of our earthly kingdom, we shall be made rulers over the "many things" of the heavenly kingdom. He who serves and suffers for Christ will reign with Him. He will be the "chiefest" in His kingdom of love. Knowing this, who would hesitate to turn the other cheek? A kingdom and a throne are to be won. Joseph was a type of all this. In slavery and in prison he reigned as king, as truly as when seated on Pharaoh’s throne or riding in Pharaoh’s chariot. (See Gen. 39:6) “So he left all that he had in Joseph’s charge, and because of him he had no concern about anything but the food he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance.” (Genesis 39:22- 23.) “ And the keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever was done there, he was the one who did it. The keeper of the prison paid no attention to anything that was in Joseph’s charge, beca use the LORD was with him. And whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed.” He became the greatest by being the least, the chiefest by being servant of all. Dear reader, are you ruling in this way, in this kind of kingdom? Are you the greatest in your small world — at home, church, or in your social circle? Then be the least. Be the servant of everyone. If not, your kingdom is not Christ’s kingdom, and your throne is not shared with Him. Accessing the secrets and power of this inner kingdom is not a fantasy . It’s not just an imagined victory. Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.”(Mathew 18:2 -3) It is a kingdom of childlike hearts, and only such can en ter it. We admire their unquestioning obedience to authority. To be the greatest in this divine kingdom, one must have the most of this child's trusting, tender, and obedient heart. It is guileless and self-forgetting. “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Fa ther who is in heaven.”( Matthew 7:21 ) .It is not saying, but doing, that will avail us here. We must be a child, or we cannot sit on the child’s throne. And to be a child means to do the Father’s will, since the very essence of true childhood is the spirit of obedience united to the spirit of trust. Become a little child. Set aside your greatness, self-assertion, and wisdom. Give up your strength and self-dependence. Consent to die to your old self. Be born again into the kingdom of God. The only way out of one life into another is by a death to one and a new birth into the other. It is the old story, therefore, reiterated so often and in so many different ways, of through death to life. Die, then, that you my live. Lose your own life that you may find Christ’s life. fields.title: The Chariots Of God
fields.body_html:
God's chariots are spiritual vehicles, often disguised as trials or hardships that carry the soul to victory and spiritual growth. Unlike visible, earthly chariots, these divine chariots are unseen and require faith to recognize. By embracing life’s challenges as Through God’s means of uplifting us, we can rise above difficulties and experience spiritual triumph. Trusting in God’s invisible power leads to true victory.

“The chariots of God are twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them; Sinai is now in the sanctuary. (Psalm 68:17.)

Chariots are for transportation and moving forward. Earthly chariots carry their riders to their destinations, overcoming all obstacles. God's chariots carry their souls. No words can express the glorious places to which that soul shall arrive who travels in the chariots of God. And our verse tells us t hey are “very many.” All around us on every side they wait for us; but we, sadly, we do not always see them. Earth’s chariots are always visible, but God’s chariots are Invisible.

“So he sent there horses and chariots and a great army, and they came by night and surrounded the city.

When the servant of the man of God rose early in the morning and went out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was all around the city. And the servant said, “Alas, my master! What shall we do?

He said, “Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them. “Then Elisha prayed and said, “O Lord, please open his eyes that he may see.” So the Lord opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.” (2 Kings 6:14 -17) This is the prayer we need to pray for ourselves and for one another, “Lord, open our eyes that we may see.” For the world all around us is full of God’s horses and chariots, waiting to carry us to plac es of glorious victory. But they do not look like chariots. They look instead like enemies, sufferings, trials, defeats, misunderstandings, disappointments, unkindnesses. They look like massive cars of misery, waiting to crush us. But they are chariots of triumph. They can take us to the heights of victory our souls long for.

If we would “ride on the high places of the earth , ” we must get into the chariots that can take us there; and only the “chariots of God” are equal to such lofty riding as this . (Deuteronomy 32:12-13) “The Lord alone guided him ; no foreign god was with him. He made him ride on the high places of the land, and he ate the produce of the field, and he suckled him with honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock.”

“Then you shall take delight in the Lord, and I will make you ride on the heights of the earth. I will feed you with the heritage of Jacob, your father, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken. (Isaiah 58:14).

We may make out of each event in our lives either a Juggernaut car to crush us, or a chariot in which to ride to heights of victory. It all depends upon how we take them; whether we lie down under our trials and let them roll over and crush us, or whether we climb up into them as into a chariot, and make them carry us triumphantly onward and upward.

“And as they still went on and talked, behold, chariots of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them. And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. And Elisha saw it and he cried, “My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! And he saw him no more. Then he took hold of his own clothes and tore them in two pieces.”(2Kings 2:11 - 12).Whenever we mount into God’s chariots , the same thing happens to us spiritually that happened to Elisha. We shall have a translation. Not into the heavens above us, as Elisha did, but into the heaven within us, which, after all, is almost a grander translation than his. We shall be carried up away from the low earthly groveling plane of life, where everything hurts and everything is unhappy, up into the “heavenly places in Christ Jesus,” where we shall ride in triumph over all below.

“And raised us with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus ,” (Ephesians 2:6). These “heavenly places” a re interior, not exterior, and the road that leads to them is also interior.

But the chariot that carries the soul over this road is generally some outward loss, or trial, or disappointment; some chastening that does not indeed seem for the present to be joyous, but grievous; but that nevertheless afterward yielded the peaceable fruits of righteousness to them that are exercised thereby.

“And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives. It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons. Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment, all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.”( Hebrews 12:5-11).

Look upon these scoldings , no matter how grievous they may be for the present, as God’s chariots sent to carry your souls into the “high places” of spiritual achievem ent and uplifting, and you will find that they are, after all, “paved with love.”

“King Solomon made himself a carriage from the wood of Lebanon. He made its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple; its interior was inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.” (Song of Solomon 3:9-10 ). Your own individual chariot may look very unlovely. It may be a cross-grained relative or friend; it may be the result of human malice, or cruelty, or neglect; but every chariot sent by God must necessari ly be paved with love, since God is love, and God’s love is the sweetest, softest, tenderest thing to rest one’s self upon that was ever found by any soul anywhere. It is His love indeed that sends the chariot.

“Was your wrath against the rivers, O Lord ? Was your anger against the rivers, or your indignation against the sea, when you rode on your horses, on your chariot of salvation? You stripped the sheath from your bow, calling for many arrows. Selah, you split the earth with rivers. The mountains saw you and writhed; the raging waters swept on; the deep gave forth its voice; it lifted its hands on high. The sun and moon stood still in their place at the light of your arrows as they sped, at the flash of your glittering spear. You marched through the earth in fury; you threshed the nations in anger. You went out for the salvation of your people, or the salvation of your anointed. (Habakkuk.3:8-13) Here, the prophet tells us that it was God’s displeasure against the obstacles that beset the path of His people that made Him come to their rescue, riding in His “chariots of salvation.” Everything becomes a “chariot of salvation” when God rides upon it. The “clouds” that darken our skies and seem to shut out the shining of the sun of righteousness are, after all, if we only knew it, His chariots, into which we may mount with Him, and “ride prosperously” over all the darkness.

“Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, in your splendor and majesty! In your majesty ride out victoriously for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness; let your right hand teach you awesome deeds!”(Psalm 45:3 - 4). “He rode on a cherub and flew; he came swiftly on the wings of the wind.” ((Psalm 18:10). “There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides through the heaven s to your help, through the skies in his majesty.” (Deuteronomy 33:26). A late writer has said that we cannot, by even the most vigorous and toilsome efforts, sweep away the clouds, but we can climb so high above them as to reach the clear atmosphere overhead; and he who rides with God rides upon the heavens far above all earth-born clouds.

“O kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing praises to the Lord, Selah to him who rides in the heavens, the ancient heavens; behold, he sends out his voice, his mighty voice. Ascribe power to God, whose majesty is over Israel, and whose power is in the skies.”(Psalm 68:32 -34 ) . This may sound fanciful, but it is really exceedingly practical when we begin to act it out in our daily lives.

I knew a lady who had a very slow servant. She was excellent in every way and very useful. But her slowness irritated her naturally quick mistress.

The lady would get angry with the girl twenty times a day. And, twenty times, she would regret it and try to control her anger. But it was in vain. Her life was made miserable by the conflict. One day, it occurred to her that she had, for a long while, been praying for patience. Perhaps this slow servant was the very chariot the Lord had sent to carry her soul into patience. She immediately accepted it as such, and from that time used the slowness of her servant as a chariot for her soul. And the result was a victory of patience that no slowness of anybody was ever able to disturb.

At one of our conventions, I knew a sister who had to sleep in a room with two others because of the crowd. She wanted to sleep, but they wanted to talk. The first night, she was disturbed. She lay there, feeling frustrated and upset, long after the others had quieted down. She could have slept. But the next day, she heard about God’s chariots. That night, she decided to see the talking sisters as her chariots.

They would help her learn sweetness and patience. She lay there, feeling peaceful and calm. But it got very late, and they should all have been as leep. So, she quietly said, “Sisters, I’m lying here riding in a chariot.” This brought complete silence. Her chariot had carried her to victory, both inside and out.

If we choose to ride in God’s chariots, not our own, we would experience the same.

“ Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the Lord! And yet he is wise and brings disaster; he does not call back his words, but will arise against the house of the evildoers and against the helpers of those who work iniquity. The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the Lord stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together. (Isaiah 31:1- 3) “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the Lord our God. They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright. ” (Psalm. 20:7 -8). Our constant temptation is to trust in the “chariots of Egypt.” We can see them. They are real and look substantial. But, God's chariots are invisible and intangible. It's hard to believe they are there. Our eyes are not opened to see them.

“By your messengers you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, ‘with my many chariots I have gone up the heights of the mountains, to the far recesses of Lebanon; I felled its tallest cedars, its choicest cypresses; I entered its farthest lodging place, its most fruitful forest.” We try to reach the high places with the “multitude of our chariots.” We first depend on one thing, then another. We do this to improve our spirit and gain spiritual victories. We “go down to Egypt for help.” (2 Kings 19: 23).

And God is obliged often to destroy all our own chariots before he can bring us to the point of mounting into His.

“And in that day, declares the Lord, I will cut off your horses from among you and will destroy your chariots ;”( Micah 5:10). “An d to overthrow the throne of kingdoms. I am about to destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the nations, and overthrow the chariots and their riders. And the horses and their riders shall go down, everyone by the sword of his brother.” (Haggai. 2:22) .We rely too much on a dear friend to aid our spiritual growth. So, the Lord must separate us from that friend. We believe our spiritual growth relies on a favorite preacher's ministry. Now, we are mysteriously removed. We see our prayer-meeting or Bible-class as our main source of spiritual strength. Now, we are unable to attend it. And the “chariot of God,” which alone can carry us to the places where we hoped to be taken by the instrumentalities upon which we have been depending, is to be found in the very deprivations we have so mourned over. God must burn up with the fire of His love every chariot of our own that stands in the way of our mounting into His.

“For behold, the Lord will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire.”(Isaiah. 66:15) .Let us be thankful, then, for every trial that will help to destroy our chariots, and will compel us to take refuge in the chariot of God, which stands ready and waiting beside us.

“For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him. He only is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be shaken. On God rests my salvation and my glory; my mighty rock, my refuge is God. Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us. Selah.” (Psalm. 62:5 -8).We have to be brought to the place where all other refuges fail us, before we can say, He only. We say, He and something else.

"His, and my experience," or "my church relationships," or "my Christian work"; and all that comes after the "and" must be taken away from us, or must be proved useless, before we can come to "He only."” As long as visible chariots are at hand, the soul will not mount into the invisible ones.

“Sing to God, si ng praises to his name; lift up a song to him who rides through the deserts; his name is the Lord; exult before him!” (Psalm. 68:4).If we want to ride with God “upon the heavens,” we have to be brought to an end of all riding upon the earth.

“Your procession is seen, O God, the procession of my God, my King, into the sanctuary.” (Psalm.

68:24). To see God’s goings, we must get into the sanctuary of his presence; and to share in His goings and go with Him, we must abandon all earthly goings.

“A man’s steps are from the Lord; how then can man understand his way?”(Proverbs.20:24). “My steps have held fast to your paths; my feet have not slipped.”(Psalm. 17:5).

“I waited patiently for the Lord; he inclined to me and heard my cry.”(Psalm.40:1). When we m ount into God’s chariot our goings are “established,” for no obstacles can hinder its triumphal course. All losses therefore are gains that bring us to this.

“But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith.” (Philippians.3:7 -9). Paul understood this, and he gloried in the losses which brought him such unspeakable gain.

“So to keep me from becoming co nceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited. Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me. But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me. For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.” (2 Corinthians.12:7 -10) Even the "thorn in the flesh," the messenger of Satan sent to trouble him, became just a chariot for his willing heart, taking him to victories he could not have reached otherwise. To "take pleasure" in one’s struggles — what is that if not turning them into the greatest of chariots?

Joseph dreamed of his future triumphs and reign. But, to the eye of sense, the chariots that carried him there were bitter failures. It was a strange road to a kingdom. It went through slavery and a prison. Yet, there was no other way for Joseph to reach his triumph. His dream, Gen. 37:5- 10 “Now Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers they hated him even more. He said to them, “Hear this dream that I have dreamed: Behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and stood upright. And behold, your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf.” His brothers said to him, Are you indeed to reign over us? Or are you indeed to rule over us? So they hated him even more for his dreams and for his words. Then he dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers and said, Behold, I have dreamed another dream. Behold, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me. But when he told it to his father and to his brothers, his father rebuked him and said to him, what is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves to t he ground before you?”

His chariots, Genesis. 37:19- 20 “They said to one another, “Here comes this dreamer. Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. Then we will say that a fierce animal has devoured him, and we will see what will b ecome of his dreams.” Genesis 27:28 “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth and plenty of grain and wine.” Genesis 39:19 -20 “As soon as his master heard the words that his wife spoke to him, “This is the way your servant treated me,” his anger was kindled. And Joseph’s master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the king’s prisoners were confined, and he was there in prison.” And Joseph’s master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the ki ng’s prisoners were confined, and he was there in prison; how he rode in his chariots, Genesis. 39:1- 6 “Now Joseph had been brought down to Egypt, and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, had bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there. The Lord was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, and he was in the house of his Egyptian master. His master saw that the Lord was with him and that the Lord caused all that he did to succeed in his hands. So Joseph found favor in his sight and attended him, and he made him overseer of his house and put him in charge of all that he had. From the time that he made him overseer in his house and over all that he had, the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; the blessing of the Lord was on all that he had, in house and field. So he left all that he had in Joseph’s charge, and because of him he had no concern about anything but the food he ate.”

Genesis 39:21- 23 “ But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison. And the keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever was done there, he was the one who did it. The keeper of the prison paid no attention to anything that was in Joseph’s charge, because the LORD was with him.

And whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed .” His triumph.

And now a word as to how one is to mount into these chariots. My answer would be simply this: Find out where God is in each one of them, and hide yourself in Him. Or, in other words, do what the little child does when trouble comes, who finds its mother and hides in her arms. The real chariot, after all that, that takes us triumphantly through is the carrying of God.

Isaiah. 46:4 “Even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save.” The baby carried in the chariot of its mother’s arms rides triumphantly through the hardest places and does not even know they are hard.

Isaiah. 63: 9 “ In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them; in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; he lifted them and carried them all the days of old.”.And how much more w e, who are carried in the chariot of the “arms of God.” Get into your chariot, then. Take each thing that is wrong in your lives as God’s chariot for you. No matter who built the wrong, it is now God's chariot for you. It must carry you to a heavenly place of triumph. Shut out all the second causes, and find the Lord in it. Say, “Lord, open my eyes that I may see, not the visible enemy, but thy unseen chariots of deliverance.”

Accept His will in the trial, whatever it may be, and hide yourself in His arm s of love. Say, “Your will be done; Your will be done!” over and over.

Shut out every other thought but the one thought of submission to His will and of trust in His love.

Make your trial your chariot. Then, your soul will "ride upon the heavens" with God in a way you never dreamed possible.

I have no doubt. If our eyes were opened, we would see our homes, businesses, and streets filled with the "chariots of God." There is no need for any of us to walk for lack of chariots.

That cross inmate of your household, who has made life a burden, may henceforth be a glorious chariot.

It will carry you to the heights of heavenly patience and longsuffering. Your misunderstanding, mortification, unkindness, disappointment, loss, and defeat are chariots. They wait to carry you to the heights of victory you have longed for.

Then, with thankful hearts, mount into them. Lose sight of all second causes in the shining of His love.

He will carry you in His arms, ensuring your safety and celebrating victory over it all.
