So, it might sever its connection with the vine for that part of its life. Of course that which sought an independent life would wither and die in the very nature of things. And just so is it with us who are branches of Christ the true vine. We can do nothing, great or small, without withering and death. The same is true for a branch of the natural vine. It will show us, at once, how fatal is the divorce I have spoken of, to the oneness with Christ, for which our souls hunger. We all know, more or less, that we cannot live our religious life without Him. But, in our socalled temporal life, who thinks our daily tasks should be done for Christ? Tasks like keeping house, doing business, making calls, darning stockings, sweeping, trimming a bonnet, or entertaining guests. Only those who abide in Him and do them in His strength can do them rightly. If it is Christ in the Christian leading the prayer meeting, then they are one. So, it must also be Christ in the Christian who is to keep the house and make the bargain. So, one duty is as religious as the other. It is the man that makes the action, not the action the man. If we "acknowledge God in all our ways," we will make our daily life as solemn and sweet as our religious occasions. We should do everything, even eating and drinking, for His glory. If our religion is truly our life, it must be in everything we do. No act, however human or natural, can escape its control and guidance. If God is always with us, He is with us in our business and social times as much as in our religious times. His presence is as solemn in one moment as in another. If we for ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘for we are indeed his offspring " (Acts 17:28), then we can do nothing without Him, whether we know it or not. And facts are stubborn things, thank God, and do not alter for all our feelings. In Psalm 127:1- 2 ‘’unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain. It is in vain that you rise early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep. ” We have a very striking illustration of this truth. The Psalmist says, "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord keeps the city, the watchman wakes in vain." It is vain for you to rise early, to sit up late, and to eat the bread of sorrows; for so He gives His beloved sleep.” The two things, done in vain unle ss the Lord is in them, are purely secular. They are simple business matters on the human plane of life. The lesson is only impressive for this: It proved God's presence in temporal things. Those were undeniable facts. In truth, the Bible is full of this fact, and the only wonder is how any believer in the Bible could have overlooked it. God is present in all daily life, from building cities to counting hairs and noting a sparrow's fall. He is the mainspring of it all. In all we do, even eating and drinking, we must do it for Him and His glory. We are urged to live and walk in the light, so our works, both temporal and spiritual, show they are "wrought in God." This brings unspeakable comfort to every loving Christian heart. It turns all of life into a sacrament. It makes the kitchen, workshop, nursery, and parlor as sacred a place of service to the Lord as the prayer meeting, mission board, or charity visit. A dear young Christian mother and housekeeper came to me, sorely grieved, because of her busy, worldly life. “There seems,” she said, “to be nothing spiritual about my life from one week’s end to the other. My large family of little children is so engrossing that I have no time for anything but attending to them and my household duties. Each night, I go to bed sick at heart. I have felt separated from my Lord all day and could do nothing for Him.” I told her what I wrote above. I assured her that all would change if she would see and acknowledge God in these homely duties. She must recognize her total dependence on Him to do them. Her heart welcomed the good news with gladness. Months later, she told me that, from then on, life had become a transformed and glorified thing. It was now filled with the Lord's presence and the sweetness of serving Him. Another Christian, a young lady from a fashionable family, came to me. She was in grief. Much of her life, she felt separated from God and sensed no presence of Him. I told her to avoid anything that could cause such a separation. But she assured me it was impossible. The things she meant were not wrong. “For instance,” she said, “it is my duty to visit my mother. Yet, nothing separates me so much from God as visits” “But how would it be,” I asked, “if you visited as service to the Lord and for His glory?” “What!” she exclaimed, “visits for God? I never heard of such a thing.” “But why not?” I asked, "If it is right to make visits at all, it ought to be done for God. We are commanded to do all for His glory. If it is not right, you ought not to do it." As a Christian,” I continued, “you must not do anything that you cannot do for Him.” “I see! I see!” she exclaimed, after a little pause, “and it makes all life look so different! “Nothing can separate me from Him but sin. But, any act done to His glory will draw me closer and make His presence more real.” These two instances will illustrate my meaning. I'm sure thousands of weary souls would be transformed if they realized and acted on these truths. An old spiritual writer says, to become a saint, we need not change our works. We must only aim them at God. We must do them for His glory, in His strength. Before, we did them for ourselves, with our own power. This means what our Lord meant when He said, "Without me you can do nothing." There is another side to this truth. It is comforting. The Psalmist develops it in the verses I quoted. “It is vain,” he says, “to rise early, to sit up late, and to eat the bread of sorrows.” Or, in other words, “What is the use of all this worry and strain? “W ork will amount to nothing unless God is in it. If he is, what folly to fret or be burdened? "His presence means He assumes care and responsibility for it all." Ah, it is vain indeed, and I wish all of God's children knew it! We mothers ought to know it. "Our ways with our children would teach us, if we had the 'eyes to see.' How many mothers have risen early, sat up late, and eaten the bread of sorrows, just to give sleep to their beloved children?" And how grieved their hearts would have been if, after all their pains, the children had refused to rest. I can appeal to some mother hearts, I am sure, as thoroughly understanding my meaning. Memories will arise of the rosy boy coming in at night, tired from play. His knees were out, and his coat was torn. We stayed up late and rose early to patch it all. We wanted the cause of all the mischief to rest undisturbed in happy childhood sleep. How vain, and worse, would it have been for that beloved darling to have sat up late, risen early, and eaten the bread of sorrows? His mother was doing it for him just so he wouldn't have to. If this is true of mothers, it must be more so of their Maker. He came among us in bodily form to bear our burdens, carry our sorrows, and do our work, so we might "enter into His rest." “For whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his. ”(Hebrews 4:10). He has learned, at last, a lesson. Without Christ, he can do nothing. But, he can do all things through Christ, who strengthens him. So, he has given up all self-effort. He has abandoned himself to God to work in him to do His will. This and this only is the rest that remains for the people of God. Scientific men are seeking to resolve all forces in nature into one primal force. Unity of origin is the present cry of science. Light, heat, sound are all said to be the products of one force differently applied, and that force is motion. All things, say the scientists, can be resolved back to this. I cannot say if they are right or wrong. But, the Bible reveals a grand primal force behind motion. It is God's force. God is at the source of everything, God is the origin of everything, and God is the explanation of everything. Without Him was not anything made that was made, and without Him is not anything done that is done. It is no mystery. It is a simple fact. Our Lord says, "Without me you can do nothing." Of Himself, He said, “I can do nothing on my own." He meant that He and His Father were so one that any independent action was impossible. It must be a glorious necessity between our souls and Christ. That is why He said we could do nothing without Him. It means He has made us one with Himself. So, we cannot act independently towards Him, as He could not towards His Father. Dear Christian, do n’t you see here a glimpse of a wonderful glory? Let’s believe that without Him, we can truly do nothing. We must believe it because it’s true. But let’s recognize this truth and start living by it from now on. Let’s turn away from living apart from Christ. From now on, let’s acknowledge Him in everything we do. Everything we do should be as a service to Him, for His glory. We rely on Him alone for wisdom, strength, patience, and everything else we need to live well. As I said before, it is not so much a change of acts that will be necessary, as a change of motive and of dependence. The house will be kept, the children cared for, and the business run, perhaps as before. Outwardly, it will be the same. But, inwardly, God will be acknowledged, depended on, and served. There will be a great difference between a life of ease in His presence and a life of painful effort apart from Him. Bringing God into our affairs will yield many benefits. We will gain divine wisdom in their conduct. There will be a greater speed in accomplishing them. We will see a surprising increase in our resources. We will better grasp the true nature of things. And, we will expand in ways that will amaze our cramped souls. I mean this literally. The house will be nicer and easier to maintain. The children will learn faster. The stockings will be mended quickly. The hosts will be better at entertaining guests. The servants will be easier to manage. The deal will be more satisfying. And life will be sweeter and more peaceful. God will be i n every moment of it, and when He’s present, everything goes well. In this simple way, the soul will develop the habit of "abiding in Christ." His presence will become the most real thing in our lives, and we will have a quiet, private connection with Him that brings us joy. A child of God may ask, "What is the quickest way to reach the highest union with God in this life?" There is no quicker way than the one I have been declaring. By the homely path of everyday duties done thus in God and for God, the sublimest heights are reached. Not as a reward, but as a natural result. If we abide in Him and refuse to leave Him, we shall be where He is. All that He is will be ours. If you wish to know, dear reader, the divine union in your soul, start today to practice what I have suggested. Offer every moment and every action of your life to God. Say to Him, “Lord, I do this in you and for your glory. You are my strength, my wisdom, and everything I need. I rely only on you.” Refuse to live even for a single moment or do anything without Him. Keep doing this until it becomes a habit for your soul. Soon, you will understand the deep desires of your soul, and they will be fulfilled in the constant presence of Christ, your life within.

fields.title: The One Hundred And Thirty-ninth Psalm
fields.body_html:
In Psalm 139, we are reminded that God is always with us, no matter where we are or what we're facing. His presence is constant, and He understands us completely, offering love and care like a devoted parent. No darkness or difficulty can separate us from Him, and His continual presence provides peace, security, and strength in every circumstance.

Your great hospitality surrounds us like a boundless sea. We cannot lose ourselves where all is home, nor drift away from you.”

Very few of us understand the full meaning of the words in Matthew. 1:23, “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel . ” This short sentence reveals the world's greatest truth. God, the Almighty Creator of Heaven and Earth, is not a distant god in a glorious Heaven.

He lives with us, in our poor, helpless lives, as close as we are to ourselves. This seems so incredible to the human heart that we are slow to believe it. But, the Bible teaches it as fact, from cover to cover.

Any honest mind cannot deny this.

In the very beginning of Genesis we read of the “presence of the Lord God amongst the trees of the garden.” Since then, He is always revealed to us. He has a daily, close relationship with His peop le everywhere. In Exodus we find Him asking them to make Him a “sanctuary that He might dwell among them.” He is recorded as having "walked" with them in the wilderness, and as "taking up His home" with them in the Promised Land. He taught them to rely on Him as an ever-present Friend and Helper.

They should consult Him about all their affairs and give Him their lives. And finally, He came in Christ in bodily form. He dwelt in the world as a man among men. He made Himself bone of our bone and flesh of our flesh. He took upon Him our nature. He revealed to us, in the most real way, a great and blessed truth. He intended to be with us always, even unto the end of the world.

Those who believe this truth will find its solution. It will solve all their life's troubles. As a little girl, I remember that, in trouble, my parents' arrival always relieved me. When I heard one say, "Daughter, I am here," every burden dropped and every anxiety stilled. It was their simple presence that did it. They did not need to promise to relieve me. They did not need to tell me their plans. Their presence was all the assurance I required. It meant everything would be set right and all would go well for me.

After their arrival, I only wanted to see how they would do it.

They must be exceptional parents. Their children are very confident. I think they were. But our God is exceptional. So, the application is absolute. His presence is all we need.

It would be enough for us, even if we had not a single promise nor a single revelation of His plans. The Bible says, "I will be with you." It has stilled all questions and fears. Who can doubt it? He meant to assure us that His infinite wisdom, love, and power are on our side. Over and over again in my childhood, have the magic words, “Oh, there is mother!” It brought me relief and comfort. In my later years, I've heard, "Oh, there is God!" spoken with reverence.” brought me a far more blessed deliverance. With Him present, what could I have to fear? He has said, “ Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you .”(Hebrews 13:5). So, I may boldly say, The Lord is my helper. I will not fear what man shall do to me. I still recall the inspiring sense of security that came with my father's presence. I never feared anything when he was by. And surely with my Heavenly Father by, there can be no possible room for fear.

I seek to make clear and definite the fact of "Emmanuel, God with us." Its practical help and comfort inspire me. I am sure that few of God's own children truly believe it. They may say they do. They may repeat a thousand times, in a devout tone, "Oh, yes, we know that God is always present with us, but, and in this "but," the whole story is told. There are no “buts” in the vocabulary of the soul that accepts His presence as a literal fact. Such a soul is joyously triumphant over every suggestion of fear or of doubt. It has God, and that is enough for it. His presence is its certain security and supply, always, and for everything.

I beg my readers to turn with me to the 139th Psalm. There, we will find a blessed revelation of this truth. The central thought of the Psalm is to be found in verses 7 to 12, “Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me. If I say, “Surely the darkness shall cover me, and the light about me be night,” even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day, for darkness is as light with you.”

This passage is the strongest proof of His constant presence with us, wherever we are or whatever we do. People seek to be in the Lord's presence. But they cannot escape it. There is no place in the universe where He is not. Not in heaven, hell, or the farthest sea. No darkness can hide from Him, even for a moment. The reason is, He "has possessed our reins." It means He is not only with us, but within us.

So, He must accompany us wherever we go.

We must accept it as true. Our Lord's words, "Look, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world," were not just a beautiful sentiment. They are an undeniable fact. He is with us, and we cannot get away from Him.

In thick darkness, we may see nothing. We may think, often think that He does not see us. But our Psalm assures us that the darkness hides not from Him. In fact, darkness and light are both alike to Him. We are as present to His view and as plainly seen in our darkest spiritual depths as in our brightest light. The darkness may hide Him from us, but it does not hide us from Him. Nor does any spiritual distance or wandering take us from His presence. Not even if we sink into sin in our wandering. In the uttermost parts of the sea, or wherever we may be, He is ever present to hold and to lead us. There is not a moment nor a place where we can be left without His care.

Sometimes, confusion makes us unaware of the loving care of our nurses. A child in confusion might cry out for its mother, and its sad cries will break her heart. Meanwhile, she is holding the child's hot hand, cooling its fevered head, and caring for it with a mother's love. The sickness may hide the mother from the child, but it doesn't hide the child from the mother.

And just so it is with our God and us. Our doubts, fears, sorrows, and sins cannot hide us from Him.

But they often hide Him from us. He has said that the darkness and light are alike to Him. If our faith accepts this, we can trust in dark times. Though we cannot see or feel Him, our God cares for us. He will never leave us.

Whether, however, this abiding presence of our God will be a joy to us or a sorrow will depend upon what we know about Him. If we think of Him as a stern tyrant, intent only on His own glory, we shall be afraid of His continual presence. If we see Him as a loving Father, we'll be glad. He wants only our happiness. So, we'll be thankful to have Him with us always. For the presence and the care of love can never mean anything but good to the one beloved.

The Psalm we are considering shows us that God's presence is love. It brings us infinite comfort and rest. He says in verses 1 to 5, “O Lord, you have searched me and known me! You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down and are acquainted with all my ways. Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O Lord, you know it altogether. You hem me in, behind and before, and lay your hand upon me.”

Our God knows us and understands us, and is acquainted with all our ways. No one else in all the world understands us. People may misinterpret our actions and misjudge our motives. Our natural characteristics are not taken into account, nor our inherited tendencies considered. No one makes allowances for our ill health; no one realizes how much we have to contend with. But our Father knows it all. He understands us. His judgment considers every part of our character, both conscious and unconscious. It also considers what controls our actions. Only an all comprehending love can be just, and our God is just. No wonder Faber can say: Nowhere on Earth are its sorrows felt more than in Heaven. Nowhere are its failings judged more kindly. Some of you may fear His justice, thinking it would be against you. But do you not see? It is all on your side, just as a mother's justice is, because He knows our frame and remembers that we are dust. No human judge can ever do this, and to me, this comprehension of God is one of my most blessed comforts. Often, I do not understand myself; all within looks confused and hopelessly tangled. But I remember that He has searched me. He knows me. He understands my perplexing thoughts. So, I may leave the whole mess to Him to unravel.

And my soul sinks at once, as on downy pillows, into a place of the most blissful rest. Then, because of His complete knowledge of our needs, what comfort it is to be told that He knows our down sitting and our uprising. He compasses our path, and takes note of our lying down. Our God does for us what a mother does for her foolish, careless, ignorant, but dearly loved little ones. When a mother is with her children, she thinks of their comfort and well-being always before her own. They must have comfortable, draught-free seats. She must endure any discomfort. Their beds must be soft and their blankets warm, let hers be what they may.

Their paths must be smooth and safe, even though she is obliged to walk in rough and dangerous ways.

Her own comfort, as compared with that of her children, is of no account in a loving mother’s eyes.

Surely, our God is not less capable of a self-sacrificing love than the mothers in this world. He must be better and greater on the line of love and self-sacrifice than any mother He ever made. He has assured us that He knows our down sitting and uprising. He compasses our path and our lying down. So, we can be sure, in all the little details of our lives, we get the very best that His love, wisdom, and power can provide. I mean this in a very literal sense. I mean that He cares for our seats and our beds. He sees that we each have the best kind for our highest development.

And just on this last point is where He is so much better than any mother can be. His love is a wise love that sees the outcome of things and cares more for our highest good than for that which is lower. A mother's weak love can't see beyond a child's comfort. It can't bear to cause any discomfort. But God's strong, wise love can permit some pain. It is for the sake of the future glory that will come from it.

At home and abroad, let us trust God. He knows all about our daily lives. So, let Him choose our seats, beds, and other small things.

For we are told in our Psalm that He “besets” our path. We have some of us have known what it was to be “beset” by unwelcome and unpleasant people or things. But we never thought, perhaps, t hat we were beset by God. He loves us so much that He cannot leave us alone.

No coldness or rebuffs can drive Him away. Yet it is gloriously true! Moreover , He besets us “behind” as well as before. Just as a mother does. She goes after her children. She picks up all they dropped and clears away their rubbish.

We mothers start this in the nursery with the blocks and toys. We do it all our lives. We try to fix what our children have left undone or wrong. It takes a lot of effort and trouble, but our love makes that effort seem small compared to caring for our children. What good mother would ever turn away a sad, crying child? Or refuse to help a boy untangle his kite strings? Even if the knots and tangles are his fault, her love understands and feels for those mistakes. So, she works even harder to help fix them.

Our God does all this, and more, for us from infancy. He does it long before we are aware of it, until the end of our earthly lives. We have seen Him before us, perhaps, but we have never thought of Him as behind us as well. Yet, it is a blessed fact. He is behind us. He longs to make crooked things straight, untangle our knots, and atone for our wrongs. If any of us has a troubling past, let us be happy. The God who is behind us will set it all straight if we commit it to Him. He can even make our mistakes work together for good. Ah! It is a grand thing to be surrounded by God.

Then again, what comfort in verses 14 to 16: "I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.

A Wonderful work are your works; my soul knows it very well. My frame was not hidden from you when I was being made in secret, intricately woven in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them.”

We often dislike, more than we admit, how we were made. Our mental or moral “make - up” does not suit us. We think that if we were created with less of this or more of that, we'd be more successful. If we were less impulsive or more enthusiastic, we could better serve God. We could also be more satisfactory to ourselves and to Him. We believe that if we were more like someone we admire, it would help too. And we are tempted sometimes to think that with our miserable make-up, it is hopeless to expect to please Him.

If we truly realized that God made us, we would see the folly of all this at once. But, we feel that He had little hand in it. We think we were put together haphazardly, leaving our characters to chance. We believe in creation in the general, but not in the particular, when it comes to ourselves. This Psalm shows that God oversaw our creation. He managed even the smallest details. Figuratively, he wrote down what each "member" was to be when none existed yet. So, we are, by nature, what God wants.

He made us do a special work. I mean, of course, our natural characteristics, not the perversion of them by sin on our parts.

There is something very glorifying to the Creator in this way of looking at it. Genius always seeks to express itself in many ways. No true artist repeats himself. Each painting or statue is a new expression of his creative power. An art exhibition should not have two identical pictures. If it did, it would lower the value of art. The same is true for us, as we are "God's workmanship." His creative power expresses itself differently in each one of us.

And in the individual "make-up," which sometimes troubles us, there is a unique power. Without it, the day of the exhibition, when we are to praise His glory, would be incomplete. He asks only this: since He made us, He should manage us. He alone understands us, so only He can do it.

The man who makes an intricate machine is best suited to manage and repair it. Anyone else who meddles is likely to spoil it. Given our complex minds and our poor control of them, we should be thankful to hand them to their Creator and leave them in His hands. We can be sure He will make the best of us. Even with our "peculiar temperaments" and flaws, we will be made into vessels of honor.

We will be sanctified and fit for the Master's use, ready for every good work.

I once read a saying from an old Quaker writer that stayed with me: "Be content to be just what God made you." It helped me understand my thoughts. I believe that to truly submit to God, we must accept ourselves as He created us, just as we accept our daily circumstances. If we did not exist, a part of God’s creation would be missing. His work would be incomplete. Besides, com plaining about ourselves is like complaining about the One who made us, which must hurt Him. Let’s be content and trust the Divine Potter to shape us as He sees best and use us as He chooses.

Verses 17 and 18 bring out another view of God’s continual pr esence with us, and that is, that He is always thinking about us, and that His thoughts are kind and loving thoughts, for the Psalmist calls them precious. “How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! How great is the sum of them!

If I should count them, they are more in number than the sand: when I awake, I am still with thee.”

So many people are tempted to think that God is not paying any attention to them. They believe their interests are beneath His notice. They feel too unworthy to hope for His attention. But they wrong Him grievously by such thoughts. A mother pays as much attention to her smallest infant as to her oldest children. She is as interested in its little needs and pleasures as in theirs. I am not sure, but she is more.

She thinks of the one who needs them most. He who made the mother's heart will care for His most helpless creatures. He hears the young lions when they cry. Not a sparrow can fall to the ground without Him. We are worth more than many sparrows. So, we need not fear neglect for a moment.

Creating anything requires constant care from the Creator. Omnipotence's glory is that it can do everything at once. It can tend to the smallest details and the grandest tasks. "Only an infinite greatness can hold all things. A greatness less than infinite would crush us."

I don't know why we see a man or woman as weak for neglecting small details in favor of big tasks.

Yet, we accuse our God of doing the same thing. But if any of my readers have been guilty of this folly, let it end now. “How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!

If I were to count them, they would be more than the sand. I awake, and I am still with you.”

The rest of the Psalm shows a perfect harmony between the soul and God. It is where this life of simple faith has begun. The soul unites with God, knowing that He is always present and cares. It loves what He loves and hates what He hates. It eagerly asks Him to search and test it, so no part of it is out of harmony with Him.

In His presence, darkness must flee. The heart will feel it cannot endure having any corner hidden from His light. “For, you make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.” (Psal m 16:11 ) An old woman, in a desolate part of England, made a lot of money selling ale and beer to travelers at her lonely cottage. But her conscience troubled her about it. She wanted to be a Christian and go to Heaven when she died. But, she felt that, if she did, she'd have to give up her profitable business. She thought that would be too much to bear. So, she was torn between the two.

One night, at a meeting she attended, a preacher spoke about the joy of God's constant presence. He said knowing this truth brings great happiness. Her heart was filled with excitement at the thought that this could be true for her. Forgetting all about the beer, she simply and sincerely accepted it as a wonderful reality. As the preacher kept speaking, she cried in her he art, “Lord Jesus, I didn’t know you were always with me! Lord, how amazing it is to know that you are always here with me, taking care of me! I will never feel lonely again !

When the meeting ended, she walked home across the fields. The joyful thought kept repeating in her heart, "Ah, Lord Jesus, you are coming home with me tonight." She said, "Never mind, Lord Jesus, old Betty won’t ever let you go again now. I know you are here with me.

Her faith in God’s presence grew stronger, and she felt more joy ful with each step. By the time she reached her cottage door, her heart was full of happiness. As she walked in, the first thing she saw was a big pot of beer on the table, ready to be sold. A thought came to her: “The Lord won’t like that pot of beer.” Her heart quickly responded, “Then it must go.” The pot was heavy, so she knelt beside it and prayed, “Lord, You have come home with me. You will live in this cottage, and I know you don’t want this beer here. Please give me the strength to pour it out.” God gave her strength, and soon the beer was running down the road. Then she went back inside, knelt, and thanked the Lord for helping her. She added, “Now, Lord, if there is anything else in this cottage that you don’t like, show me, and I will get rid of it too. Isn’t this a perfect example of the message at the end of our Psalm?

"Lord, don’t I hate those who hate you? Am I not troubled by those who oppose you? I hate them completely and see them as my enemies.

Search me, O God, and know my heart. Test me and know my thoughts.

If there is anything wrong in me, show me, and lead me on the right path forever Just as light drives out darkness, so does the realized presence of God drive out sin. The soul that by faith abides in His presence knows a very real and wonderful Deliverance.

And now I trust that some will ask, “How can I find this presence to be real to myself?” I will close, so, with a few practical directions. First, convince yourself from the Scriptures that it is a fact. Facts must always ground our experiences. Without them, the experiences are worthless. It is not the feeling that causes the fact, but the fact that produces the feeling. What every soul needs, first of all, is this.

God's own words must convince them, beyond question. They must know, as an unalterable fact, that His presence with us is constant.

Then, this point settled, we must make it real. We must "practice His presence," as an old writer said, always and everywhere, in everything. You must obey the Scripture command. It says, "In all your ways acknowledge Him." So, at every hour and moment, say, "The Lord is here." Do everything, even eating and drinking, in His presence and for Him. Literally, “whether, therefore, you eat or drink, or whatsoever you do, do all to the glo ry of God.” By this continual "practice of His presence," the soul gains a habit of faith. It becomes, finally, as hard to doubt His presence as it was to believe it at first.

This requires no great effort, just an unwavering faith. It is not studied reasoning or elaborate meditations that will help you here. The soul must, by simple faith, recognize that God is present. It must then, in freedom and simplicity, talk to Him about everything, all the time. He does not need great things of us. He asks for so little. A little remembrance of His presence. A few words of love and confidence. A brief lifting of the heart to Him as we go about our daily tasks. A constant appeal to Him, a present and loving friend. A desire to live in a sense of His presence, and to let our hearts "dwell at ease" because of it. The least remembrance is welcome to Him. It helps make His presence real to us.

Whoever remains faithful in this exercise will soon discover a blessed realization. Of all I've tried to tell in this book, and of far more that I cannot, I hope you will understand, beyond words, those wonderful words about our Lord: "They must call Him Emmanuel, which means, 'God with us."

THE END
fields.body_text: In Psalm 139, we are reminded that God is always with us, no matter where we are or what we're facing. His presence is constant, and He understands us completely, offering love and care like a devoted parent. No darkness or difficulty can separate us from Him, and His continual presence provides peace, security, and strength in every circumstance. Your great hospitality surrounds us like a boundless sea. We cannot lose ourselves where all is home, nor drift away from you.” Very few of us understand the full meaning of the words in Matthew. 1:23, “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel . ” This short sentence reveals the world's greatest truth. God, the Almighty Creator of Heaven and Earth, is not a distant god in a glorious Heaven. He lives with us, in our poor, helpless lives, as close as we are to ourselves. This seems so incredible to the human heart that we are slow to believe it. But, the Bible teaches it as fact, from cover to cover. Any honest mind cannot deny this. In the very beginning of Genesis we read of the “presence of the Lord God amongst the trees of the garden.” Since then, He is always revealed to us. He has a daily, close relationship with His peop le everywhere. In Exodus we find Him asking them to make Him a “sanctuary that He might dwell among them.” He is recorded as having "walked" with them in the wilderness, and as "taking up His home" with them in the Promised Land. He taught them to rely on Him as an ever-present Friend and Helper. They should consult Him about all their affairs and give Him their lives. And finally, He came in Christ in bodily form. He dwelt in the world as a man among men. He made Himself bone of our bone and flesh of our flesh. He took upon Him our nature. He revealed to us, in the most real way, a great and blessed truth. He intended to be with us always, even unto the end of the world. Those who believe this truth will find its solution. It will solve all their life's troubles. As a little girl, I remember that, in trouble, my parents' arrival always relieved me. When I heard one say, "Daughter, I am here," every burden dropped and every anxiety stilled. It was their simple presence that did it. They did not need to promise to relieve me. They did not need to tell me their plans. Their presence was all the assurance I required. It meant everything would be set right and all would go well for me. After their arrival, I only wanted to see how they would do it. They must be exceptional parents. Their children are very confident. I think they were. But our God is exceptional. So, the application is absolute. His presence is all we need. It would be enough for us, even if we had not a single promise nor a single revelation of His plans. The Bible says, "I will be with you." It has stilled all questions and fears. Who can doubt it? He meant to assure us that His infinite wisdom, love, and power are on our side. Over and over again in my childhood, have the magic words, “Oh, there is mother!” It brought me relief and comfort. In my later years, I've heard, "Oh, there is God!" spoken with reverence.” brought me a far more blessed deliverance. With Him present, what could I have to fear? He has said, “ Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you .”(Hebrews 13:5). So, I may boldly say, The Lord is my helper. I will not fear what man shall do to me. I still recall the inspiring sense of security that came with my father's presence. I never feared anything when he was by. And surely with my Heavenly Father by, there can be no possible room for fear. I seek to make clear and definite the fact of "Emmanuel, God with us." Its practical help and comfort inspire me. I am sure that few of God's own children truly believe it. They may say they do. They may repeat a thousand times, in a devout tone, "Oh, yes, we know that God is always present with us, but, and in this "but," the whole story is told. There are no “buts” in the vocabulary of the soul that accepts His presence as a literal fact. Such a soul is joyously triumphant over every suggestion of fear or of doubt. It has God, and that is enough for it. His presence is its certain security and supply, always, and for everything. I beg my readers to turn with me to the 139th Psalm. There, we will find a blessed revelation of this truth. The central thought of the Psalm is to be found in verses 7 to 12, “Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me. If I say, “Surely the darkness shall cover me, and the light about me be night,” even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day, for darkness is as light with you.” This passage is the strongest proof of His constant presence with us, wherever we are or whatever we do. People seek to be in the Lord's presence. But they cannot escape it. There is no place in the universe where He is not. Not in heaven, hell, or the farthest sea. No darkness can hide from Him, even for a moment. The reason is, He "has possessed our reins." It means He is not only with us, but within us. So, He must accompany us wherever we go. We must accept it as true. Our Lord's words, "Look, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world," were not just a beautiful sentiment. They are an undeniable fact. He is with us, and we cannot get away from Him. In thick darkness, we may see nothing. We may think, often think that He does not see us. But our Psalm assures us that the darkness hides not from Him. In fact, darkness and light are both alike to Him. We are as present to His view and as plainly seen in our darkest spiritual depths as in our brightest light. The darkness may hide Him from us, but it does not hide us from Him. Nor does any spiritual distance or wandering take us from His presence. Not even if we sink into sin in our wandering. In the uttermost parts of the sea, or wherever we may be, He is ever present to hold and to lead us. There is not a moment nor a place where we can be left without His care. Sometimes, confusion makes us unaware of the loving care of our nurses. A child in confusion might cry out for its mother, and its sad cries will break her heart. Meanwhile, she is holding the child's hot hand, cooling its fevered head, and caring for it with a mother's love. The sickness may hide the mother from the child, but it doesn't hide the child from the mother. And just so it is with our God and us. Our doubts, fears, sorrows, and sins cannot hide us from Him. But they often hide Him from us. He has said that the darkness and light are alike to Him. If our faith accepts this, we can trust in dark times. Though we cannot see or feel Him, our God cares for us. He will never leave us. Whether, however, this abiding presence of our God will be a joy to us or a sorrow will depend upon what we know about Him. If we think of Him as a stern tyrant, intent only on His own glory, we shall be afraid of His continual presence. If we see Him as a loving Father, we'll be glad. He wants only our happiness. So, we'll be thankful to have Him with us always. For the presence and the care of love can never mean anything but good to the one beloved. The Psalm we are considering shows us that God's presence is love. It brings us infinite comfort and rest. He says in verses 1 to 5, “O Lord, you have searched me and known me! You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down and are acquainted with all my ways. Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O Lord, you know it altogether. You hem me in, behind and before, and lay your hand upon me.” Our God knows us and understands us, and is acquainted with all our ways. No one else in all the world understands us. People may misinterpret our actions and misjudge our motives. Our natural characteristics are not taken into account, nor our inherited tendencies considered. No one makes allowances for our ill health; no one realizes how much we have to contend with. But our Father knows it all. He understands us. His judgment considers every part of our character, both conscious and unconscious. It also considers what controls our actions. Only an all comprehending love can be just, and our God is just. No wonder Faber can say: Nowhere on Earth are its sorrows felt more than in Heaven. Nowhere are its failings judged more kindly. Some of you may fear His justice, thinking it would be against you. But do you not see? It is all on your side, just as a mother's justice is, because He knows our frame and remembers that we are dust. No human judge can ever do this, and to me, this comprehension of God is one of my most blessed comforts. Often, I do not understand myself; all within looks confused and hopelessly tangled. But I remember that He has searched me. He knows me. He understands my perplexing thoughts. So, I may leave the whole mess to Him to unravel. And my soul sinks at once, as on downy pillows, into a place of the most blissful rest. Then, because of His complete knowledge of our needs, what comfort it is to be told that He knows our down sitting and our uprising. He compasses our path, and takes note of our lying down. Our God does for us what a mother does for her foolish, careless, ignorant, but dearly loved little ones. When a mother is with her children, she thinks of their comfort and well-being always before her own. They must have comfortable, draught-free seats. She must endure any discomfort. Their beds must be soft and their blankets warm, let hers be what they may. Their paths must be smooth and safe, even though she is obliged to walk in rough and dangerous ways. Her own comfort, as compared with that of her children, is of no account in a loving mother’s eyes. Surely, our God is not less capable of a self-sacrificing love than the mothers in this world. He must be better and greater on the line of love and self-sacrifice than any mother He ever made. He has assured us that He knows our down sitting and uprising. He compasses our path and our lying down. So, we can be sure, in all the little details of our lives, we get the very best that His love, wisdom, and power can provide. I mean this in a very literal sense. I mean that He cares for our seats and our beds. He sees that we each have the best kind for our highest development. And just on this last point is where He is so much better than any mother can be. His love is a wise love that sees the outcome of things and cares more for our highest good than for that which is lower. A mother's weak love can't see beyond a child's comfort. It can't bear to cause any discomfort. But God's strong, wise love can permit some pain. It is for the sake of the future glory that will come from it. At home and abroad, let us trust God. He knows all about our daily lives. So, let Him choose our seats, beds, and other small things. For we are told in our Psalm that He “besets” our path. We have some of us have known what it was to be “beset” by unwelcome and unpleasant people or things. But we never thought, perhaps, t hat we were beset by God. He loves us so much that He cannot leave us alone. No coldness or rebuffs can drive Him away. Yet it is gloriously true! Moreover , He besets us “behind” as well as before. Just as a mother does. She goes after her children. She picks up all they dropped and clears away their rubbish. We mothers start this in the nursery with the blocks and toys. We do it all our lives. We try to fix what our children have left undone or wrong. It takes a lot of effort and trouble, but our love makes that effort seem small compared to caring for our children. What good mother would ever turn away a sad, crying child? Or refuse to help a boy untangle his kite strings? Even if the knots and tangles are his fault, her love understands and feels for those mistakes. So, she works even harder to help fix them. Our God does all this, and more, for us from infancy. He does it long before we are aware of it, until the end of our earthly lives. We have seen Him before us, perhaps, but we have never thought of Him as behind us as well. Yet, it is a blessed fact. He is behind us. He longs to make crooked things straight, untangle our knots, and atone for our wrongs. If any of us has a troubling past, let us be happy. The God who is behind us will set it all straight if we commit it to Him. He can even make our mistakes work together for good. Ah! It is a grand thing to be surrounded by God. Then again, what comfort in verses 14 to 16: "I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. A Wonderful work are your works; my soul knows it very well. My frame was not hidden from you when I was being made in secret, intricately woven in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them.” We often dislike, more than we admit, how we were made. Our mental or moral “make - up” does not suit us. We think that if we were created with less of this or more of that, we'd be more successful. If we were less impulsive or more enthusiastic, we could better serve God. We could also be more satisfactory to ourselves and to Him. We believe that if we were more like someone we admire, it would help too. And we are tempted sometimes to think that with our miserable make-up, it is hopeless to expect to please Him. If we truly realized that God made us, we would see the folly of all this at once. But, we feel that He had little hand in it. We think we were put together haphazardly, leaving our characters to chance. We believe in creation in the general, but not in the particular, when it comes to ourselves. This Psalm shows that God oversaw our creation. He managed even the smallest details. Figuratively, he wrote down what each "member" was to be when none existed yet. So, we are, by nature, what God wants. He made us do a special work. I mean, of course, our natural characteristics, not the perversion of them by sin on our parts. There is something very glorifying to the Creator in this way of looking at it. Genius always seeks to express itself in many ways. No true artist repeats himself. Each painting or statue is a new expression of his creative power. An art exhibition should not have two identical pictures. If it did, it would lower the value of art. The same is true for us, as we are "God's workmanship." His creative power expresses itself differently in each one of us. And in the individual "make-up," which sometimes troubles us, there is a unique power. Without it, the day of the exhibition, when we are to praise His glory, would be incomplete. He asks only this: since He made us, He should manage us. He alone understands us, so only He can do it. The man who makes an intricate machine is best suited to manage and repair it. Anyone else who meddles is likely to spoil it. Given our complex minds and our poor control of them, we should be thankful to hand them to their Creator and leave them in His hands. We can be sure He will make the best of us. Even with our "peculiar temperaments" and flaws, we will be made into vessels of honor. We will be sanctified and fit for the Master's use, ready for every good work. I once read a saying from an old Quaker writer that stayed with me: "Be content to be just what God made you." It helped me understand my thoughts. I believe that to truly submit to God, we must accept ourselves as He created us, just as we accept our daily circumstances. If we did not exist, a part of God’s creation would be missing. His work would be incomplete. Besides, com plaining about ourselves is like complaining about the One who made us, which must hurt Him. Let’s be content and trust the Divine Potter to shape us as He sees best and use us as He chooses. Verses 17 and 18 bring out another view of God’s continual pr esence with us, and that is, that He is always thinking about us, and that His thoughts are kind and loving thoughts, for the Psalmist calls them precious. “How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! How great is the sum of them! If I should count them, they are more in number than the sand: when I awake, I am still with thee.” So many people are tempted to think that God is not paying any attention to them. They believe their interests are beneath His notice. They feel too unworthy to hope for His attention. But they wrong Him grievously by such thoughts. A mother pays as much attention to her smallest infant as to her oldest children. She is as interested in its little needs and pleasures as in theirs. I am not sure, but she is more. She thinks of the one who needs them most. He who made the mother's heart will care for His most helpless creatures. He hears the young lions when they cry. Not a sparrow can fall to the ground without Him. We are worth more than many sparrows. So, we need not fear neglect for a moment. Creating anything requires constant care from the Creator. Omnipotence's glory is that it can do everything at once. It can tend to the smallest details and the grandest tasks. "Only an infinite greatness can hold all things. A greatness less than infinite would crush us." I don't know why we see a man or woman as weak for neglecting small details in favor of big tasks. Yet, we accuse our God of doing the same thing. But if any of my readers have been guilty of this folly, let it end now. “How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them! If I were to count them, they would be more than the sand. I awake, and I am still with you.” The rest of the Psalm shows a perfect harmony between the soul and God. It is where this life of simple faith has begun. The soul unites with God, knowing that He is always present and cares. It loves what He loves and hates what He hates. It eagerly asks Him to search and test it, so no part of it is out of harmony with Him. In His presence, darkness must flee. The heart will feel it cannot endure having any corner hidden from His light. “For, you make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.” (Psal m 16:11 ) An old woman, in a desolate part of England, made a lot of money selling ale and beer to travelers at her lonely cottage. But her conscience troubled her about it. She wanted to be a Christian and go to Heaven when she died. But, she felt that, if she did, she'd have to give up her profitable business. She thought that would be too much to bear. So, she was torn between the two. One night, at a meeting she attended, a preacher spoke about the joy of God's constant presence. He said knowing this truth brings great happiness. Her heart was filled with excitement at the thought that this could be true for her. Forgetting all about the beer, she simply and sincerely accepted it as a wonderful reality. As the preacher kept speaking, she cried in her he art, “Lord Jesus, I didn’t know you were always with me! Lord, how amazing it is to know that you are always here with me, taking care of me! I will never feel lonely again ! When the meeting ended, she walked home across the fields. The joyful thought kept repeating in her heart, "Ah, Lord Jesus, you are coming home with me tonight." She said, "Never mind, Lord Jesus, old Betty won’t ever let you go again now. I know you are here with me. Her faith in God’s presence grew stronger, and she felt more joy ful with each step. By the time she reached her cottage door, her heart was full of happiness. As she walked in, the first thing she saw was a big pot of beer on the table, ready to be sold. A thought came to her: “The Lord won’t like that pot of beer.” Her heart quickly responded, “Then it must go.” The pot was heavy, so she knelt beside it and prayed, “Lord, You have come home with me. You will live in this cottage, and I know you don’t want this beer here. Please give me the strength to pour it out.” God gave her strength, and soon the beer was running down the road. Then she went back inside, knelt, and thanked the Lord for helping her. She added, “Now, Lord, if there is anything else in this cottage that you don’t like, show me, and I will get rid of it too. Isn’t this a perfect example of the message at the end of our Psalm? "Lord, don’t I hate those who hate you? Am I not troubled by those who oppose you? I hate them completely and see them as my enemies. Search me, O God, and know my heart. Test me and know my thoughts. If there is anything wrong in me, show me, and lead me on the right path forever Just as light drives out darkness, so does the realized presence of God drive out sin. It is not the feeling that causes the fact, but the fact that produces the feeling. What every soul needs, first of all, is this. God's own words must convince them, beyond question. THE END

fields.title: Understanding Libraries
fields.body_html:
What a library is and what it does Setting up a library starts with understanding what a library truly is. It is not simply a room filled with books, but a vibrant, active space that holds knowledge, stories, and opportunities. Think of it as a doorway to discovery. Your library should bring together the different kinds of resources your community needs: children’s storybooks, students’ textbooks, magazines, newspapers, maps, DVDs, and even digital resources such as eBooks and online journals. When these materials are gathered and arranged in a clear, simple structure, the library becomes a gateway that helps people learn, explore new ideas, and grow in ways they may never have imagined.

But a good library is more than the materials on its shelves—it is also the experience it offers. As you set up your library, consider how it will serve the people who use it. Create areas where children can enjoy stories, students can study comfortably, and adults can read quietly or search for information that supports their daily needs. If possible, provide computers or Wi-Fi so that even those without access at home can learn and connect. Above all, ensure the library is warm, safe, and welcoming. When people feel comfortable, they are more likely to return, take part in activities, and discover the joy of reading and learning.

Because of these important services, libraries play a unique role in every part of society: In schools, Libraries help students and teachers succeed. They provide textbooks, storybooks, research materials, and digital tools that support the curriculum. They teach learners how to find information, think critically, and develop a lifelong love of reading. A school library is often the heart of academic life, encouraging curiosity and helping pupils build strong learning habits.

In communities, Libraries act as centres for learning, connection, and social support. They help job seekers create CVs, and offer people a comfortable place to read, learn new skills, or participate in activities.

In organisations, Libraries support professional growth and informed decision-making. Whether in a company, government office, hospital, or NGO, a library provides reliable information that helps professionals carry out research, plan projects, and improve services. These specialised collections ensure staff have the knowledge they need to excel.

In families, Libraries bring learning into the home. Parents can borrow books for their children, find educational materials, or join family-friendly activities like storytelling sessions, reading clubs, or homework support programs. For some families, the library is a safe, free, and inspiring place to spend time together.

Different Types of Libraries Even though all libraries share the same purpose — to provide access to information — they serve different groups and therefore operate in different ways.

Public Libraries These are open to everyone and are usually funded by the government or community. They offer book lending, internet access, children’s programs, literacy training, and community events.

Their mission is to serve the public equally, regardless of age, education level, or income.

Academic Libraries Found in colleges and universities, they support advanced study and research. Their collections include textbooks, scholarly journals, academic databases, and research tools. Trained librarians help students and researchers find in-depth information for assignments, dissertations, and scientific work.

School Libraries Located in primary, secondary, and high schools, these libraries help learners grow academically and personally. They provide age-appropriate books, curriculum resources, reading programs, and support for research skills. Their goal is to encourage reading, support classroom learning, and help young people become independent learners.

Special Libraries These libraries serve specific groups and have highly focused collections. They can be found in hospitals, law firms, museums, government departments, NGOs, or corporations. Their resources are tailored to the unique needs of the organisation — for example, medical journals in a hospital library or legal texts in a law library.

Core Principles That Guide All Good Libraries Despite their differences, all good libraries are built on the same foundation of values: Organization Materials are arranged in a clear, logical way so people can find what they need quickly. This includes proper shelving, cataloguing, and classification.

Access Libraries work to ensure that everyone — regardless of age, background, or ability — can freely use their resources and services. This includes eliminating barriers such as cost, distance, or lack of technology.

Service Libraries exist to help people. Trained staff guide users, answer questions, assist with technology, and help them find the information they need.

Fairness and Inclusion A library must be a place where everyone feels welcome. Collections should represent different cultures, points of view, management, and interests. Services should be accessible to all.

Knowledge Sharing Libraries preserve and share the knowledge of society. They do this by lending materials, hosting programs, supporting research, and creating spaces for learning and community discussion.

Special Libraries These libraries serve specific groups and have highly focused collections. They can be found in hospitals, law firms, museums, government departments, NGOs, or corporations. Their resources are tailored to the unique needs of the organisation — for example, medical journals in a hospital library or legal texts in a law library. Core Principles That Guide All Good Libraries Despite their differences, all good libraries are built on the same foundation of values: Organization Materials are arranged in a clear, logical way so people can find what they need quickly. This includes proper shelving, cataloguing, and classification. Access Libraries work to ensure that everyone — regardless of age, background, or ability — can freely use their resources and services. This includes eliminating barriers such as cost, distance, or lack of technology. Service Libraries exist to help people. Trained staff guide users, answer questions, assist with technology, and help them find the information they need. Fairness and Inclusion A library must be a place where everyone feels welcome. Collections should represent different cultures, points of view, management, and interests. Services should be accessible to all. Knowledge Sharing Libraries preserve and share the knowledge of society. They do this by lending materials, hosting programs, supporting research, and creating spaces for learning and community discussion.

fields.title: Library Administration & Governance
fields.body_html:
How to Lead, Organise, and Guide Your Library Successfully eading a library is a task that combines leadership, service, and discipline. When you take responsibility for a library — whether it is a school library, a community library, or a small organisational resource centre — you are taking on more than a room full of books. You are stepping into a leadership role. Your decisions will shape how the library feels, how it functions, and how well it serves the people who depend on it. This is to help you understand how to run your library with confidence, clarity, and purpose.

1. The Role of a Librarian: What You Are Responsible For Far beyond issuing books, a librarian is responsible for: • Organising the collection: arranging books, maintaining order, and making sure everything is easy to find.

• Helping users: answering questions, guiding research, assisting with computers, and supporting reading.

• Planning programs: storytime sessions, reading clubs, study workshops, or community activities.

• Maintaining the space: keeping it clean, safe, welcoming, and accessible.

• Managing records: tracking borrowed books, updating user information, and keeping simple statistics.

• Protecting the collection: repairing books, preventing damage, and ensuring materials are used responsibly.

Imagine a library without a librarian.

Books would be misplaced. Borrowers wouldn’t know where things are. Damaged books would go unnoticed. The library would feel confusing instead of helpful.

Example A student walks in looking for a history textbook for their exam. The librarian doesn’t just point at a shelf—they guide the student, check availability, offer alternatives, and suggest other helpful resources, such as past papers or online materials.

In simple terms, the librarian is the heart of the library , keeping everything running smoothly.

2. Library Leadership or Committees: Who Makes the Big Decisions?

Some libraries — especially school, public, or organisational libraries — have a leadership team, governing board, or committee. These people help guide the library’s long-term direction.

They are responsible for: • Setting the overall vision • Approving budgets • Supporting the librarian’s work • Making decisions about big purchases • Establishing policies • Planning development or expansion • Ensuring the library serves its community fairly Think of governance as the “steering wheel.”

The librarian may run the daily engine, but the committee helps steer the library in the right direction—deciding where the library wants to go and how it plans to get there.

3. Policies and Procedures: The Rules That Keep the Library Running Every good library needs policies and procedures .

These are simply the written rules and step-by-step instructions that help everyone understand how things work.

Policies (The Rules) Policies explain what should happen. Examples include: • Borrowing rules (how many books, for how long) • Fines or penalties for lost books • Opening and closing times • Behaviour expectations • Use of computers or the internet • Donation guidelines Policies help maintain fairness, protect the collection, and keep the library organised.

Procedures (The Steps) Procedures explain how things should be done. For example: • How to register a new user • How to issue and return books • How to handle damaged materials • How to close the library at the end of the day • How to record statistics If you set good procedures, the library runs smoothly even when different staff or volunteers take turns working.

4. Staff and Volunteer Roles: How Everyone Contributes Not every library has a large team, but many have at least a few helpers. Each person plays a valuable role.

Here are common roles: Librarian or Library Manager Leads daily operations, supports users, and manages the collection.

Library Assistant Helps with shelving, issuing books, guiding users, and basic administration.

Volunteers Support activities like reading sessions, shelving, and organising events — especially in community or church libraries.

ICT/Technology Support Helps with computers, digital catalogues, and internet services (in libraries that use technology).

Security or Custodial Support Keeps the environment safe and clean.

Your library may have only one staff member, but it’s important to understand these roles — they help clarify responsibilities and identify areas where help is needed.

5. Planning, Goal Setting, and Measuring Progress To grow a strong library, you need a plan.

This plan does not have to be complicated — even a simple one-page document can guide your work for the entire year.

Your library’s plan should include: • What you want to achieve (goals) • How you will achieve it (strategies) • What resources do you need (budget, staff, materials) • When you expect to complete it (timeline) Examples of simple goals include: • Increasing membership • Improving the children’s corner • Buying new textbooks or storybooks • Starting a reading club • Providing weekly ICT lessons Measuring Progress At the end of each month or term, you can track things like: • Number of users • Books borrowed • New materials added • Programs run • Feedback from users Planning is like planting seeds.

You may not see the results immediately, but each action grows into a stronger, more helpful library. These simple records help you see what is working — and what needs improvement.

6. Professional Ethics and Standards: How Library Workers Should Behave As a library worker, you hold a position of trust.

People come to you for help, guidance, and sometimes private information. It is important to act professionally and ethically.

Good library ethics include: • Respecting all users: treating everyone fairly and kindly • Protecting privacy: not sharing private information about users • Being honest and reliable: following rules, returning money, and keeping clear records • Staying neutral: not judging people based on what they read or believe • Promoting learning: encouraging reading, curiosity, and discovery • Caring for resources: using materials responsibly and teaching others to do the same Example If a user forgets their library card, the librarian should follow the identification procedure—not bend rules for friends or relatives.

Ethics are like the moral compass of the library—they guide behaviour and ensure trust. These principles help build a library that people trust and return to.

fields.title: Managing Library Collections
fields.body_html:
How libraries take care of their books and materials.

Alibrary is only as strong as the collection it keeps. The books, magazines, digital materials, and other resources you gather will shape how your library serves its people.

Managing these materials is not a one-time task—it is a journey that continues as long as your library is alive. In this chapter, we walk together through the process of building, organising, protecting, and refreshing a library collection that people can trust and enjoy.

Choosing and Acquiring Books Every collection begins with a choice. When you select a book for your library, you are making a promise: a promise that this book will help someone learn, grow, imagine, or solve a problem.

That is why choosing materials with care is so important.

Start by understanding the needs of the people who will use your library. A school library will choose storybooks, readers, textbooks, and subject guides. A community library may choose books on farming, health, business, language learning, and children’s reading materials. A special library may focus on medical, legal, or technical knowledge. When you know your users, you know what to collect.

Libraries receive books in many ways. Some are purchased using a budget or donations. Others come through requests from organisations or government programs. Many community and school libraries receive donated books from well-wishers. Donations can be a blessing, but they must be checked carefully. A library should not become a storage place for unwanted or outdated items. Accept only books that are clean, relevant, and in good condition. A single useful book is more valuable than a box full of unsuitable ones.

Cataloguing and Classification: Giving Each Book a Home When new books arrive, the next step is to help them “introduce themselves” to the library. This process is called cataloguing. Here, you record important details like the title, author, subject, and year of publication. These details become part of your library’s catalogue—the master list of everything the library owns.

Once a book is described, it needs a place to live on the shelves. This is where classification comes in. By grouping books according to their subjects, you create an organised map that helps people find what they need. A science book, a storybook, and a history book all get their own unique “address.” When a book has a clear title, users can find it easily without confusion.

Good cataloguing and classification save everyone time. They make the library simpler to use, especially for children, new readers, and community members who may be interacting with a library for the first time.

Processing New Books: Preparing Them for Use Before a book reaches the shelves, it needs a little attention—almost like a new student preparing for the first day of school. This preparation is called processing.

Processing may include stamping the library’s name inside the book, adding a spine label with its call number, covering it with protective plastic, and giving it a barcode or unique number for tracking. These small details make a big difference. They protect the book, help you keep records, and ensure that each item can be borrowed, returned, and easily found again.

Processing is the final step before a book becomes part of your library family.

Arranging Books on the Shelves A well-arranged shelf is an invitation. When books are neat, accessible, and clearly labelled, people feel comfortable exploring the library on their own.

Shelve books according to their call numbers so that they follow a natural order. Place children’s books on lower shelves where young readers can easily reach them. Create welcoming spaces for storybooks, textbooks, novels, and subject areas. Newspapers and magazines can be displayed separately so readers can quickly pick up the latest issue.

Some librarians set aside special areas for “New Arrivals” or “Recommended Reading.” These small touches make the library feel alive and changing, not static.

When your shelves are tidy, users sense that the library is cared for—and they care for it in return.

Preserving Books: Helping Them Last Longer Books age the way people do—slowly, quietly, and sometimes unexpectedly. Preservation is the work of protecting your collection so it remains useful for many years.

Keep books in a clean, dry, well-ventilated space. Avoid direct sunlight, which fades covers and weakens pages. Dust shelves regularly. Teach users, especially children, to turn pages gently and return books properly. Repair small tears early so they do not become big ones later.

Often, preservation requires more attention than money. A little care every day keeps your collection healthy.

Weeding: Removing What No Longer Serves the Library A good library grows not only by adding books, but also by removing those that no longer help the community. This process is called weeding. Some books become outdated, especially in subjects like science, health, or technology. Others may become too worn out to continue using.

Some may simply sit untouched for years.

Weeding keeps your shelves relevant, attractive, and easy to search. It prevents users from relying on wrong or outdated information. Think of weeding as pruning a tree—it helps the library stay strong and vibrant.

When removing books, always follow a simple rule: keep what is useful, safe, and relevant. Let go of what no longer supports your mission.

Keeping Inventory: Knowing What You Own A responsible librarian always knows the state of the library’s collection. Inventory is the process of checking each book against your records to confirm that it still exists, is in the right place, and is in good condition.

Inventory helps you track missing items, repair damaged ones, and decide what needs to be purchased. It also helps you communicate clearly with donors, administrators, or partners about the true size and condition of your collection.

Doing an inventory once or twice a year keeps your library organised and trustworthy.

Bringing It All Together Managing a library collection is an act of care. You choose materials thoughtfully, organise them with purpose, protect them with love, and update them responsibly. When you do these things consistently, your library becomes much more than a room of books—it becomes a resource your community can depend on, year after year.

A well-managed collection invites people to learn, explore, and discover. And that is the gift every library is meant to offer.
