And do not carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath or do any work” (Jeremiah 17:21–22). And in the words that follow, the continual presence of a king is made to hinge on obedience to burdens. Nehemiah was so urgent that he set his servants at the city gates, as they crowned the grey summit of Zion. " As soon as it began to grow dark at the gates of Jerusalem before the Sabbath, I commanded that the doors should be shut and gave orders that they should not be opened until after the Sabbath. And I stationed some of my servants at the gates, that no load might be brought in on the Sabbath day” (Nehemiah 13:19). And what was true in those bygone days is always true. True Sabbath keeping is impossible if burdens enter the soul. As well as try to sleep when a party of high-spirited, healthy children is tearing up and down the house and playing hide-and-seek in all the rooms. Care will break the rest of the soul as much as sin does. We will not know the peace that passes all understanding. We must learn to shut the door to the burden-carrying thoughts from the world below. They come up the hill, filling our spirits with their noise and cries. We do not need to stay to describe the results that burden-bearing brings to the heavy-laden. They are evident in the careworn look, the weary eye, and the heavy step. But, deeper than these, there is no power in prayer. There is no joy in God. There are no green pastures, no waters of rest. As snowflakes in the arctic or sand grains in the tropics will build a rampart before some lowly dwelling, enough to exclude the light, so will worries, each tiny in itself, shut out the light of God from the soul and make midnight where God meant midday. Burden-bearing sadly dishonours God. As men of the world see the faces of those who claim to be God's children, they may wonder what sort of Father He is. Their faces are dark with the same shadows as those on their own. Whatever a man’s profession is, we cannot help judging him by his children's faces. If we judge God by the views of some of His children, His foes' harshest criticisms are almost true. The unbeliever may argue: "Either there is no God, or He is powerless, uncaring, or indifferent." "What good will religion be to me?" We are either a libel or a Bible; harbour lights or warning signals; magnetic or repellent. Which we are depends on how we treat our burdens. Of course, there is a difference between care and pain. We can bear our anxieties. But we must suffer according to God's will. We must not take lightly the sufferings our Father sends. They teach lessons only learned in the school where our Lord learned obedience. The chastened spirit must go softly and withdraw itself to suffer. But accepting the sufferings sent from God is very different from burden- bearing. The Father’s care will be clear. There will be no worries and no fears about the future. To the eye of faith, it gleams like the sunlit sea on the horizon, though dark clouds brood above. Before we are fully awake in the morning, we feel a hint of depression, as if all is not right. A voice seems to tell a long tale of burdens to be carried and difficulties to be faced as the hours pass. “Ah!” says the voice, “a miserable day will this be.” “How so?” we inquire, fearfully. A creditor must be met, a skein untangled, an irritation soothed, and some tempers confronted. It is no use praying. Better linger where you are, and then drag through the day as you can. You are like a martyr being led to his death.” We have too often yielded to the suggestion. We have dragged ourselves wearily through the hours, doing our daily tasks. Our hands are engaged and our strength spent by the burdens we have assumed. God is pledged to give strength for all duties that He sets, but not for the burdens that we elect to take on as well. The one cure for burden-bearing is to cast all burdens on the Lord. The margin of the Revised Version of Psalm 55:22 thus reads: “Cast your burden on the LORD.” Whatever burden the Lord has given you, give it back to Him. Treat the burden of care as you once did the burden of sin; kneel down and deliberately hand it over to Jesus. Say to Him, “Lord, I entrust You with this, and this, and this. I cannot carry them; they are crushing me, but I definitely commit all of them to You to manage, adjust, and arrange. You have taken my sins. Take my sorrows, and in exchange give me Your peace, and Your rest.” As George Herbert says, “We must put them all into Christ’s bag.” Won’t our Lord Jesus be at least as true and faithful as the best earthly friend we have ever known? Have there not been, at times, a weariness in us all? We have been too tired or helpless to help ourselves. In those moments, we have anxiously handed our troubles to a strong man. We were sure he would not rest until he had solved them. Surely, He who loved us enough to die for us may be trusted to arrange all the smaller matters of our daily lives! Of course, we must meet one or two conditions. Then, we can hand our burdens to the Lord Jesus and leave them with Him in perfect confidence. 1. We must have cast our sins on Him before we can cast our cares. 2. We must be at peace with God through our Saviour's work. Then, we can have the peace of God through faith in His grace. 3. We must live by God's plan. We must obey His laws and execute His plans, as far as we know them. We must also wait under the cloud. 4. We must also feed faith with promise, for this food is essential to make it thrive. And when we have done all this, we shall not find it so difficult to kneel, and cast our load, even while we pray upon our God. Then rise with lightened cheer. Hand Over to Christ the Burden of How to Grow in Grace. This is a very great burden to some earnest people. They go from convention to convention, from one speaker to another, notebook in hand. They are eager to get the "blessing," as they call it. They often care more for the gift than for the Giver. They hear of others' unknown experiences. So, they feel disappointed and self-reproachful. Equally, a child in kindergarten might fret because he is not entered in the higher classes of the school. But why should he worry about his future progress? His one business is to acquire the lessons set to him by his teacher. Once those are learned, it will be for the teacher to teach his pupil more. He should advance the pupil to positions where quicker progress may be made. We must learn the lessons that the Lord Jesus sets before us each day. We should let Him lead us to a deeper knowledge and love of God. Thomas was one of the dull pupils in our Master’s school. He could not see what was clear to all beside. But instead of chiding him and leaving him in the dark, the Master paid him a visit. He made the fact of His resurrection so simple that the doubter was able to rejoice with the rest. Don't worry about being dull. It will only mean that the dear Master will give you more personal attention. Mothers give most pain to the sickly, weak, and slow among their children. Hand Over to Christ the Burden of Maintaining a Christian Profession. A secret fear keeps many from openly identifying with the Lord's people. They doubt they can hold out. They fear bringing disgrace to their Christian faith and sullying Christ's name. Almost unconsciously, they repeat the words of David, “ Then David said in his heart, “Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will despair of seeking me any longer within the borders of Israel, and I shall escape out of his hand . ”(1 Samuel 27:1). Anxiety about such sacred matters will hide Christ. Like vapour wreaths hide snow-capped peaks. And it is quite needless. He who saved can uphold. As is His heart of love, so is His arm of might. He is able to keep us from stumbling and present us faultless before the presence of His glory. But we shall never know the sufficiency of that keeping while we cling to the boat or even keep one hand upon its side. Only by stepping onto the water, trusting the Master's power, shall we know how surely He keeps what is entrusted to Him against that day. We must not carry even the burden of daily abiding in Him. Let us rather trust Him to keep us trusting and abiding in Himself. He will not fail us if we do. He will reward our faith with a desire for prayer, Bible study, and communion. These are the keys to unbroken fellowship. Hand Over to Christ the Burden of Christian Work. How to maintain our congregations? How to hold our ground amid the competition from neighboring workers? How to sustain the vigor and efficiency of our machinery? How to resolve differences among fellow and subordinate workers? How to find enough material for sermons and addresses? These burdens weigh on us. How many workers break down under them! They could bear the work but not the worry. And yet the responsibility of the work is not ours but our Master’s. He is bearing this world in His arms, as a mother her sick child. He is ministering to the infinite need of man. He is carrying on His great redemptive scheme for the glory of His Father. All He wants of us is a faithful performance of the daily tasks He gives. Let the sailor lad sleep soundly in his hammock; the captain knows exactly the ship’s course. Let the errand boy be content to fetch and carry as bidden. The firm heads know what they are about. They have resources to meet all their needs. And let the Christian worker guard against bearing burdens that the Lord alone can carry. The Lord would never have sent us to His work without first calculating His ability to carry us through. Hand Over to Christ the Burden of the Ebb and Flow of Feeling. Our feelings are as changeable as April weather. They are affected by countless subtle causes. These include our physical health, the atmosphere, fatigue, and lack of sleep. Also, there are spiritual and inward causes. No stringed instruments are more liable to be affected by minute changes than we are. And we are apt to take it sorely to heart when we see the tide of emotion running out fast. We should question ourselves at such times. Is our lack of feeling due to sin or worry? If not, we can trust Him. He knows our frame and remembers we are dust. As we pass down the dark staircase, let us hold fast to the handrail of His will, willing to do His will, though in the dark. “I am as much Your own, equally devoted to You now in the depths of my soul, as when I felt happiest in Your love.” Hand Over to Christ All Other Burdens. Servants with their frequent changes. Employers with unreasonable demands. Unkind gossip and slanderous tales about you. The perplexities and adversities of business. The difficulties of making ends meet. The question of changing your house and finding a new job. Children with childish ailments and youthful waywardness. Provision for sickness and old age. Some have businesses that cause great anxiety. Others are haunted by poverty. Any one of these will break our rest. One barking dog may break our slumber in the stillest night. One grain of dust in the eye will ruin our enjoyment of the fairest view. There is nothing for us, then, but to roll our burden, and indeed ourselves, on God. “Cast your burden on the Lord, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved.” (Psalm 55:22). A little boy, trying to help his father move some books, fell on the stairs under the weight of a heavy volume. The father ran to his aid. He caught up with the boy and carried them both to his room. And will our Father do less? He must love us infinitely and be ever at hand. “ Casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you ” (1 Peter 5:7). It is a good way to deal with God. If you are unsure of His will, say that you will stay where you are. Or, go on doing what you have been doing. Do this until He makes clear what He wants and empowers you to do it. Entrust your worries to God. “Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established.” (Proverbs 16:3). Expect Him to make any changes clearly known to you, so you won't mistake it, even if you're dull. Don’t worry about dress, ornaments, or doubtful things. Satan loves to turn the soul’s attention from Christ to itself. It is as if a girl should spend an hour in her room, choosing a dress for her impatient lover, who is waiting. Let her go to him, and if she desires it, he will reveal his preferences to her directly in due time. Get into the presence of Jesus. You will not be left to hazy doubts. You will be told clearly His will, always about one point at a time. Archbishop Leighton sweetly says: "When you must do or suffer anything, tell God." Burden Him with it. Then, you have done enough." No more care, but sweet, quiet diligence in thy duty, and dependence on Him for the carriage of thy matters. Roll over on God, make one bundle of all: roll thy cares, and thyself with them, as one burden, all on thy God." If individuals bring no burdens into the soul and give them to the Lord, the peace of God will fill the inner temple. Though the world may be restless, these things will endure. They are the presence of God. Meanwhile, the soul keeps an unbroken Sabbath. It is like the calm ocean depths, untouched by the hurricanes that churn the surface into foam. “And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:7).

fields.title: How to Bear Sorrow
fields.body_html:
As believers our comfort must be in God, who refines us through trials rather than punishing us, as Christ bore all punishment on the cross. Sorrow reveals and strengthens virtues like patience, sympathy, and hope. Though friends may not fully understand, Jesus is a constant source of compassion and comfort. Instead of isolating ourselves, we find healing in helping others. This suffering, while painful, sows seeds of future joy, wisdom, and strength that will one day be realized.

You are passing through a time of deep sorrow. The love in which you placed your trust has failed you without warning. It has dried up like a brook in the desert that is now a dwindling stream, then shallow pools, and at last drought. You are always listening for footsteps that do not come. Waiting for a word that is not spoken, pining for a reply that tarries overdue. The savings of your life have vanished without warning. Instead of helping others, someone must help you. You must leave the warm nest that sheltered you from life’s storms. You must venture alone into a hostile world. Or, you receive an unexpected call to take on another's life. You must take no rest until you have guided it through dark, difficult seas to safety.

Your health, sight, and energy are failing. You carry a death sentence. The anguish of awaiting the future is almost unbearable. In other cases, there is a sense of recent loss.

The gap in the forest shows where the woodsman has been felling trees. At such times life seems almost insupportable. Will every day be as long as this? Will the slow-moving hours ever again quicken their pace?

Will life ever array itself in another garb than the torn autumn remnants of past summer glory? “Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?” (Psalm 77:9).

This road has been trodden by myriads. Think of the wars that have devastated every land. Of the Nimrods, the Nebuchadnezzars, the Timurs, and the Napoleons. Of the merciless slave trade. And of all the tyranny, oppression, and wrongs the weak have suffered at the hands of their fellows. Of the unutterable sorrows of women and children. You must see that most of our race shares your grief.

Jesus Christ Himself trod this difficult path, leaving traces of His blood on its flints. Apostles, prophets, confessors, and martyrs have passed by the same way. It is comforting to know that others have crossed the same dark valley. The vast crowd before the Lamb, wearing victory palms, came out of great tribulation. Where they were, we are; and, by God’s grace, where they are, we will be.

Do Not Talk About Punishment. You may talk of chastisement or correction. Our Father deals with us as with sons. You may speak of reaping the results of mistakes and sins, once planted in life's furrows. Or, you may bear the consequences of others' sins and mistakes. But, do not speak of punishment.

Jesus took on all the guilt and penalty of sins, and He removed them forever. His were the stripes and the chastisement of our peace. If God punishes us for our sins, Christ's sufferings were incomplete.

If He began to punish us, life would be too short for the infliction of all that we deserve. Also, how could we explain life's anomalies? The saints endure suffering, while the ungodly live peacefully. Surely, if our sufferings were penal, there would be a reversal of lots of these.

Sorrow is a refiner’s crucible. Another's neglect or cruelty may cause it. It might be due to uncontrollable circumstances or a dark past. But, since God allowed it, we must accept it. It is His test, a furnace to search and purify the soul. Suffering searches us as fire does metal. We think we completely devote ourselves to God until the cleansing fire of pain exposes us. Then we discover, as Job did, how much dross there is in us, and how little real patience, submission, and faith. Nothing detaches us from this world, its pleasures, and earthly loves more than this. Nothing but the life of Jesus in our mortal flesh can likely stop the self-life's power.

But God always keeps the discipline of sorrow in His own hands. Our Lord said, “My Father is the husbandman.” His hand holds the pruning knife. His eye watches the crucible. His gentle touch is on the pulse while the operation is in progress. He will not allow even the devil to have his own way with us. As in the case of Job, so always. The team allocates the moments with care. The test's severity is exact. It lies in unrecognized reserves of grace and strength. They will be sought and used under the pain of great pressure.

He holds the winds in His fist and the waters in the hollow of His hand. He doesn’t dare risk the loss of that which has cost Him the blood of His Son. “ No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it . (1 Corinthians 10:13).

In sorrow, the Comforter is near. “Very present in times of trouble.” He sits by the crucible, a Refiner of silver. He regulates the heat, marking every change. He waits for the scum to float away and for the clear, molten metal to mirror his face. No earthly friend may tread the winepress with you. But, the Savior is there, His garments stained with the blood of the grapes of your sorrow. Dare to repeat it often, though you do not feel it, and though Satan insists that God has left you, “You are with me.” Mention His name again and again, “Jesus, Jesus, You are with me.” So you will become conscious that He is there.

When friends come to console you, they speak of time's healing touch. They think forgetting is the best cure for sorrow. In their kindness, they suggest travel or fun. But they fail to see the dark night that hangs over your soul. So you turn from them sick at heart and prepared to say, as Job, “Miserable comforters are you all.” But, Jesus is nearer than they are. He knows their pain. He feels for them. His love is too deep for words. He waits to comfort them, like a mother with a suffering baby.

Study the art of this divine comfort. Then, you can comfort those in any affliction with the comfort you received from God (2 Corinthians 1:4). Some trials may come to us, as they do to our Lord. They exist to help us give "sympathy to others." We should observe each symptom of the pain with attention. We should also note each prescription of the Great Physician. We may have to help those with similar experiences in the future. So, we learn from our suffering. When we are perfect, we can help tormented souls. Our help will be priceless and eternal.

Do Not Shut Yourself Up with Your Sorrow. A friend, in deep grief, wrote that he must give up the Christian ministries he had loved. I replied, urging him not to. There is no solace for heart pain like ministry. Great suffering tempts us to isolate and withdraw. We want to sit alone and be silent. Do not yield to it. Break through the icy chains of the reserve, if they have already gathered. Arise, anoint your head and wash your face; go forth to your duty, with willing though chastened steps. All selfishness, in action or thought, is hurtful. It shuts out God's help and love.

Sorrow is apt to be selfish. The soul, full of grief and refusing comfort, becomes a Dead Sea. It is a place where no birds fly and nothing grows. And thus we miss the very lesson that God would teach us. His constant war is against the self-life, and every pain He inflicts is to lessen its hold upon us. But we may thwart His purpose. We may extract poison from His gifts, as men do with opium and alcohol from innocent plants.

A Hindu woman, a beautiful Eastern legend tells us, lost her only child. Wild with grief, she implored a prophet to give back her little one to her love. He looked at her tenderly for a long while and said: “Go, my daughter, bring me a handful of rice from a house into which Death has never entered, and I will do as you desire.” The woman at once began her search. She went from dwelling to dwelling and easily got rice. But, when they granted it, she asked, "Is everyone at the hearth—father, mother, children—none missing?"

The people invariably shook their heads, with sighs and looks of sadness. As far and wide as she wandered, there was always some vacant seat by the hearth. The legend says, as she passed on, her grief faded. The sorrow everywhere had overwhelmed her. Her heart, once consumed by its own pain, now yearned to share in the world's suffering. Her anguish turned to pity; her passion to compassion. She lost herself in the interest of all. She found redemption in redeeming.

Refrain from criticizing yourself for your intense feelings. Tears are natural. Jesus wept. A rainless thunderstorm is perilous. The pattering raindrops cool the air and relieve the charged atmosphere. The swollen brooks state that the snow is melting on the hills and spring is near. “Daughters of Jerusalem,” said our Lord, “Weep for yourselves and for your children.” (Luke 23:28). To bear sorrow with dry eyes and a stolid heart may befit a Stoic, but not a Christian. We should not scold nature, longing for its mate, its lost joy, the touch of a vanished hand, the sound of a still voice. We ask only that you surrender the will. This is the one consideration for those who suffer, is the will right? If it isn’t, God Himself cannot comfort. If it is, then the path will lead from the valley of the shadow of death to the banqueting table and the overflowing cup.

Many say, “I cannot feel surrendered. It is bad enough to have my grief to bear, but I have this added trouble, that I cannot feel surrendered.” My constant reply is: “You probably never can feel surrender, but you can.

The Lord Jesus, in the Garden of Gethsemane, has shown us how to suffer. He chose His Father’s will. Satan prompted Judas to mix the cup and give it to the Savior. But the Savior looked past Judas to the Father, who allowed his cruel act. He then said, "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given me?" He then added, "If I cannot pass this unless I drink it, may your will be done." He gave up His own way, saying, "If you are willing, remove this cup from me." Still, not my will, but yours, be done.”

Let all sufferers who read these lines go apart and dare to say the same words: “Your will, and not mine. Your will be done in the earth of my life, as in the heaven of Your purpose. I choose Your will.” Say this thoughtfully and deliberately. Not because you feel it, but because you will. Not because the way of the cross is pleasant, but because it must be right. Say it, whenever the pain returns, whenever the wound bleeds. “Not my will, but Yours be done.” Dare to say yes to God.

“Even so, Father, for so it seems good in Your sight.”

And so you will be led to feel that all is right and well. A great calm will settle on your heart. It will be a peace beyond understanding. You will find a rest that coexists with suffering.

It will walk amid it, like the three young men in the fiery furnace. The burning coals must have felt like the dewy grass of a forest glade. The doctor told us my little child was dying. I felt like a stone. But in a moment, I seemed to give up my hold on her. She appeared no longer mine, but God’s.”

Be Sure to Learn God’s Lessons. Each sorrow carries at its heart a germ of holy truth. If you get and sow in your heart, you will bear fruit, as seed-corns from mummy cases do in modern soil. God has a meaning in each blow of His chisel, each incision of His knife. He knows the way that He takes. But his object is not always clear to us. In suffering, God touches the minor chords. He develops the passive virtues.

He reveals the treasures of darkness, the constellations of promise, the rainbow of hope, and the silver light of the covenant. What is character without sympathy, submission, patience, and trust? What is it without hope that grips the unseen as an anchor? But these Graces are only possible through sorrow.

Sorrow is a garden. Its trees bear the fruits of righteousness. They are peaceful. Do not leave without bringing them with you. Sorrow is a mine, its walls glistening with precious stones. Do not return to daylight without some specimens. Sorrow is a school.

You are sent to sit on its hard benches and learn from its black-lettered pages lessons that will make you wise forever; do not trifle away your chance of graduating there. Miss Havergal used to talk of “turned lessons."

Count on the afterward. God will not always be causing grief. He ploughs the dull brown acres. He wants to sow precious seed.

Believe that in days of sorrow, He is sowing light for the righteous and gladness for the upright in heart. Look forward to the reaping. Expect the joy ahead. It will fill your heart with song when patience has done her perfect work.

You will live to recognize the wisdom of God’s choice for you. One day, you will see that the thing you wanted was only second best. You will be surprised to remember. You nearly broke your heart and wasted your life on something that would not have satisfied you. It was like a child chasing a butterfly or a soap bubble. You will meet your beloved again. You will have your love again. You will gain a deep character, great sympathy, and patience. You will understand and help others. If you give these to Christ, you will be glad you were afflicted. You will see God’s plan and purpose; you will reap His harvest; you will behold His face and be satisfied. Each wound will have its pearl. Each carcass will have a swarm of bees. Each foe will yield its goodly spoil, like Midian did to Gideon.

The way of the cross, rightly borne, is the only way to the everlasting light. Only the path through Gethsemane and over Calvary's hill leads to the Easter visions and the Ascension's glories. If we do not drink His cup, or are not baptized with His baptism, we cannot expect to share in the joys of His espousals and the ecstasy of His triumph. We must also fill up what is lacking in His sufferings. If we meet these conditions, we will not miss a note in the everlasting song or an element in the bliss possible to men.

Not possible to remove the adverb. The death of Hallam was the birthday of Tennyson’s beautiful poem “In Memoriam.” The cloud of insanity that brooded over Cowper gave us the hymn “God Moves in a Mysterious Way.” Milton’s blunders taught him to sing of “Holy light, offspring of heaven’s first-born.” Rist used to say, “The cross has pressed many songs out of me.” No one likely suffers without helping to ease grief, to triumph good over evil, love over hate, and light over darkness.

If you believe this, could you not bear to suffer? Isn't the worst part of suffering its loneliness? And, its aimlessness? Then dare to believe that no man dies to himself. Fall into the ground, bravely and cheerfully, to die. If you refuse, you will be alone. But if you yield, you will bear fruit. It will sweeten and strengthen the lives of others.

They may never know your name or thank you for your help.

He doesn’t dare risk the loss of that which has cost Him the blood of His Son. “ No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it . (1 Corinthians 10:13). In sorrow, the Comforter is near. “Very present in times of trouble.” He sits by the crucible, a Refiner of silver. He regulates the heat, marking every change. He waits for the scum to float away and for the clear, molten metal to mirror his face. No earthly friend may tread the winepress with you. But, the Savior is there, His garments stained with the blood of the grapes of your sorrow. Dare to repeat it often, though you do not feel it, and though Satan insists that God has left you, “You are with me.” Mention His name again and again, “Jesus, Jesus, You are with me.” So you will become conscious that He is there. When friends come to console you, they speak of time's healing touch. They think forgetting is the best cure for sorrow. In their kindness, they suggest travel or fun. But they fail to see the dark night that hangs over your soul. So you turn from them sick at heart and prepared to say, as Job, “Miserable comforters are you all.” But, Jesus is nearer than they are. He knows their pain. He feels for them. His love is too deep for words. He waits to comfort them, like a mother with a suffering baby. Study the art of this divine comfort. Then, you can comfort those in any affliction with the comfort you received from God (2 Corinthians 1:4). Some trials may come to us, as they do to our Lord. They exist to help us give "sympathy to others." We should observe each symptom of the pain with attention. We should also note each prescription of the Great Physician. We may have to help those with similar experiences in the future. So, we learn from our suffering. When we are perfect, we can help tormented souls. Our help will be priceless and eternal. Do Not Shut Yourself Up with Your Sorrow. A friend, in deep grief, wrote that he must give up the Christian ministries he had loved. I replied, urging him not to. There is no solace for heart pain like ministry. Great suffering tempts us to isolate and withdraw. We want to sit alone and be silent. Do not yield to it. Break through the icy chains of the reserve, if they have already gathered. Arise, anoint your head and wash your face; go forth to your duty, with willing though chastened steps. All selfishness, in action or thought, is hurtful. It shuts out God's help and love. Sorrow is apt to be selfish. The soul, full of grief and refusing comfort, becomes a Dead Sea. It is a place where no birds fly and nothing grows. And thus we miss the very lesson that God would teach us. His constant war is against the self-life, and every pain He inflicts is to lessen its hold upon us. But we may thwart His purpose. We may extract poison from His gifts, as men do with opium and alcohol from innocent plants. A Hindu woman, a beautiful Eastern legend tells us, lost her only child. Wild with grief, she implored a prophet to give back her little one to her love. He looked at her tenderly for a long while and said: “Go, my daughter, bring me a handful of rice from a house into which Death has never entered, and I will do as you desire.” The woman at once began her search. She went from dwelling to dwelling and easily got rice. But, when they granted it, she asked, "Is everyone at the hearth—father, mother, children—none missing?" The people invariably shook their heads, with sighs and looks of sadness. As far and wide as she wandered, there was always some vacant seat by the hearth. The legend says, as she passed on, her grief faded. The sorrow everywhere had overwhelmed her. Her heart, once consumed by its own pain, now yearned to share in the world's suffering. Her anguish turned to pity; her passion to compassion. She lost herself in the interest of all. She found redemption in redeeming. Refrain from criticizing yourself for your intense feelings. Tears are natural. Jesus wept. A rainless thunderstorm is perilous. The pattering raindrops cool the air and relieve the charged atmosphere. The swollen brooks state that the snow is melting on the hills and spring is near. “Daughters of Jerusalem,” said our Lord, “Weep for yourselves and for your children.” (Luke 23:28). To bear sorrow with dry eyes and a stolid heart may befit a Stoic, but not a Christian. We should not scold nature, longing for its mate, its lost joy, the touch of a vanished hand, the sound of a still voice. We ask only that you surrender the will. This is the one consideration for those who suffer, is the will right? If it isn’t, God Himself cannot comfort. If it is, then the path will lead from the valley of the shadow of death to the banqueting table and the overflowing cup. Many say, “I cannot feel surrendered. It is bad enough to have my grief to bear, but I have this added trouble, that I cannot feel surrendered.” My constant reply is: “You probably never can feel surrender, but you can. The Lord Jesus, in the Garden of Gethsemane, has shown us how to suffer. He chose His Father’s will. Satan prompted Judas to mix the cup and give it to the Savior. But the Savior looked past Judas to the Father, who allowed his cruel act. He then said, "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given me?" He then added, "If I cannot pass this unless I drink it, may your will be done." He gave up His own way, saying, "If you are willing, remove this cup from me." Still, not my will, but yours, be done.” Let all sufferers who read these lines go apart and dare to say the same words: “Your will, and not mine. Your will be done in the earth of my life, as in the heaven of Your purpose. I choose Your will.” Say this thoughtfully and deliberately. Not because you feel it, but because you will. Not because the way of the cross is pleasant, but because it must be right. Say it, whenever the pain returns, whenever the wound bleeds. “Not my will, but Yours be done.” Dare to say yes to God. “Even so, Father, for so it seems good in Your sight.” And so you will be led to feel that all is right and well. A great calm will settle on your heart. It will be a peace beyond understanding. You will find a rest that coexists with suffering. It will walk amid it, like the three young men in the fiery furnace. The burning coals must have felt like the dewy grass of a forest glade. The doctor told us my little child was dying. I felt like a stone. But in a moment, I seemed to give up my hold on her. She appeared no longer mine, but God’s.” Be Sure to Learn God’s Lessons. Each sorrow carries at its heart a germ of holy truth. If you get and sow in your heart, you will bear fruit, as seed-corns from mummy cases do in modern soil. God has a meaning in each blow of His chisel, each incision of His knife. He knows the way that He takes. But his object is not always clear to us. In suffering, God touches the minor chords. He develops the passive virtues. He reveals the treasures of darkness, the constellations of promise, the rainbow of hope, and the silver light of the covenant. What is character without sympathy, submission, patience, and trust? What is it without hope that grips the unseen as an anchor? But these Graces are only possible through sorrow. Sorrow is a garden. Its trees bear the fruits of righteousness. They are peaceful. Do not leave without bringing them with you. Sorrow is a mine, its walls glistening with precious stones. Do not return to daylight without some specimens. Sorrow is a school. You are sent to sit on its hard benches and learn from its black-lettered pages lessons that will make you wise forever; do not trifle away your chance of graduating there. Miss Havergal used to talk of “turned lessons." Count on the afterward. God will not always be causing grief. He ploughs the dull brown acres. He wants to sow precious seed. Believe that in days of sorrow, He is sowing light for the righteous and gladness for the upright in heart. Look forward to the reaping. Expect the joy ahead. It will fill your heart with song when patience has done her perfect work. You will live to recognize the wisdom of God’s choice for you. One day, you will see that the thing you wanted was only second best. You will be surprised to remember. You nearly broke your heart and wasted your life on something that would not have satisfied you. It was like a child chasing a butterfly or a soap bubble. You will meet your beloved again. You will have your love again. You will gain a deep character, great sympathy, and patience. You will understand and help others. If you give these to Christ, you will be glad you were afflicted. You will see God’s plan and purpose; you will reap His harvest; you will behold His face and be satisfied. Each wound will have its pearl. Each carcass will have a swarm of bees. Each foe will yield its goodly spoil, like Midian did to Gideon. The way of the cross, rightly borne, is the only way to the everlasting light. Only the path through Gethsemane and over Calvary's hill leads to the Easter visions and the Ascension's glories. If we do not drink His cup, or are not baptized with His baptism, we cannot expect to share in the joys of His espousals and the ecstasy of His triumph. We must also fill up what is lacking in His sufferings. If we meet these conditions, we will not miss a note in the everlasting song or an element in the bliss possible to men. Not possible to remove the adverb. The death of Hallam was the birthday of Tennyson’s beautiful poem “In Memoriam.” The cloud of insanity that brooded over Cowper gave us the hymn “God Moves in a Mysterious Way.” Milton’s blunders taught him to sing of “Holy light, offspring of heaven’s first-born.” Rist used to say, “The cross has pressed many songs out of me.” No one likely suffers without helping to ease grief, to triumph good over evil, love over hate, and light over darkness. If you believe this, could you not bear to suffer? Isn't the worst part of suffering its loneliness? And, its aimlessness? Then dare to believe that no man dies to himself. Fall into the ground, bravely and cheerfully, to die. If you refuse, you will be alone. But if you yield, you will bear fruit. It will sweeten and strengthen the lives of others. They may never know your name or thank you for your help.

fields.title: In the Secret of His Presence
fields.body_html:
Though God is omnipresent to all creation, many often fail to feel His presence due to our unawareness. Figures like Brother Lawrence found God's nearness even in humble tasks, while others felt divine connection through stillness and purity. This chapter encourages us to cultivate a sense of God’s presence through prayer, purity, and meditation on Scripture. God’s presence brings peace, purity, and strength, transforming life.

In one sense, God is always near us. He is not an absentee; he does not need anyone to bring him down from the heavens or up from the deep. He is near at hand. His Being pervades all being. Every world that floats like an island in space shows signs of His presence. It's like how your friend's home is full of clues of his house. They prove he lives there, though you have not seen his face. Every crocus pushing through the dark mould. Every firefly in the forest. Every bird that springs up from its nest before your feet. All that exists is as full of God's presence as the burning bush. Before it, Moses bared his feet in acknowledgment of God. But we do not always realise it. We often pass hours, and days, and weeks.

We sometimes pray. We go back and forth to His house, where the ladder of communication rests. Still, He is a shadow, a name, a tradition, a dream of days gone by. “Oh that I knew where find him!

That even come to his seat! I seek him, but he's not there.

Behold, I go forward, but he is not there,and backward, but I do not perceive him; on the left hand when he is working, I do not behold him; he turns to the right hand, but I do not see him.” (Job 23:3, 8–9).

How different is this failure to see God's presence from the bliss of those who felt His nearness! Brother Lawrence, a simple cook, felt God's presence for over sixty years. He felt it while doing his humble duties.

Office as when partaking of the Holy Supper. John Howe, on the blank page of his Bible, wrote in Latin: "This morning I awoke from a most delightful dream. A bright stream of celestial rays from the Divine Majesty's throne seemed to dart into my open and expanded breast. I have often reflected on that great pledge of Divine favor. It has brought me much joy.”

Are not these, so blessed and inspiring, experiences like those of the author of the longest, and in some ways, the sublimest Psalm in the Psalter? He had been pounding out the golden ore of thought through the paragraphs of great power and beauty. Then, he seemed to sense that He of whom he had been speaking was near and bending over him.

The sense of the presence of God was born upon this inner consciousness. And, lifting up a face on which reverence and ecstasy met and mingled, he cried, “But you are near, O Lord, and all your commandments are true.” (Psalm 119:151).

If only such an experience of the nearness of God were always ours, enfolding us as air or light; if only we could feel, as the great apostle put it on Mars’ Hill, that God is not far away but the element in which we have our being, as sea flowers live in deep, still lagoons: then we should understand what David meant when he spoke about dwelling in the house of the Lord all the days of his life, beholding His beauty, inquiring in His temple, and hiding in the secret of His pavilion. “One thing have I asked of the Lord, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the Lord and to inquire in his temple. For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his tent; he will lift me high upon a rock. (Psalm 27:4–5). Then, too, we should get the blessed secret of peace, purity, and power.

In the Secret of His Presence There Is Peace. “I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.” (John 16:33). People say a certain insect can surround itself with a film of air. It then drops into muddy, stagnant pools and remains unhurt. The believer knows that a divine presence surrounds him. It protects him like an envelope protects a far-travelled letter. "They draw nigh that follow after mischief." But, You are nearer than the nearest. I dwell in the inner ring of Your presence. The horses and chariots of Your protection fill the mountains around me. No weapon formed against me can prosper. It can only reach me through You. It will touch you and then shift its gaze to the side without causing any harm. To be in God is to be in a well-fitted house when the storm has slipped its leash. Or, it is to be in a sanctuary, the doors of which shut out a pursuer.

In the Secret of His Presence There Is Purity. The sight of the distant, snow-capped Alps, across Lake Geneva, elevates the soul. It destroys all evil things that might intrude upon it.

A little child's pure innocence can disarm passion. It's like a beam of light, falling in a reptile-haunted cave that scatters the snakes. But what will not Your presence do for me, if I get a perpetual sense of it, and live in its secret place? In the heart of that fire, despite being black cinder, I must remain pure, glowing, and intense!

In the Secret of His Presence There Is Power. My cry, day and night, is for power—spiritual power. Not the power of intellect, oratory, or human might. These cannot avail to vanquish the serried ranks of evil. You say with sincerity that it is not by might nor by power. Yet, human souls that touch You become magnetised. They gain a spiritual force the world cannot deny or resist. Oh! Let me touch you! Let me dwell in unbroken contact with You. Let divine energy flow into and through my eager spirit. It should flow, but never ebb. Lift me into a life of blessed ministry. Make deserts blossom like the garden of the Lord.

But how must we get and keep this sense of God’s nearness? Not possible to remove the adverb. Ah, have stood beside him, with an unanointed eye. We would have seen no ladder and heard no voice. The patriarch would find God in the bleak, joyless moors of our lives. We had trodden them without reverence.

Must we travel to the cave's mouth? There, Elijah stood, thrilled by the music of the still small voice, sweeter than the thunder and the storm. Alas! Some have stood beside him, unaware of that Presence. If alive now, Elijah would sense it in the wind, the babbling of babies, and the rhythm of heartbeats.

If we had stood beside Paul at the third heaven, we would have seen only a tentmaker's shop or a dingy, rented room. We would be in the dark while he was in transports. If he lived again, he would see angels on our steamships, visions in our temples, and doors to heaven in our bleak skies.

In point of fact, we carry everywhere our circumference of light or dark. God is as much in the world as He was when Enoch walked with Him and Moses communed with Him face-to-face.

He is as willing to be a living, bright, glorious reality to us about them. But the fault is with us. We have unanointed eyes because our hearts are not right. The pure in heart still see God. To those who love Him and keep His commandments, He still shows Himself as He does not to the world. Let us stop to blame our times; let us blame ourselves. We are degenerate, not them. What, then, is that temper of soul that perceives the presence and nearness of God with the greatest ease? Let us endeavor to learn the blessed secret of abiding ever in the secret of His presence and of being hidden in His pavilion. “In the cover of your presence you hide them, from the plots of men; you store them in your shelter from the strife of tongues (Psalm 31:20).

Remember, at the outset, that neither you nor our race can have that glad consciousness of the presence of God except through Jesus. “All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.”(Luke 10:22); “ Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”(John 14:6).

God's presence, apart from Jesus, terrifies devils and sinners. The latter hide among trees, weaving aprons for cover. But in Him, we break down all barriers, rent all veils, and disperse all clouds. The weakest believer may live where Moses sojourned, in the fire. No impurity can stand before its consuming flames.

Not possible to remove the adverb.” Sinners draw near through the blood of His Cross. His death revealed God's tender love. It also put away our sins. And, it wove us garments of pure beauty. In these, the King welcomes us into his inner chamber. Remember God said, “ There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you about all that I will give you in commandment for the people of Israel. ”(Exodus 25:22). You will realize His deep nearness when you fully join in His death and live in the spirit of His memorial supper. Now, as at Emmaus, He loves to make Himself known in the breaking of bread.

“And is this all? For I have heard this many times, and still fail to live in the secret place as I would." Exactly. Thus, to do what we cannot, our Lord has received from His Father the promise of the Holy Spirit. He should bring into our hearts the very presence of God. Understand that since you are Christ’s, the blessed Comforter is yours.

He is within you as He was within your Lord. As you live in the Spirit and walk in Him, you will become His Presence-chamber, filled with His glory. And as you realise that He is in you, you will realise that you are ever in Him. Thus the beloved apostle wrote, “By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.” (1 John 4:13). "I know all this. Yet, I fail to see the marvellous fact of the Spirit's indwelling in me. How can I then realise my indwelling in Him?" “It is because your life is so hurried.

You do not take enough time for meditation and prayer. You cannot discern the Spirit of God within you or the Presence of God without you when pleasure occupies your senses, your pulse races, or rushing thoughts fill your mind. It is when water stands that it becomes clear and reveals the pebbly beach below. Be still, and know that God is within you and around you. In the hush of the soul, the unseen becomes visible and the eternal real.

The eye dazzled by the sun cannot detect the beauties of its pavilion till it has had time to rid itself of the glare. Let no day pass without its season of silent waiting before God. Are there any other conditions that I should fulfil, so that I may abide in the secret of His presence?” Be pure in heart.

Every permitted sin encrusts the soul's windows with grime. It obscures the vision of God. But every victory over impurity and selfishness clears the spiritual vision. As if scales fall from the eyes.

In the power of the Holy Spirit, deny self, give no quarter to sin, resist the devil, and you will see God. The unholy soul could not see God, even though it was set down in the midst of heaven. But holy souls see God in the mundane. They find an open vision everywhere. Such could not be nearer God, though they stood by the sea of glass. Their only advantage would be a more perfect vision. They would tear the veil of their mortal, sinful natures. Keep His commandments. Let there be not one jot or tittle unrecognised and unkept. “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And my Father will love anyone who loves me, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” (John 14:21). Moses, the faithful servant, was also the prophet, and he spoke with God face to face as a man speaks with his friend.

Continue in the spirit of prayer. At times, the vision may be delayed. It tests your desire. At other times, it will come as the dawn steals over the sky. Before you are aware, you will sense His presence. He was even used to glide, unannounced, into His disciples' midst through unopened doors. “Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen.” (Psalm 77:19).

Not possible to remove the adverb. Because He was a quickening power. As soon as He entered, He awoke my slumbering soul. He moved and pierced my heart, which was strange, stony, hard, and sick.

My soul could then bless the Lord. All within me praised His Holy Name.” Cultivate the habit of speaking aloud to God. We don't always express our desires because they are often too sacred or deep to put into words. But it is good to get the habit of speaking to God as a present friend while sitting in the house or walking by the way.

Talk things over with God. Share your letters, plans, hopes, mistakes, sorrows, and sins. Things look very different when brought into the calm light of His presence. One cannot talk long with God aloud without feeling that He is near.

Meditate much upon the Word. This is the garden where the Lord God walks. It is the temple where He dwells, and the presence-chamber where He holds court. Those who seek Him find it. It is through the word that we feed upon the Word. And He said, “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.” (John 6:56). Be diligent in Christian work. The place of prayer is the place of His presence. But, that presence would fade if we lingered there after the duty bell rang. We will ever meet it as we go about our necessary work: “You meet him who joyfully works righteousness, those who remember you in your ways. Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved?” (Isaiah 64:5).

As we go forth to our daily tasks, the angel of His presence comes to greet us and turns to go at our side. “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.” (Matthew 28:19–20). We can be in the secret of His presence everywhere. Not just in temple courts, secluded glens, or sickrooms. But also in daily duties and common places. In the dullness of life, we can say, " Now Elijah the Tishbite, of Tishbe in Gilead, said to Ahab, “As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word.”

" And the angel answered him, “I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news ” (see 1 Kings 17:1; Luke 1:19).

Cultivate the habit of recognizing the presence of God. “Blessed is the one you choose and bring near, to dwell in your courts! We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!” (Psalm 65:4). There is no life like this. To feel that God is with us. He never leads us through a place too narrow for Him to pass as well.

We can never be lonely again, not for a moment. We are beset by Him behind and before, and covered by His hand. He could not be nearer to us, even if we were in heaven. To have Him as Friend, and Referee, and Counselor, and Guide. To know that, without the Captain of the Lord's host, there can be no Jericho in our lives. His invisible but mighty legions will make all walls fall. What wonder that saints of old waxed valiant in fight as they heard Him say, “ No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you. ”(Joshua 1:5). Be gone fear and sorrow and dread of the dark valley! “In the cover of your presence you hide them from the plots of men; you store them in your shelter from the strife of tongues.”(Psalm 31:20).
