A wise preacher, by the power of the Holy Spirit, seeks to break apart the hardened clods of the heart so that it may receive the heavenly seed. Many truths serve as sharp ploughshares. People must be made to feel that they have sinned and must be led to repentance. They must receive Christ not merely with intellectual agreement but with the heart, “for with the heart one believes and is justified.” There must be genuine emotion and conviction. The ploughshare of the law must cut into the heart. A farmer who is too tender-hearted to tear and harrow his field will never see a harvest. This is the failure of certain preachers: they fear hurting anyone’s feelings and therefore avoid truths that might awaken fear or grief. They keep no sharp ploughshare in their shed and are therefore unlikely to gather a harvest into their barn. They fish without hooks so as not to injure the fish. They fire guns without bullets out of respect for the birds’ feelings. This kind of love is cruelty to souls. It is like a surgeon who allows a patient to die rather than cause pain with a necessary incision or amputation. Such tenderness is dreadful — it leaves people to perish rather than disturb them. It may be pleasant to speak only smooth words, but woe to the one who does so at the cost of truth. Was this Christ’s spirit? Did He hide the sinner’s danger? Did He cast doubt upon the unquenchable fire and the undying worm? Did He soothe souls with flattering speech? No. With honest love and deep concern, He warned of wrath and urged people to repent or perish. Let Christ’s servants follow their Master. Let them plough deeply with a sharp blade that will not be turned aside by hard soil. If we truly love souls, we must prove it through faithful speech. The hard heart must be broken, or it will continue to reject the Savior who binds up the brokenhearted. There are certain things people may or may not experience and still be saved. But the realities associated with this ploughing are indispensable. There must be holy fear and humble trembling before God. There must be acknowledgment of guilt and a penitent plea for mercy. In short, there must be a thorough ploughing of the soul before we can expect the seed to bear fruit. II. At Times Ministers Labor in Vain The text also teaches that sometimes ministers labor without visible success. “Shall horses run upon the rock? Will one plough there with oxen?” A ploughman quickly senses whether his plough can cut the ground. So does a minister. He may preach the same words in two different places. In one setting he feels hope and joy; in another, heaviness and resistance. The plough seems to leap out of the furrow. The blade chips against the stone. He says to himself, “I do not understand why I make no progress here,” and realizes he has been assigned particularly hard soil. All who labor for Christ know this experience. You may have felt it in a Sunday school class, in a cottage meeting, or in any setting where you have tried to teach Christ. At one time you turned up rich soil that yielded easily under the oxen. At another time, though the horse strains and the oxen labor until their shoulders are sore, no furrow can be cut. The rock resists to the very end. Such hearers exist in every congregation. They receive the word with joy, yet do not hold fast to it. They listen attentively, but never put it into practice. They hear about repentance but never repent. They hear about faith but never believe. They are capable judges of gospel preaching, yet have never personally accepted it. They insist that good bread be served, yet refuse to eat it. fields.title: The Parable Of The Sower
fields.body_html:
The sower scatters seed freely, yet not all soil receives it. Hearts may be hardened, distracted, or entangled, preventing growth. God’s Word calls for receptive ground, patience, and perseverance, reminding us that fruit depends on divine grace, not human effort.

“And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable: ‘A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.’ As he said these things, he called out, ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear.’” Luke 8:4–8.

In our country, when a farmer goes out to sow, he usually works in an enclosed field, scattering seed from his basket along every ridge and furrow. But in the East, near small towns, farmland was often an open stretch of ground. It was divided into different properties, but there were no visible fences—only ancient boundary markers or perhaps small ridges of stones.

Footpaths ran through these open fields. The most traveled paths were called highways, though they were nothing like our paved roads—just well-worn tracks, hardened by constant use. There were also smaller side paths, made by travelers seeking safer routes or shortcuts. Over time, these too became worn and firm.

When the sower went out to sow, he worked soil that had been scratched by a simple, primitive plow. He aimed to scatter most of his seed there. But since a path ran through the middle of the field, unless he left a wide strip unused, some seed would fall on the path. In another place, a rock might rise close to the surface, covered only by a thin layer of soil. Seed would fall there as well.

In yet another corner, the ground might be tangled with the roots of nettles and thistles.

The farmer would scatter seed there too, and both the grain and the weeds would grow together— until the stronger thorns choked the young plants so that they produced no mature fruit.

Remembering that the Bible was written in the East, and that its images come from that setting, often helps us understand its meaning more clearly than if we picture only English farming customs. The preacher of the Gospel is like that sower. He does not create the seed; it is given to him by his divine Master. No one can create even the smallest grain that grows in the earth, much less the heavenly seed that gives eternal life. The minister goes to his Master in private prayer and asks to be taught the gospel. In that way, he fills his basket with the good seed of the kingdom.

Then he goes out in his Master’s name and scatters the precious truth. If he knew exactly where the best soil was—where hearts had already been prepared by conviction—he might focus only there. But since he cannot see into human hearts, he must preach the gospel to every creature. He must scatter seed on hardened hearts, on distracted minds, and on those entangled in the cares and pleasures of this world.

He must leave the results to the Lord who gave him the seed. He is not responsible for the harvest; he is responsible only for faithfully and diligently doing his work. Even if not a single ear of grain should ever make the reaper glad, the sower will still be rewarded by his Master if he has planted the right seed with careful hands. Without this assurance, how could we avoid crying out with the prophet, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1, ESV).

Our duty is not determined by the character of our hearers but by the command of our God. We must preach the gospel whether people listen or refuse. We must sow beside all waters. Whatever condition hearts may be in, the minister must preach—to the rock as well as the furrow, to the path as well as the plowed field.

Now I will speak about the four kinds of hearers described in our Lord’s parable. First, those like the path—hearers only. Second, those like rocky ground—briefly moved, but without lasting fruit. Third, those among thorns—where the word begins to grow, but is choked by life’s cares, the deceitfulness of riches, and worldly pleasures.

And lastly, that small group—may God greatly increase it—the good soil, in whom the Word produces abundant fruit.

I. The Path “Some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.” Many of you do not come to worship seeking a blessing. You do not intend to worship God or to be changed by what you hear. You are like the path, never meant to be a field of grain. If even one seed of truth were to grow in you, it would be as surprising as wheat growing in the middle of a busy street.

If the seed is skillfully scattered, some may rest briefly on your thoughts. You may not understand it fully, but if it is presented attractively, you might discuss it for a time—until something more entertaining captures your attention. Even that small benefit is short-lived. Soon you forget everything you heard.

We wish we could hope that the Word would remain with you, but your heart is so hardened by constant traffic that there is no place for the seed to take root. Satan continually passes over it with blasphemies, lusts, lies, and empty distractions. Pride rolls across it like heavy wheels. Greed tramples it down until it becomes hard as stone.

The seed finds no resting place. Thoughts rush back and forth constantly. Your soul has become a marketplace where everything is traded. You are busy buying and selling, yet you do not realize that you are selling the truth and buying your own destruction.

You say you have no time to think about spiritual things. The road of your heart is so crowded that there is no room for the seed to grow. If it ever begins to sprout, some new amusement or distraction crushes it before it matures. Just as grain could never grow in the busiest streets of a city, so truth cannot grow in a heart filled with constant noise, pride, worry, and rebellion against God.

We have looked at this hardened roadside; now let us consider what becomes of the good word when it falls on such a heart.

The seed would have grown if it had fallen on proper soil. But it has landed in the wrong place, and it remains as dry as when it first left the sower’s hand. The word of the gospel lies on the surface of that heart but never enters it. It is like snow falling on a busy street: it touches the wet pavement, melts, and disappears at once. The word has no time to awaken life in the soul. It rests there briefly, but it never takes root or produces any lasting effect.

Why do people come to hear if the word never enters their hearts? That question has often puzzled us. Some would not miss a Sunday for anything. They enjoy gathering for worship. Yet no tear falls from their eyes. Their souls never rise to heaven in praise. They do not truly join in confession of sin. They do not think seriously about coming judgment or the future state of their souls. Their hearts are like iron; the minister might as well preach to a heap of stones.

What brings such unfeeling sinners here? At times it seems we would have as much hope of converting wild beasts as these untamed, unresponsive hearts. Has all feeling vanished? Do people attend worship merely because it is respectable? Or does coming help them feel more comfortable in their sins? If they stayed away, conscience might trouble them; but by attending, they persuade themselves that they are religious.

Oh, my hearers, your condition could make an angel weep. The sun of the gospel shines on your face, yet your eyes remain blind. The music of heaven sounds in your ears, yet you do not truly hear it. You can appreciate a turn of phrase. You can admire an illustration. But the spiritual meaning—the living power within the message—you do not grasp. You sit at the wedding feast, but you do not taste the food. Heaven rejoices over redeemed souls, yet you remain unredeemed, without God and without Christ. Though we plead with you, pray for you, and weep over you, you remain as hardened and careless as ever. May God have mercy on you and break up your hard heart so that his word may dwell within you.

The picture is not yet complete. The passage tells us that the birds of the air devoured the seed. Is there a wayside hearer here? Perhaps he did not intend to listen carefully today. When the sermon ends, someone invites him into questionable company. He goes along, and the good seed is quickly devoured.

There are many influences ready to snatch the gospel from a heart. The devil himself—whom Scripture calls the “prince of the power of the air”—is always eager to steal away a good thought.

And he does not work alone. He has countless helpers. A spouse, children, friends, enemies, customers, creditors—any of these may become instruments to consume the seed, and they often succeed. What a tragedy that heavenly seed should become food for the devil—that God’s grain should feed unclean birds.

If you have heard the gospel since childhood, how many wagonloads of sermons have been wasted on you? In your younger days, you may have heard a faithful preacher who prayed for his congregation until his eyes were red with tears. Do you remember the Sundays when you said to yourself, “I will go to my room and pray”? But you did not. The birds devoured the seed, and you continued in sin.

Even now, you are rarely absent from church. Yet the gospel falls on your soul as if it dropped onto iron. The law may be preached with thunder—you do not mock it, but neither are you moved.

Christ may be lifted up before you. His wounds may be described. His blood may be set before your eyes. You may be urged earnestly to look to him and live. But it is like sowing seed along the seashore.

What shall I do for you? Shall I stand here and weep over this hardened path? My tears cannot soften it; it has been trampled too long. Shall I bring the plow of the gospel? The blade cannot penetrate soil so compacted. What then? O God, you alone know how to melt the hardest heart through the precious blood of Jesus. Do it now, we pray. Glorify your grace by causing the good seed to live and produce a heavenly harvest.

Now consider the second kind of hearer. Some seed fell upon rock, and as it grew up, it withered away because it lacked moisture. You can picture that rock in the middle of the field, covered only by a thin layer of soil. The seed falls there as it does everywhere else. It sprouts quickly. It grows rapidly. Then it withers and dies.

Only those who deeply love souls can understand the hopes, joys, and bitter disappointments that these rocky places have caused. There are hearers whose hearts seem soft and responsive. While others feel nothing, these are visibly moved. Whether the message speaks of judgment or of Christ’s love at the cross, they are stirred. Strong impressions are made.

They resolve to change, yet they delay. They are not hardened opponents of God. They appear open and eager. Rejoicing, we direct the message toward them, and it seems to penetrate. But there is hidden armor beneath the surface. No lasting wound is made.

Scripture describes them this way: “And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away” (Mark 4:16–17, ESV).

Have we not seen many who receive the word with joy? They have no deep conviction of sin, yet they quickly profess faith in Christ. Their belief appears genuine. The seed has sprouted. There is a green blade. We thank God, thinking a soul has been saved. But our joy is premature. The same lack of depth that made them respond quickly also causes them to wither when difficulty comes.

We see this often. Someone asks to join the church and tells us how deeply a sermon moved them.

They say they believed at once and have never felt such happiness. We ask about conviction of sin. They believe they were convicted. What they know for certain is that religion brings them great pleasure.

We ask if they will continue, and they are confident that they will. Everything seems new. They claim to hate what they once loved. And all of this has happened suddenly, without deep plowing of the heart. It is as if a field were instantly covered with wheat by magic. Perhaps they are received into fellowship. Within weeks they are less regular. When gently corrected, they explain that opposition has made things difficult. Soon they disappear entirely. A little ridicule or inconvenience has driven them back. The minister feels like a farmer who saw his field green and flourishing, only to wake and find every shoot destroyed by frost.

If it is tragic to be a wayside hearer, it is hardly better to be like the rock. This second group gives more initial hope. They gather eagerly, especially around a new minister. They seem devoted. But time tests everything. What appeared strong proves shallow. When trials come, they fade away.

Some of you may belong to this group. You have felt deeply. You have resolved often. Yet years pass, and nothing changes. There is no depth, no steady work of the Spirit. Must it remain so?

Shall one day your life be remembered as a plant that sprouted but never ripened? God forbid.

May the Spirit work deeply and effectively in you, so that you may yet bear fruit for God and bring honor to Christ.

III. I shall briefly treat of the third class, and may the Spirit of God help me to deal faithfully with you.

“And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprang up with it, and choked it.” Now, this was good soil. The first two characters were bad; the wayside was not the proper place, the rock was not a suitable situation for the growth of any plant; but this is good soil, for it grows thorns.

Wherever a thistle will spring up and flourish, there wheat would flourish too. This was rich, fertile soil; it was no wonder therefore that the farmer dealt generously there, and threw handful after handful upon that corner of the field. See how happy he is when in a month or two he visits the spot. The seed has sprung up. True, there is a suspicious little plant down there of about the same size as the wheat. “Oh!” he thinks, “that is not much, the corn will outgrow that. When it is stronger it will choke these few thistles that have unfortunately mixed with it.” Ah, Mr. Farmer, you do not understand the power of evil, or you would not dream like this! He comes again, and the seed has grown, there is even corn in the ear; but the thistles, the thorns, and the briers have become intertwined with one another, and the poor wheat can hardly get a ray of sunshine. It is so choked with thorns on every side, that it looks quite yellow; the plant is starved. Still it keeps on growing, and it does seem as if it would bring forth a little fruit. Alas, it never comes to anything. With it the reaper never fills his arm.

We have this class very largely among us. These hear the word and understand what they hear.

They take the truth home; they think it over; they even go so far as to make a profession of religion.

The wheat seems to spring up and form an ear; it will soon come to perfection. Do not be in a hurry; these men and women have a great deal to look after; they have the cares of a large business; their establishment employs so many hundreds; do not be mistaken about their godliness—they have no time for it. They will tell you that they must live; that they cannot neglect this world; that they must somehow look after the present, and as for the future, they will give it proper attention by and by. They continue to attend gospel preaching, and the poor little stunted blade of religion keeps on growing in a fashion.

Meanwhile they have grown rich; they come to the place of worship in a carriage; they have all that heart can wish. Ah! now the seed will grow, will it not? No, no.

They have no cares now; the shop is given up, they live in the country; they no longer have to ask, “Where shall the money come from to meet the next bill?” or “How shall we provide for an increasing family?” Now they have too much instead of too little, for they have riches, and they are too wealthy to be gracious. “But,” says one, “they might spend their riches for God.” Certainly they might, but they do not, for riches are deceitful. They have to entertain much company, and go along with the world, and so Christ and his church are left behind.

Yes, but they begin to spend their riches, and they have surely overcome that difficulty, for they give generously to the cause of Christ, and they are liberal in charity; the little blade will grow, will it not? No, for now look at the thorns of pleasure. Their generosity to others involves generosity to themselves; their pleasures, amusements, and vanities choke the wheat of true religion; the good grains of gospel truth cannot grow because they must attend that musical party, that ball, and that soirée, and so they cannot think about the things of God. I know several examples of this class. I knew one, high in court circles, who confessed to me that he wished he were poor, for then he might enter the kingdom of heaven. He said to me, “Ah, sir, these politics, these politics, I wish I were rid of them, they are eating the life out of my heart. I cannot serve God as I would.”

I know of another, burdened with riches, who said to me, “Ah, sir, it is an awful thing to be rich; one cannot keep close to the Saviour with all this earth around him.”

Ah, my dear readers, I will not ask that God lay you on a bed of sickness, that he strip you of all your wealth, and bring you to poverty; but, oh, if he were to do it, and you were to save your souls, it would be the best bargain you could ever make. If those mighty ones who now complain that the thorns choke the seed could give up all their riches and pleasures, if those who live in luxury every day could take the place of Lazarus at the gate, it would be a happy change for them if their souls might be saved. A man may be honorable and rich, and yet go to heaven; but it will be hard work, for “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” God does cause some rich people to enter the kingdom of heaven, but hard is their struggle. Steady, young man, steady! Do not hurry to climb to wealth! It is a place where many heads are turned. Do not ask God to make you popular; those who have popularity are wearied by it. Cry with Agur, “Give me neither poverty nor riches.” God grant that I may walk in the golden mean, and may I always have in my heart that good seed, which shall bring forth fruit a hundredfold to his own glory.

IV. I now close with the last character, namely, the good ground. Of the good soil, as you will notice, we have but one in four. Will one in four of our hearers, with a well-prepared heart, receive the Word?

The ground is described as “good”; not that it was good by nature, but it had been made good by grace. God had ploughed it; he had stirred it up with the plough of conviction, and there it lay in ridge and furrow as it should lie. When the gospel was preached, the heart received it, for the man said, “That is exactly the blessing I want. Mercy is what a needy sinner requires.” So the preaching of the gospel brought comfort to this disturbed and ploughed soil. Down fell the seed to take good root. In some cases it produced fervent love, largeness of heart, and devotedness of purpose of a noble kind, like seed which produces a hundredfold. The man became a mighty servant for God; he spent himself and was spent. He took his place in the front ranks of Christ’s army, stood in the hottest part of the battle, and did deeds of courage which few could accomplish—the seed produced a hundredfold. It fell into another heart of the same kind; the man could not do the most, but still he did much. He gave himself to God, and in his business he had a word to say for his Lord; in his daily walk he quietly adorned the doctrine of God his Saviour—he brought forth sixtyfold. Then it fell on another, whose abilities and talents were small; he could not be a star, but he would be a glow-worm; he could not do as the greatest, but he was content to do something, however humble.

The seed had brought forth in him tenfold, perhaps twentyfold. How many are there of this sort here? Is there one who prays within himself, “God be merciful to me, a sinner”? The seed has fallen in the right place. Soul, your prayer shall be heard. God never sets a person longing for mercy without intending to give it. Does another whisper, “Oh that I might be saved”? Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you, even you, will be saved. Have you been the chief of sinners? Trust Christ, and your great sins shall vanish as a millstone sinks beneath the flood. Is there no one here who will trust the Saviour? Can it be possible that the Spirit is entirely absent? that he is not moving in one soul? not giving life in one spirit? We will pray that he may now descend, that the word may not be in vain.

But time tests everything. What appeared strong proves shallow. When trials come, they fade away. Some of you may belong to this group. You have felt deeply. You have resolved often. Yet years pass, and nothing changes. There is no depth, no steady work of the Spirit. Must it remain so? Shall one day your life be remembered as a plant that sprouted but never ripened? God forbid. May the Spirit work deeply and effectively in you, so that you may yet bear fruit for God and bring honor to Christ. III. I shall briefly treat of the third class, and may the Spirit of God help me to deal faithfully with you. “And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprang up with it, and choked it.” Now, this was good soil. The first two characters were bad; the wayside was not the proper place, the rock was not a suitable situation for the growth of any plant; but this is good soil, for it grows thorns. Wherever a thistle will spring up and flourish, there wheat would flourish too. This was rich, fertile soil; it was no wonder therefore that the farmer dealt generously there, and threw handful after handful upon that corner of the field. See how happy he is when in a month or two he visits the spot. The seed has sprung up. True, there is a suspicious little plant down there of about the same size as the wheat. “Oh!” he thinks, “that is not much, the corn will outgrow that. When it is stronger it will choke these few thistles that have unfortunately mixed with it.” Ah, Mr. Farmer, you do not understand the power of evil, or you would not dream like this! He comes again, and the seed has grown, there is even corn in the ear; but the thistles, the thorns, and the briers have become intertwined with one another, and the poor wheat can hardly get a ray of sunshine. It is so choked with thorns on every side, that it looks quite yellow; the plant is starved. Still it keeps on growing, and it does seem as if it would bring forth a little fruit. Alas, it never comes to anything. With it the reaper never fills his arm. We have this class very largely among us. These hear the word and understand what they hear. They take the truth home; they think it over; they even go so far as to make a profession of religion. The wheat seems to spring up and form an ear; it will soon come to perfection. Do not be in a hurry; these men and women have a great deal to look after; they have the cares of a large business; their establishment employs so many hundreds; do not be mistaken about their godliness—they have no time for it. They will tell you that they must live; that they cannot neglect this world; that they must somehow look after the present, and as for the future, they will give it proper attention by and by. They continue to attend gospel preaching, and the poor little stunted blade of religion keeps on growing in a fashion. Meanwhile they have grown rich; they come to the place of worship in a carriage; they have all that heart can wish. Ah! now the seed will grow, will it not? No, no. They have no cares now; the shop is given up, they live in the country; they no longer have to ask, “Where shall the money come from to meet the next bill?” or “How shall we provide for an increasing family?” Now they have too much instead of too little, for they have riches, and they are too wealthy to be gracious. “But,” says one, “they might spend their riches for God.” Certainly they might, but they do not, for riches are deceitful. They have to entertain much company, and go along with the world, and so Christ and his church are left behind. Yes, but they begin to spend their riches, and they have surely overcome that difficulty, for they give generously to the cause of Christ, and they are liberal in charity; the little blade will grow, will it not? No, for now look at the thorns of pleasure. Their generosity to others involves generosity to themselves; their pleasures, amusements, and vanities choke the wheat of true religion; the good grains of gospel truth cannot grow because they must attend that musical party, that ball, and that soirée, and so they cannot think about the things of God. I know several examples of this class. I knew one, high in court circles, who confessed to me that he wished he were poor, for then he might enter the kingdom of heaven. He said to me, “Ah, sir, these politics, these politics, I wish I were rid of them, they are eating the life out of my heart. I cannot serve God as I would.” I know of another, burdened with riches, who said to me, “Ah, sir, it is an awful thing to be rich; one cannot keep close to the Saviour with all this earth around him.” Ah, my dear readers, I will not ask that God lay you on a bed of sickness, that he strip you of all your wealth, and bring you to poverty; but, oh, if he were to do it, and you were to save your souls, it would be the best bargain you could ever make. If those mighty ones who now complain that the thorns choke the seed could give up all their riches and pleasures, if those who live in luxury every day could take the place of Lazarus at the gate, it would be a happy change for them if their souls might be saved. A man may be honorable and rich, and yet go to heaven; but it will be hard work, for “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” God does cause some rich people to enter the kingdom of heaven, but hard is their struggle. Steady, young man, steady! Do not hurry to climb to wealth! It is a place where many heads are turned. Do not ask God to make you popular; those who have popularity are wearied by it. Cry with Agur, “Give me neither poverty nor riches.” God grant that I may walk in the golden mean, and may I always have in my heart that good seed, which shall bring forth fruit a hundredfold to his own glory. IV. I now close with the last character, namely, the good ground. Of the good soil, as you will notice, we have but one in four. Will one in four of our hearers, with a well-prepared heart, receive the Word? The ground is described as “good”; not that it was good by nature, but it had been made good by grace. God had ploughed it; he had stirred it up with the plough of conviction, and there it lay in ridge and furrow as it should lie. When the gospel was preached, the heart received it, for the man said, “That is exactly the blessing I want. Mercy is what a needy sinner requires.” So the preaching of the gospel brought comfort to this disturbed and ploughed soil. Down fell the seed to take good root. In some cases it produced fervent love, largeness of heart, and devotedness of purpose of a noble kind, like seed which produces a hundredfold. The man became a mighty servant for God; he spent himself and was spent. He took his place in the front ranks of Christ’s army, stood in the hottest part of the battle, and did deeds of courage which few could accomplish—the seed produced a hundredfold. It fell into another heart of the same kind; the man could not do the most, but still he did much. He gave himself to God, and in his business he had a word to say for his Lord; in his daily walk he quietly adorned the doctrine of God his Saviour—he brought forth sixtyfold. Then it fell on another, whose abilities and talents were small; he could not be a star, but he would be a glow-worm; he could not do as the greatest, but he was content to do something, however humble. The seed had brought forth in him tenfold, perhaps twentyfold. How many are there of this sort here? Is there one who prays within himself, “God be merciful to me, a sinner”? The seed has fallen in the right place. Soul, your prayer shall be heard. God never sets a person longing for mercy without intending to give it. Does another whisper, “Oh that I might be saved”? Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you, even you, will be saved. Have you been the chief of sinners? Trust Christ, and your great sins shall vanish as a millstone sinks beneath the flood. Is there no one here who will trust the Saviour? Can it be possible that the Spirit is entirely absent? that he is not moving in one soul? not giving life in one spirit? We will pray that he may now descend, that the word may not be in vain.

fields.title: The Principal Wheat
fields.body_html:
The farmer sows the principal wheat, giving chief care to what matters most. So must we in life: identify the greatest good—salvation, holiness, and Christ—and devote our minds, hearts, and actions to cultivating it above all else.

“The principal wheat.” Isaiah 28:25 The prophet mentions it as a matter of wisdom on the part of the farmer, that he knows what is the principal thing to cultivate, and makes it his chief care. The text, with the connection, runs thus: “Does not the farmer sow the principal wheat?” He does not go to the granary and take out wheat, and cummin, and barley, and rye, and scatter these about carelessly, but he estimates the value of each grain, and arranges them in his mind accordingly. He does not think that cummin and caraway, which he grows merely to flavor his meal, are of half such importance as his bread-corn; and, though rye and barley have their value, yet he does not consider even these equal to what he calls “the principal wheat.” He is a man of judgment; he arranges things; he places the most important crop in the front rank, and spends upon it the most care.

Here let us learn a lesson. Do keep things clear in your minds—not mixed and muddled by careless thought. Do not live a confused life, without care and discretion, running everything together; but sort things out, and divide and distinguish between the precious and the worthless. See what this is worth, and what the other is worth, and set your matters in rank and order, making some of them principal, and others of them secondary. I suggest to you young people especially that, in starting life, you say to yourselves, “What shall we live for? There is a principal thing for which we ought to live; what shall it be?” Have you really considered that question, or have you gone at it at random? What are you living for? What is your principal aim? Is it to be that of the old gentleman in Horace who said to his boy, “Get money; get it honestly, if you can; but, by all means, get money”? Will you be a money-maker? Shall money be your principal corn?

Or will you choose a life of pleasure—“a short life and a merry one,” as so many fools have said to their deep regret? Is it in dissipation that your life is to be spent? Are thistles to be your principal crop? Because there is a certain pleasure in looking at a Scotch thistle, do you intend to grow acres of pleasurable vice? And will you make your bed upon them when you come to die? Search and see what is worthy to be the principal object in life; and, when you have found it, then ask the Holy Spirit to help you to choose that one thing, and to give all your powers and faculties to cultivating it. The farmer, who finds that wheat ought to be his principal crop, makes it so, and directs his efforts with that end in view; learn from this to have a main object, and to give your whole mind to it.

This farmer was wise, because he counted that to be principal which was most necessary. His family could do without cummin, which was only a flavoring. Perhaps the mistress might complain, or the cook might grumble, but that did not matter so much as it would if the children cried for bread. They certainly must have wheat, for bread is the staff of life. It is bread that strengthens man’s heart, and therefore the farmer must grow wheat if he grows nothing else. What is necessary he regarded as the principal thing. Is not this simple common sense? If we were wisely to sit down and consider, should we not say, “To have my sins forgiven, to be right with God, to be holy, to be fit to live eternally in heaven, is the greatest and most necessary thing for me, and therefore I will make it the principal object of my pursuit”? A creature cannot be satisfied unless he is fulfilling the purpose for which he was created; and the purpose of every intelligent creature is first, to glorify God, and next, to enjoy God. What a joy it must be to enjoy God himself for ever and ever! Other things may be desirable, but this one thing is necessary. A sufficient income, a measure of respect among men, a degree of health—all these are the flavoring of life; but to be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation is life itself. Jesus Christ is the bread by which our soul’s best life is sustained. Oh, that we were all wise enough to feel that to be one with Christ is the one thing necessary; that to be at peace with God is the principal thing; that to be brought into harmony with the Most High is the true music of our being. Other herbs may take their place in proper order, but grace is the principal wheat, and we must cultivate it.

This farmer was wise, because he made that the principal thing which was most fit to be so. Of course, barley is useful as food, for nations have lived on barley bread, and lived healthily too; and rye has been the nourishment of millions; neither have they starved on oats and other grains.

Still, give me a piece of wheaten bread, for it is the best support for life’s journey. This farmer knew that wheat was the most suitable food for man, and so he did not put the inferior grain, which might serve as a substitute, into the prominent place; but he gave his wheat the preference. He did not say, “the principal barley,” or “the principal rye,” much less “the principal cummin,” or “the principal fitches,” but “the principal wheat.”

And what is there, brethren, that is so fit for the heart, the mind, the soul of man, as to know God and his Christ? Other mental foods, such as the fruits of knowledge and the delights of science, excellent though they may be, are inferior nourishment and unsuitable to build up the inner man.

In my God and my Saviour, I find my heaven and my all. My soul feeds on a crumb of truth about Jesus, and finds deep satisfaction in living upon it. The more we know God, and enjoy God, and become like God, and the more Christ is our daily bread, the more we perceive the fitness of all this for our new-born natures. O beloved, make that your principal object which is the fittest pursuit of an immortal mind.

“Religion is the chief concern Of mortals here below; May I its great importance learn, Its sovereign virtue know!” “More needful this than glittering wealth, Or aught the world bestows; Not reputation, food, or health, Can give us such repose.”

Moreover, this farmer was wise, because he made that the principal thing which was most profitable. Under certain circumstances, in our own country, wheat is not the most profitable crop a man can grow; but ordinarily, it is the best crop the earth yields, and therefore the text speaks of “the principal wheat.” Our grandfathers used to rely upon the wheat stack to pay their rent. They looked to their corn as the source of their strength; and though it may not be so now, it was so of old, and perhaps it may yet be so again.

In any case, the illustration holds true with regard to true religion. That is the most profitable thing.

I am told that rich men find it very hard to secure anything that yields five percent nowadays; but this blessed fear of the Lord is an extraordinarily profitable investment, for it does not yield a hundred percent, or a thousand percent, but a man begins with nothing and all things become his by faith.

Being freely forgiven of our sins, we are by overflowing grace greatly enriched, so that we count among our possessions heaven itself, Christ himself, God himself. All things are ours. Oh, what a blessed crop to sow! What a harvest comes from it! Godliness is profitable for the present life, and for the life to come. Godliness is a blessing to a man’s body—it keeps him from drunkenness and vice; and it is a blessing to his soul—it makes him gentle and pure. It is a blessing to him in every way. If I had to die like a dog, I would prefer to live like a Christian. If there were no hereafter, still, for comfort and joy, give me the life of one who strives to live like Christ. There is a practical everyday truth in the verse— “’It is religion that can give Sweetest pleasures while we live; ’It is religion must supply Solid comfort when we die.” Only that religion must not be of the common sort; it must have as its root a sincere faith in Jesus Christ. See to it. Our religion must be either everything or nothing, either first or nowhere. Make it “the principal wheat,” and it will richly repay you.

II. Secondly, the husbandman is a lesson to us because he gives this principal thing the principal place. I find that the Hebrew is rendered by some eminent scholars, "He puts the wheat into the principal place." That little handful of cummin for the wife to flavor the cakes with he grows in a corner; and the various herbs he places in their proper borders. The barley he sets in its plot, and the rye in its acre; but if there is a good bit of rich soil—the best he has—he appropriates it to the principal wheat. He gives his choicest fields to that which is to be the main means of his living.

Now, here is a lesson for you and for me. Let us give to true godliness our principal powers and abilities. Let us give to the things of God our best and most intense thought.

I pray you, do not take religion at second hand from what I tell you, or from what somebody else tells you; but think it over. Read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest the word of God. The thoughtful Christian is the growing Christian. Remember, the service of God deserves our first consideration and endeavor. We are poor things at our prime, but we ought to give the Lord nothing short of our best. God would not have us serve him heedlessly, but he would have us use all the brain and intellect and mind that we have in studying and practicing his word. "Acquaint now yourself with him, and be at peace" (Job 22:21). "Meditate on these things; give yourself wholly to them" (1 Timothy 4:15). If your mind is more clear and active at one time than at another, then sow the principal wheat. If you feel more fresh and more inclined to think at one time of the day than at another, let your mind then go towards the best things.

Be sure, also, to yield to this subject your most earnest love. The best field in the little estate of manhood is not the head, but the heart; sow the principal wheat there. Oh, to have true religion in the heart; to love what we know—intensely to love it; to hold it fast as with the grip of life and death—never to let it go! The Lord says, "My son, give me your heart" (Proverbs 23:26, ESV), and he will not be contented with anything less than our heart. Oh, when your zeal is most burning, and your love is most fervent, let the warmth and the fervency all go towards the Lord your God, and to the service of him who has redeemed you with his precious blood. Let the principal wheat have the principal part of your nature. Towards God and his Christ also turn your most fervent desires. When you enlarge your desire, desire Christ; when you become ambitious let your ambition be all for God. Let your hunger and your thirst be after righteousness. Let your aspirations and your longings be all towards holiness, and the things that shall make you like to Christ. Give to this principal wheat your principal desires.

Then let the Lord have the attentive respect of your life. Let the principal wheat be sown in every action. If we are truly Christians we must be as much Christians outside the church as in it. We shall try to make our eating and our drinking, and everything we do, tend to the glory of God.

Draw no line between the secular and the religious part of your conduct, but let the secular be made religious by a devout desire to glorify God in the one as much as in the other (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Let us worship God in the commonest duties of life, even as they do who stand before his throne.

So it ought to be. Let us sow the principal wheat in all the fields of our conversation, in business, in the family, among our friends, and with our children.

May we each one feel, "For me to live is Christ. I cannot live without Christ, or for anything but Christ" (Philippians 1:21, ESV). Let your whole nature yield itself to Jesus, and to none else.

We should give to this principal wheat our most earnest labors. We should spend ourselves for the spread of the gospel. A Christian man ought to lay himself out to serve Jesus. I hate to see a professing man zealous in politics and lukewarm in devotion; all on fire at a parish vestry, and chill as winter when he comes to a prayer-meeting. Some fly like eagles when they are serving the world, but they have a broken wing in the service of God. This should not be. If anything could rouse us up, and make the lion within us roar in his strength, it should be when we confront the foes of Jesus or fight in his cause. Our Lord's service is the principal wheat; let us labor most in connection with it.

This, I think, should also take possession of us so as to lead to our greatest sacrifices. The love of Christ ought to be so strong as to swallow up self, and make sacrifice our daily joy. For Christ's name's sake we should be willing to endure poverty, reproach, slander, exile, death. Nothing should be dear to a Christian in comparison with Christ. Now, I will put it to you whether it is so or no. Is the love of Jesus the principal wheat with us? Are we giving our religion the chief place or not? I am afraid some people treat religion as certain gentlemen treat an off-hand farm; they put a bailiff into it, and only give an eye to it now and then. Their minister is the bailiff, and they expect him to see to it for them. These off-hand farms are losing concerns.

Look at these half-and-half brethren. They have religion? Certainly. But they are like the man of whom the child spoke at the Sunday-school. "Is your father a Christian?" said the teacher. "Yes," said the child, "but he has not worked much at it lately." I could point out several of this sort, who are sowing their wheat very sparingly, and choosing the most barren patch to sow it in. They profess to be Christians, but religion is a tenth-rate article on their farm. Some have a large acreage for the world, and a poor little plot for Christ. They are growers of worldly pleasure and self- indulgence, and they sow a little religion by the roadside for appearance’s sake. This will not do.

God will not thus be mocked (Galatians 6:7). If we despise him and his truth we shall be lightly esteemed. O come, let us give our principal time, talent, thought, effort to that which is the chief concern of immortal spirits. May we imitate the husbandman who gives the principal wheat the principal place in his farm.

III. Let us learn a third lesson. The husbandman selects the principal seed-corn when he is sowing his wheat. When a farmer is setting aside wheat for sowing, he does not choose the tail corn and the worst of his produce, but if he is a sensible man he likes to sow the best wheat in the world.

Many farmers search the country round for a good sample of wheat for sowing, for they do not expect to get a good harvest out of bad seed. The husbandman is taught of God to put into the ground "the principal wheat." Let me learn that if I am going to sow to the Lord and be a Christian, I should sow the best kind of Christianity.

I should try to do this, first, by believing the weightiest doctrines. I would believe not this "ism," nor that, but the unadulterated truth which Jesus taught; for a holy character will only grow by the Spirit of God out of true doctrine. Falsehood breeds sin; truth begets and fosters holiness. You and I therefore ought to select our seed carefully, and cast out all error. If we are wise we shall think most of the most important truths, for I have known people attach the greatest importance to the smallest things. They fight over the fitches, and leave the wheat to the crows. As for me, those who will may dispute over vials and trumpets; I shall mainly preach the doctrine of the precious blood and the glorious truths of substitution and atonement. These doctrines are the principal wheat, and therefore these shall have my choice.

Next to that, we ought to sow the noblest examples. Many men are dwarfed because they choose a bad model to start with. They imitate dear old Mr. So-and-so till they grow wonderfully like him with the best of him left out. A minister happens to be of a gloomy turn of mind, and he preaches the deep experience of the children of God, and in consequence a band of good people think it their duty to be melancholy. Why need they fall into a ditch because their leader has splashed himself?

We should never copy any man's infirmities. To be like Paul there is no need to have weak eyes; to be like Thomas there is no necessity to doubt. If you copy any good man, there is a point at which you ought to stop short. If I must have a human model, I would prefer one of the bravest of the saints of God; but oh how much better to follow that perfect pattern which you have in Christ Jesus!

We should sow the best wheat by seeing that we have the purest spirit. Alas! how soon do spirits become soiled by self or pride, or despondency or sloth, or some earthly taint. But what a grand thing it is to live in the spirit of Christ! May we be humble, lowly, bold, self-sacrificing, pure, chaste, and holy.

And then, there is one more mode of sowing selected seed. We should endeavor to live in the closest communion with God. A dear brother prayed just now that we might have as much grace as we were capable of receiving, and that God would bring us into such a state that we might not hinder him in anything which he willed to do by us. This is a good prayer. It should be our desire to rise to the highest form of spiritual life. If you sow this principal wheat, get the best sort of it.

There is a spirit and a spirit; and there are doctrines and doctrines; the best is the best for you. O young men, if you mean to have piety, go in for it thoroughly. Do not sneak through the world as if you were ashamed of your Lord. If you are Christ's, show your colors. Rally to his banner, gather to his trumpet call, and then stand up, stand up for Jesus. If there is any manhood in you, this great cause calls for it all; exhibit it, and may the Spirit of God help you so to do.

IV. Fourthly, the husbandman grows the principal wheat with the principal care. Some critics say that the proper translation is that the husbandman plants his wheat in rows. It is said that the large crops in Palestine in olden times were due to the fact that they planted the wheat. They set it in lines so that it was not checked or suffocated by being too thick in one place, neither was there any fear of its being too thin in another. The wheat was planted, and then streams of water were turned by the foot to each particular plant. No wonder, therefore, that the land brought forth abundantly.

This is a lesson for us. We must not give a careless, half-hearted attention to the things of God.

The principal wheat requires careful cultivation—our hearts, minds, and lives must be deliberately trained for holiness. As it is written, “And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it” (Matthew 13:7). Let us avoid sowing the best of our hearts in a distracted, worldly manner, or we shall find our fruitfulness choked.

Just as the husbandman waters each row, so must we nurture every part of our spiritual life. “But the seed falling on good soil refers to someone who hears the word and understands it. This is the one who produces a crop, yielding a hundred, sixty, or thirty times what was sown” (Matthew 13:23). The care we give to our principal wheat—our devotion to Christ, our love for God, our obedience—determines the abundance of the harvest. Do not neglect the principal; give your best thought, your deepest love, your strongest efforts, to the cultivation of your soul in Christ.

Let the principal wheat have the principal care in your life. Let your heart, mind, and conduct all be devoted to God. Sow diligently, water faithfully, guard carefully. Then you will see the blessing of a fruitful harvest, and your life will yield abundantly to God’s glory.

We should give our main attention to the most important thing. Our godliness should be carried out with care and thoughtfulness. Brothers, are we careful enough in our spiritual walk? Have you examined the depth of your profession? Why are you a member of a particular church? Because your mother was? That is some reason, but it is not enough to justify you before God. I urge you to honestly assess your standing. If any Christian minister is afraid to call you to this duty, I question him. I am not afraid. I ask you to examine everything I teach, for I do not want to be responsible for another man’s beliefs. Like the Bereans, check and see whether these things are true according to Scripture (Acts 17:11).

One of the greatest blessings for the church would be a spirit of inquiry that tests everything against the Word of God. If people speak contrary to Scripture, it is because there is no light in them. Serve God as carefully as an Eastern farmer planted his wheat, placing it in orderly rows with care and precision. You serve a precise God, so serve Him precisely. He is a jealous God, so be careful to avoid even the smallest error or form of self-worship (Exodus 20:5).

Also, water every part of your spiritual life as the farmer waters each plant. Pray for grace from above, so that no part of your faith, hope, or love ever dries up. Serve each part of your soul as a farmer serves his wheat. Make grace your main concern, for it deserves it.

With this I conclude: focus on this, because from it you can expect your main harvest. If religion is the most important thing, you can expect your main reward from it. The harvest will come in various ways. You will achieve the greatest success in life if you live wholly for God’s glory.

Success or failure depends largely on the focus of our efforts. It is useless for me to try to conduct a choir—I am not made for that—but I may succeed in preaching, because that is my calling.

Christian, if you live for the world, you will not prosper, for you are not made for it. Grace has made you unsuitable for sin. If you live for God with all your heart, you will succeed, because God made you for this purpose. Just as He made the fish for water and the birds for air, He made the believer for holiness and for serving Him. You will be out of your element, like a fish out of water or a bird in the stream, if you abandon God’s service. The Eastern farmer’s success depends on his wheat; yours depends on your devotion to God. Look to godliness for your joy. Is there any happiness like knowing you are in Christ and loved by the Lord? It is in your faith that you will find comfort on a sick and dying bed, and that time may come soon.

In the life to come, what a harvest will result from serving the Lord! What does the world give?

Only smoke. A man may make a million dollars and die—what has he gained? A man’s fame may spread across the earth, yet he dies—what remains? Living for the world is like children playing in the street for coins or shells. Life for God is real and lasting; everything else is waste. Let us remember this and dedicate ourselves to serving the Lord. May the Spirit help us to sow the “principal wheat” and live in joyful expectation of reaping a harvest, as promised: “Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy” (Psalm 126:5).
